source_paragraphs: There was once a little Kid whose growing horns made him think he was a grown-up Billy Goat and able to take care of himself. So one evening when the flock started home from the pasture and his mother called, the Kid paid no heed and kept right on nibbling the tender grass. A little later when he lifted his head, the flock was gone.

He was all alone. The sun was sinking. Long shadows came creeping over the ground. A chilly little wind came creeping with them making scary noises in the grass. The Kid shivered as he thought of the terrible Wolf. Then he started wildly over the field, bleating for his mother. But not half-way, near a clump of trees, there was the Wolf!
The Kid knew there was little hope for him.
"Please, Mr. Wolf," he said trembling, "I know you are going to eat me. But first please pipe me a tune, for I want to dance and be merry as long as I can."
The Wolf liked the idea of a little music before eating, so he struck up a merry tune and the Kid leaped and frisked gaily.

Meanwhile, the flock was moving slowly homeward. In the still evening air the Wolf's piping carried far. The Shepherd Dogs pricked up their ears. They recognized the song the Wolf sings before a feast, and in a moment they were racing back to the pasture. The Wolf's song ended suddenly, and as he ran, with the Dogs at his heels, he called himself a fool for turning piper to please a Kid, when he should have stuck to his butcher's trade.
_Do not let anything turn you from your purpose._
translated_paragraphs: 从前有只小山羊，头上刚冒出犄角，就觉得自己已经是只成年的公山羊，能照顾自己了。一天傍晚，羊群离开草场回家，妈妈唤他，他理也不理，低头接着啃嫩草。过了一会儿，他抬头一望，羊群不见了。
只剩他一个。太阳往下沉，长长的影子沿着地面悄悄爬来。一阵凉飕飕的风也跟着爬过来，在草丛里发出吓人的响声。小山羊想起可怕的狼，浑身打了个哆嗦。他撒腿奔过田野，咩咩地叫着妈妈。还没跑到半路，就在一小片树丛旁边，狼来了！
小山羊知道，自己几乎没指望逃命了。
“求求您，狼先生，”他哆哆嗦嗦地说，“我知道您要吃我。可请您先吹支曲子吧，趁还能快活一会儿，我想跳个舞。”
狼觉得，开饭前先听点音乐倒不错，就吹起了一支快活的曲子。小山羊听着曲子，欢欢喜喜地蹦跳起来。
这时候，羊群正慢慢往家走。暮色里四下静悄悄的，狼的笛声传出老远。牧羊犬们竖起耳朵，认出这是狼大吃一顿之前爱吹的调子，转眼便飞奔着赶回草场。狼的曲子一下子断了。他一路逃命，几只狗紧跟脚后。他骂自己糊涂，明明是个杀羊的，偏为讨好一只小山羊，改行做起了吹笛手！
认准了要做的事，别叫旁的事分了心。

source_paragraphs: The Tortoise, you know, carries his house on his back. No matter how hard he tries, he cannot leave home. They say that Jupiter punished him so, because he was such a lazy stay-at-home that he would not go to Jupiter's wedding, even when especially invited.

After many years, Tortoise began to wish he had gone to that wedding. When he saw how gaily the birds flew about and how the Hare and the Chipmunk and all the other animals ran nimbly by, always eager to see everything there was to be seen, the Tortoise felt very sad and discontented. He wanted to see the world too, and there he was with a house on his back and little short legs that could hardly drag him along.
One day he met a pair of Ducks and told them all his trouble.

"We can help you to see the world," said the Ducks. "Take hold of this stick with your teeth and we will carry you far up in the air where you can see the whole countryside. But keep quiet or you will be sorry."
The Tortoise was very glad indeed. He seized the stick firmly with his teeth, the two Ducks took hold of it one at each end, and away they sailed up toward the clouds.
Just then a Crow flew by. He was very much astonished at the strange sight and cried:
"This must surely be the King of Tortoises!"
"Why certainly----" began the Tortoise.
But as he opened his mouth to say these foolish words he lost his hold on the stick, and down he fell to the ground, where he was dashed to pieces on a rock.
_Foolish curiosity and vanity often lead to misfortune._
translated_paragraphs: 你知道，乌龟把房子背在背上。不管怎么努力，他也出不了家门。听说这是朱庇特给他的惩罚。当初他太懒，只爱待在家里，连朱庇特特地邀请他参加婚礼，他也不肯去。
好多年过去，乌龟渐渐后悔没去赴宴。他看见鸟儿快活地飞来飞去，野兔、花栗鼠和别的动物从身旁敏捷地跑过，恨不得把天下好看的东西看个遍，越想越不舒坦。他也想出去见见世面呀。偏偏背上驮着一座房子，四条小短腿，连挪动自己都很费劲。
一天，他碰上一对野鸭，就把自己的烦恼全说了出来。
“我们能带你去看看世界，”野鸭说，“你用牙咬住这根棍子，我们带你飞到高高的天上，四周的田野村庄尽收眼底。千万别开口，不然准会后悔。”
乌龟真是高兴极了。他牢牢咬住棍子，两只野鸭各叼一端，乘风直上，飞向云端。
恰好一只乌鸦飞过，看见这番奇景，大为惊讶，叫道：
“这一定就是乌龟大王了！”
“嘿，那当——”乌龟开口说。
他张嘴要说这句蠢话，牙就松开了棍子。他直坠而下，撞在岩石上，摔得粉碎。
不知轻重的好奇心和虚荣心，往往会招来不幸。

sections.title_en: THE YOUNG CRAB AND HIS MOTHER
source_paragraphs: "Why in the world do you walk sideways like that?" said a Mother Crab to her son. "You should always walk straight forward with your toes turned out."
"Show me how to walk, mother dear," answered the little Crab obediently, "I want to learn."
So the old Crab tried and _tried_ to walk straight forward. But she could walk sideways only, like her son. And when she wanted to turn her toes out she tripped and fell on her nose.
_Do not tell others how to act unless you can set a good example._
translated_paragraphs: “你走路怎么总横着走呀？”蟹妈妈说，“脚尖朝外，直直地往前走才对。”
“好妈妈，你走给我看吧。”小螃蟹乖乖地答道，“我想学。”
蟹妈妈试了一遍，又试一遍，想要朝正前方走。可她跟儿子一样，只能横着走。她努力把脚尖朝外一撇，扑通！摔了个嘴啃泥。
教别人怎么做之前，自己先做给人家看。

source_paragraphs: An Ox came down to a reedy pool to drink. As he splashed heavily into the water, he crushed a young Frog into the mud. The old Frog soon missed the little one and asked his brothers and sisters what had become of him.
"A _great big_ monster," said one of them, "stepped on little brother with one of his huge feet!"
"Big, was he!" said the old Frog, puffing herself up. "Was he as big as this?"
"Oh, _much_ bigger!" they cried.
The Frog puffed up still more.

"He could not have been bigger than this," she said. But the little Frogs all declared that the monster was _much, much_ bigger and the old Frog kept puffing herself out more and more until, all at once, she burst.
_Do not attempt the impossible._
translated_paragraphs: 一头牛来到长满芦苇的池塘边喝水。他笨重地跨进水中，哗啦一声，把一只小青蛙踩进了泥里。老青蛙很快发现少了个孩子，便问他的兄弟姐妹，小弟弟怎么了。
“有个好大好大的怪物，”一只小青蛙说，“一只巨大的脚，一下子就踩住了小弟弟！”
“很大，是吗？”老青蛙吸气，鼓起了自己。“有这么大？”
“哎呀，大得多呢！”小青蛙们喊。
老青蛙又鼓大了些。
“总不能比这个还大吧？”她说。可孩子们齐声说，那个怪物可要大得多、大得多呢。老青蛙拼命地鼓啊，鼓啊，突然，肚子撑破了。
别硬做根本做不到的事。

sections.title_en: THE DOG, THE COCK, AND THE FOX
source_paragraphs: A Dog and a Cock, who were the best of friends, wished very much to see something of the world. So they decided to leave the farmyard and to set out into the world along the road that led to the woods. The two comrades traveled along in the very best of spirits and without meeting any adventure to speak of.

At nightfall the Cock, looking for a place to roost, as was his custom, spied nearby a hollow tree that he thought would do very nicely for a night's lodging. The Dog could creep inside and the Cock would fly up on one of the branches. So said, so done, and both slept very comfortably.

With the first glimmer of dawn the Cock awoke. For the moment he forgot just where he was. He thought he was still in the farmyard where it had been his duty to arouse the household at daybreak. So standing on tip-toes he flapped his wings and crowed lustily. But instead of awakening the farmer, he awakened a Fox not far off in the wood. The Fox immediately had rosy visions of a very delicious breakfast. Hurrying to the tree where the Cock was roosting, he said very politely:
"A hearty welcome to our woods, honored sir. I cannot tell you how glad I am to see you here. I am quite sure we shall become the closest of friends."
"I feel highly flattered, kind sir," replied the Cock slyly. "If you will please go around to the door of my house at the foot of the tree, my porter will let you in."
The hungry but unsuspecting Fox, went around the tree as he was told, and in a twinkling the Dog had seized him.
_Those who try to deceive may expect to be paid in their own coin._
translated_paragraphs: 有一只狗和一只公鸡，是顶要好的朋友。他们很想出去看看外面的世界，就决定离开农家院，沿着那条通向树林的大路去闯荡。两个伙伴一路兴高采烈，也没遇上什么值得一提的奇遇。
天黑了，公鸡照例要找个地方栖身。他看见近旁有棵空心树，觉得正好借宿一夜。狗可以钻进树洞，公鸡可以飞上树枝。说办就办，两位都睡得很舒坦。
天边刚露出一线晨光，公鸡便醒了。他一时忘记身在何处，还以为自己仍在农家院里，天一亮就该由他来唤醒全家呢。他踮高脚，振起翅膀，扯开嗓子啼叫起来。结果农夫没叫醒，却叫醒了林子里不远处的一只狐狸。狐狸眼前立刻浮现出一顿美妙的早饭。他急忙跑到公鸡栖身的树下，彬彬有礼地说：
“尊敬的先生，衷心欢迎您来我们树林。见您到访，我真是说不出的高兴。我敢肯定，咱们会成为最亲密的朋友。”
“承蒙抬爱，好心的先生。”公鸡不动声色地答道，“劳驾，绕到树脚下，那里有我家的门。守门人会放您进来的。”
狐狸正饿得慌，丝毫没有起疑，照公鸡的话绕到树后。说时迟，那时快，狗一口就把他捉住了。
想算计别人的人，可得当心，别人也会用同样的办法对付他。

source_paragraphs: The Mice once called a meeting to decide on a plan to free themselves of their enemy, the Cat. At least they wished to find some way of knowing when she was coming, so they might have time to run away. Indeed, something had to be done, for they lived in such constant fear of her claws that they hardly dared stir from their dens by night or day.
Many plans were discussed, but none of them was thought good enough. At last a very young Mouse got up and said:

"I have a plan that seems very simple, but I know it will be successful. All we have to do is to hang a bell about the Cat's neck. When we hear the bell ringing we will know immediately that our enemy is coming."
All the Mice were much surprised that they had not thought of such a plan before. But in the midst of the rejoicing over their good fortune, an old Mouse arose and said:
"I will say that the plan of the young Mouse is very good. But let me ask one question: Who will bell the Cat?"
_It is one thing to say that something should be done, but quite a different matter to do it._
translated_paragraphs: 老鼠们开了个会，商量怎样摆脱它们的死对头猫。至少得有个办法，能知道猫什么时候来，好来得及跑呀！实在得想想办法了。它们整天担心给猫爪子逮住，白天黑夜都不大敢出洞。
大伙儿议了一个主意又一个，没一个让大家满意。最后，一只年纪很小的老鼠站了起来。
“我有个办法，看着挺简单，我敢说一定行。我们只要在猫脖子上挂一只铃铛！铃一响，立马就知道敌人来了。”
老鼠们都吃了一惊，这么好的办法，从前怎么就没想到呢！大伙儿正欢欢喜喜地庆祝这桩好事，一只上了年纪的老鼠站了起来。
“这位小朋友的主意，我说很好。不过容我问一句，谁去给猫挂铃铛？”
说一声“该这么办”，跟自己动手去办，是两回事。

source_paragraphs: An Eagle, swooping down on powerful wings, seized a lamb in her talons and made off with it to her nest. A Jackdaw saw the deed, and his silly head was filled with the idea that he was big and strong enough to do as the Eagle had done. So with much rustling of feathers and a fierce air, he came down swiftly on the back of a large Ram. But when he tried to rise again he found that he could not get away, for his claws were tangled in the wool. And so far was he from carrying away the Ram, that the Ram hardly noticed he was there.
The Shepherd saw the fluttering Jackdaw and at once guessed what had happened. Running up, he caught the bird and clipped its wings. That evening he gave the Jackdaw to his children.
"What a funny bird this is!" they said laughing, "what do you call it, father?"
"That is a Jackdaw, my children. But if you should ask him, _he_ would say he is an Eagle."
_Do not let your vanity make you overestimate your powers._
translated_paragraphs: 一只鹰展动有力的翅膀俯冲下来，利爪一把攫起一只羊羔，直带回巢里。一只寒鸦看见了，傻乎乎地认定自己也长得够大，力气也足，鹰能干的事他一样能干。他把羽毛抖得沙沙响，摆出凶狠的架势，飞快扑向一头大公羊的背。可是等他想再飞起来，却脱不了身，两只爪子都被羊毛缠住了。别说把羊带走，公羊几乎连背上多了个谁都没察觉。
牧羊人看见寒鸦拍打着翅膀，一下就猜到了事情的原委。他跑上前去，捉住寒鸦，剪短了他的翅羽。当天晚上，他把寒鸦送给了孩子们。
“好一只滑稽的鸟！”孩子们笑着说，“爸爸，这叫什么？”
“孩子们，这是只寒鸦。不过要是你们问他自己，他准说自己是只鹰。”
别让虚荣叫你高估了自己的本事。

source_paragraphs: A Boy was given permission to put his hand into a pitcher to get some filberts. But he took such a great fistful that he could not draw his hand out again. There he stood, unwilling to give up a single filbert and yet unable to get them all out at once. Vexed and disappointed he began to cry.
"My boy," said his mother, "be satisfied with half the nuts you have taken and you will easily get your hand out. Then perhaps you may have some more filberts some other time."
_Do not attempt too much at once._
translated_paragraphs: 一个男孩得了允许，可以把手伸进罐子里拿榛子。他一把抓得太多，拳头卡在里面，怎么也抽不出来。他就那么站着，一颗也舍不得放，又没办法一下子全拿走。又气又失望，他哭了。
“孩子，”妈妈说，“放掉一半，手不就拿出来了吗？也许过些时候，你还可以再来拿一点呀。”
别想着一下子把什么都做了。

source_paragraphs: A Farmer was driving his wagon along a miry country road after a heavy rain. The horses could hardly drag the load through the deep mud, and at last came to a standstill when one of the wheels sank to the hub in a rut.

The farmer climbed down from his seat and stood beside the wagon looking at it but without making the least effort to get it out of the rut. All he did was to curse his bad luck and call loudly on Hercules to come to his aid. Then, it is said, Hercules really did appear, saying:

"Put your shoulder to the wheel, man, and urge on your horses. Do you think you can move the wagon by simply looking at it and whining about it? Hercules will not help unless you make some effort to help yourself."
And when the farmer put his shoulder to the wheel and urged on the horses, the wagon moved very readily, and soon the Farmer was riding along in great content and with a good lesson learned.
_Self help is the best help._
_Heaven helps those who help themselves._
translated_paragraphs: 一场大雨过后，农夫赶着大车走在泥泞的乡间路上。马儿拉着沉重的货物，很难穿过深泥。有个轮子陷进车辙，泥都淹到轮毂了，车终于再也走不动了。
农夫爬下座位，站在车旁干看着，一点儿也没动手把轮子从辙里弄出来。他只顾咒骂自己倒霉，高声呼唤大力神赫拉克勒斯来帮忙。据说大力神当真现了身，说道：
“伙计，用肩膀顶住车轮，使把劲，吆喝你的马儿往前走。你以为光瞧着、哼哼唧唧，就能把车弄动吗？你自己不先出把力，大力神也不会帮你。”
农夫果真拿肩去顶轮子，又赶着马往前拉，车很容易就动了。没过多久，他又称心如意地坐在车上赶路了，心里还记住了一个好道理。
最管用的帮手是自己。
肯自助的人，天也助他。

source_paragraphs: A frisky young Kid had been left by the herdsman on the thatched roof of a sheep shelter to keep him out of harm's way. The Kid was browsing near the edge of the roof, when he spied a Wolf and began to jeer at him, making faces and abusing him to his heart's content.
"I hear you," said the Wolf, "and I haven't the least grudge against you for what you say or do. When you are up there it is the roof that's talking, not you."
_Do not say anything at any time that you would not say at all times._
translated_paragraphs: 牧人为了不让一只活蹦乱跳的小山羊遇险，把他留在羊棚的茅草顶上。小山羊正在屋顶边上啃草，忽然看见一只狼，便尽情朝他扮鬼脸，嘲笑他，骂得好不痛快。
“我听着呢，”狼说，“你说什么、做什么，我一点儿也不怪你。你站得那么高，说这些话的是屋顶，不是你。”
倘若换个时候你就不敢说，那句话在任何时候都不该说。

sections.title_en: THE TOWN MOUSE AND THE COUNTRY MOUSE
source_paragraphs: A Town Mouse once visited a relative who lived in the country. For lunch the Country Mouse served wheat stalks, roots, and acorns, with a dash of cold water for drink. The Town Mouse ate very sparingly, nibbling a little of this and a little of that, and by her manner making it very plain that she ate the simple food only to be polite.

After the meal the friends had a long talk, or rather the Town Mouse talked about her life in the city while the Country Mouse listened. They then went to bed in a cozy nest in the hedgerow and slept in quiet and comfort until morning. In her sleep the Country Mouse dreamed she was a Town Mouse with all the luxuries and delights of city life that her friend had described for her. So the next day when the Town Mouse asked the Country Mouse to go home with her to the city, she gladly said yes.

When they reached the mansion in which the Town Mouse lived, they found on the table in the dining room the leavings of a very fine banquet. There were sweetmeats and jellies, pastries, delicious cheeses, indeed, the most tempting foods that a Mouse can imagine. But just as the Country Mouse was about to nibble a dainty bit of pastry, she heard a Cat mew loudly and scratch at the door. In great fear the Mice scurried to a hiding place, where they lay quite still for a long time, hardly daring to breathe. When at last they ventured back to the feast, the door opened suddenly and in came the servants to clear the table, followed by the House Dog.
The Country Mouse stopped in the Town Mouse's den only long enough to pick up her carpet bag and umbrella.
"You may have luxuries and dainties that I have not," she said as she hurried away, "but I prefer my plain food and simple life in the country with the peace and security that go with it."
_Poverty with security is better than plenty in the midst of fear and uncertainty._
translated_paragraphs: 城里鼠去乡下看亲戚。午饭时，乡下鼠端上了麦穗、草根和橡子，又倒了一点凉水给她喝。城里鼠这边啃一点，那边咬一口，看她那副模样就知道，她吃这些简简单单的东西，全是为了不失礼。
吃过饭，她们聊了好久。说得确切一点，是城里鼠一直在讲她的城里日子，乡下鼠一直在听。夜里她们睡在树篱中暖乎乎的窝里，一觉安安稳稳到天亮。乡下鼠做了个梦，梦见自己也变成城里鼠，亲戚说的那些享受、那些好玩的事，全都归她了。第二天，城里鼠请她一道回城，她高高兴兴地答应了。
到了城里鼠住的大宅子，她们发现饭厅桌上还剩着宴会上的好东西。有蜜饯，有果冻，有点心，还有喷香的奶酪。老鼠能想出来的好吃的，这儿几乎都有。
乡下鼠刚要尝一小口点心，就听见门外好大一声猫叫，还有抓门的声音。两只老鼠吓得赶紧躲了起来，趴了好久一动不动，大气也不敢出。好容易壮着胆子回到宴席边，门又突然开了。这回是仆人来收拾桌子了，后面还跟着一条看家狗。
乡下鼠回到亲戚的窝里，只停了拿手提包和雨伞的那一小会儿。
“你有好吃的，有好用的，我都没有，”她急急忙忙地往外走，“可我还是喜欢我的粗茶淡饭，乡下的日子简简单单，我能过得安心呀。”
日子清苦些，能安心过，也比吃喝不愁却成天担惊受怕好。

source_paragraphs: A Fox one day spied a beautiful bunch of ripe grapes hanging from a vine trained along the branches of a tree. The grapes seemed ready to burst with juice, and the Fox's mouth watered as he gazed longingly at them.

The bunch hung from a high branch, and the Fox had to jump for it. The first time he jumped he missed it by a long way. So he walked off a short distance and took a running leap at it, only to fall short once more. Again and again he tried, but in vain.
Now he sat down and looked at the grapes in disgust.
"What a fool I am," he said. "Here I am wearing myself out to get a bunch of sour grapes that are not worth gaping for."
And off he walked very, very scornfully.
_There are many who pretend to despise and belittle that which is beyond their reach._
translated_paragraphs: 葡萄藤顺着枝条爬上了一棵树。一天，狐狸望见藤上垂下来一串漂亮的熟葡萄。每一颗都饱满得像要迸出汁来。狐狸仰着头，眼馋得直流口水。
葡萄挂在高枝上，要跳起来才够得着。它第一回跳，离葡萄还差老远。它退开几步，跑过去猛地一蹿，还是差了一截。它试了一回又一回，一回也没够着。
狐狸一屁股坐下来，这回瞧着葡萄的眼神可嫌弃了。
“我真傻，”它说，“累成这样，就为一串酸葡萄？这有什么好眼馋的！”
它摆出一副十分、十分瞧不起葡萄的样子，走了。
有些人够不着一样东西，就偏装作瞧不起，还要把它说得一文不值。

source_paragraphs: A certain Father had a family of Sons, who were forever quarreling among themselves. No words he could say did the least good, so he cast about in his mind for some very striking example that should make them see that discord would lead them to misfortune.

One day when the quarreling had been much more violent than usual and each of the Sons was moping in a surly manner, he asked one of them to bring him a bundle of sticks. Then handing the bundle to each of his Sons in turn he told them to try to break it. But although each one tried his best, none was able to do so.
The Father then untied the bundle and gave the sticks to his Sons to break one by one. This they did very easily.

"My Sons," said the Father, "do you not see how certain it is that if you agree with each other and help each other, it will be impossible for your enemies to injure you? But if you are divided among yourselves, you will be no stronger than a single stick in that bundle."
_In unity is strength._
translated_paragraphs: 一位父亲有几个儿子，兄弟们总在吵架。父亲说什么都没用，他就琢磨，怎样才能让他们亲眼看明白，兄弟不和会惹来麻烦。
有一天，他们吵得比平日还厉害，一个个拉着长脸，各自生闷气。父亲叫一个儿子抱来一捆树枝，把这捆树枝挨个儿递到儿子手里，请他们折一折。每个人都使尽了力气，谁也没折断。
父亲解开绳子，让他们一根一根折。咔嚓，咔嚓，这回轻易就折断了。
父亲说：“孩子们，看明白了吗？你们几个要是齐心，彼此照应，敌人就伤不了你们。可要是各顾各的，你们每个人也就跟那捆树枝里的一根一样，轻轻一折就断了。”
合在一起，才有力量。

source_paragraphs: A Wolf had been feasting too greedily, and a bone had stuck crosswise in his throat. He could get it neither up nor down, and of course he could not eat a thing. Naturally that was an awful state of affairs for a greedy Wolf.
So away he hurried to the Crane. He was sure that she, with her long neck and bill, would easily be able to reach the bone and pull it out.
"I will reward you very handsomely," said the Wolf, "if you pull that bone out for me."
The Crane, as you can imagine, was very uneasy about putting her head in a Wolf's throat. But she was grasping in nature, so she did what the Wolf asked her to do.
When the Wolf felt that the bone was gone, he started to walk away.
"But what about my reward!" called the Crane anxiously.
"What!" snarled the Wolf, whirling around. "Haven't you got it? Isn't it enough that I let you take your head out of my mouth without snapping it off?"
_Expect no reward for serving the wicked._
translated_paragraphs: 一只狼贪吃得过了头，有根骨头横着卡在喉咙里。咳又咳不出，咽又咽不下，这下自然什么也吃不成了。对一只贪嘴的狼而言，这副光景可真糟透了。
他赶紧去找鹤。他相信，凭她那么长的脖子和尖嘴，肯定能轻轻松松够着骨头，把它取出来。
“你要是替我取出这根骨头，”狼说，“我一定重重酬谢你。”
你可以想见，把脑袋伸进狼喉咙里，鹤心里可没底。但她生性贪财，还是照狼的要求做了。
狼感觉骨头没了，抬脚就要走。
“可是我的报酬呢？”鹤急切地喊。
“什么！”狼猛地转过身，龇牙低吼，“你还没得到吗？我让你从我嘴里把脑袋完完整整地拔出来，没一口咬断它，这还不够吗？”
为恶人效力，就别指望报酬。

source_paragraphs: An Ass was being driven along a road leading down the mountain side, when he suddenly took it into his silly head to choose his own path. He could see his stall at the foot of the mountain, and to him the quickest way down seemed to be over the edge of the nearest cliff. Just as he was about to leap over, his master caught him by the tail and tried to pull him back, but the stubborn Ass would not yield and pulled with all his might.
"Very well," said his master, "go your way, you willful beast, and see where it leads you."
With that he let go, and the foolish Ass tumbled head over heels down the mountain side.
_They who will not listen to reason but stubbornly go their own way against the friendly advice of those who are wiser than they, are on the road to misfortune._
translated_paragraphs: 主人正赶着驴沿山路往山下走。驴的傻脑瓜里忽然冒出个念头，要自己选条路。他能看见山脚下的驴棚，在他看来，从身旁最近的悬崖边上直下去，就是最快的路。他正要往下跳，主人揪住他的尾巴，想把他拽回来。可是犟驴不肯让步，拼尽力气往前拽。
“好吧，”主人说，“你这任性的家伙，走你的路吧，瞧它会把你带到哪儿去。”
说完他松了手。蠢驴一头栽下去，沿着山坡滚了下去。
不肯听道理，连更有见识的人好心劝告也听不进，只管固执地走自己的路，这条路通向不幸。

source_paragraphs: A pair of Oxen were drawing a heavily loaded wagon along a miry country road. They had to use all their strength to pull the wagon, but they did not complain.

The Wheels of the wagon were of a different sort. Though the task they had to do was very light compared with that of the Oxen, they creaked and groaned at every turn. The poor Oxen, pulling with all their might to draw the wagon through the deep mud, had their ears filled with the loud complaining of the Wheels. And this, you may well know, made their work so much the harder to endure.
"Silence!" the Oxen cried at last, out of patience. "What have you Wheels to complain about so loudly? We are drawing all the weight, not you, and we are keeping still about it besides."
_They complain most who suffer least._
translated_paragraphs: 两头牛拉着满载货物的大车，走在一条泥泞的乡间路上。他们得使出全身力气才拉得动，却一句也不抱怨。
车轮就不一样了。跟牛的活儿相比，他们的差事实在轻得多，可每转一圈，都要吱吱呀呀哼几声。可怜的牛拼尽力气，把车从深泥里往前拖，耳朵却被车轮响亮的抱怨灌得满满的。你准能想到，这让他们的活儿更难熬了。
“安静点儿！”牛终于忍不住喊道，“你们这些轮子，有什么值得这么大声抱怨的？这么重的一车是我们在拉，又不是你们。我们可一声没吭。”
吃苦最少的，抱怨声最大。

source_paragraphs: A Lion lay asleep in the forest, his great head resting on his paws. A timid little Mouse came upon him unexpectedly, and in her fright and haste to get away, ran across the Lion's nose. Roused from his nap, the Lion laid his huge paw angrily on the tiny creature to kill her.
"Spare me!" begged the poor Mouse. "Please let me go and some day I will surely repay you."
The Lion was much amused to think that a Mouse could ever help him. But he was generous and finally let the Mouse go.

Some days later, while stalking his prey in the forest, the Lion was caught in the toils of a hunter's net. Unable to free himself, he filled the forest with his angry roaring. The Mouse knew the voice and quickly found the Lion struggling in the net. Running to one of the great ropes that bound him, she gnawed it until it parted, and soon the Lion was free.
"You laughed when I said I would repay you," said the Mouse. "Now you see that even a Mouse can help a Lion."
_A kindness is never wasted._
translated_paragraphs: 树林里，一头狮子把大脑袋枕在爪子上，睡着了。一只胆小的老鼠没留神，走到他跟前。她吓得急忙逃开，慌乱中竟从狮子的鼻子上跑了过去。狮子被吵醒了，气呼呼地伸出大爪子，按住小家伙，要她的命。
“饶了我吧！”可怜的老鼠说，“请放我一回，总有一天我会报答你。”
一只老鼠，还能帮上狮子的忙？狮子觉得怪好笑。不过，他倒也宽厚，到底放了她。
几天后，狮子在林中悄悄追着猎物，不料自己撞进了猎人的网。他怎么挣也挣不脱，气得吼声传遍了树林。小老鼠认出了他的声音，很快就找到了正在网里挣扎的狮子。她跑到一根捆住他的粗绳跟前，啃呀啃，一直把它咬断。没一会儿，狮子就脱了身。
“我说要报答你，你还笑我呢。”老鼠说，“这下你瞧见啦，哪怕是一只老鼠，也帮得上狮子。”
你给出去的一点善意，总有它的用处。

sections.title_en: THE SHEPHERD BOY AND THE WOLF
source_paragraphs: A Shepherd Boy tended his master's Sheep near a dark forest not far from the village. Soon he found life in the pasture very dull. All he could do to amuse himself was to talk to his dog or play on his shepherd's pipe.
One day as he sat watching the Sheep and the quiet forest, and thinking what he would do should he see a Wolf, he thought of a plan to amuse himself.

His Master had told him to call for help should a Wolf attack the flock, and the Villagers would drive it away. So now, though he had not seen anything that even looked like a Wolf, he ran toward the village shouting at the top of his voice, "Wolf! Wolf!"

As he expected, the Villagers who heard the cry dropped their work and ran in great excitement to the pasture. But when they got there they found the Boy doubled up with laughter at the trick he had played on them.
A few days later the Shepherd Boy again shouted, "Wolf! Wolf!" Again the Villagers ran to help him, only to be laughed at again.
Then one evening as the sun was setting behind the forest and the shadows were creeping out over the pasture, a Wolf really did spring from the underbrush and fall upon the Sheep.
In terror the Boy ran toward the village shouting "Wolf! Wolf!" But though the Villagers heard the cry, they did not run to help him as they had before. "He cannot fool us again," they said.
The Wolf killed a great many of the Boy's sheep and then slipped away into the forest.
_Liars are not believed even when they speak the truth._
translated_paragraphs: 村子附近有片黑黝黝的树林，一个放羊娃在林边替主人照看羊群。他很快就觉得草场上的日子乏味透顶。能给自己解闷的，无非是跟狗说说话，或者吹一吹牧羊笛。
有一天，他坐着看羊，也看那片安安静静的树林，琢磨万一遇上狼该怎么办。想着想着，他倒想出个取乐的主意。
主人叮嘱过他，要是有狼扑向羊群，就大声求救，村里人会来把狼赶走。于是，他明明连个长得像狼的影子也没看见，却奔向村子，扯着嗓门大喊：“狼来了！狼来了！”
果然不出他所料，村民们一听就放下手里的活，慌慌张张跑到草场。等到了，只见那孩子为自己耍的花招笑弯了腰。
过了几天，放羊娃又喊：“狼来了！狼来了！”村民们又跑来帮忙，又一次遭到他的嘲笑。
后来，一个傍晚，太阳落到了树林后头，地上的影子朝草场慢慢爬过来。那密丛里真的蹿出一头狼，扑向羊群。
放羊娃吓坏了，往村子里奔去，大喊：“狼来了！狼来了！”村民们听到了，却谁也没像前两回那样跑来帮他。“他别想再骗我们了。”他们说。
狼咬死了好些羊，才溜回树林里去。
常说谎的人，讲真话时也没人相信。

source_paragraphs: A Gnat flew over the meadow with much buzzing for so small a creature and settled on the tip of one of the horns of a Bull. After he had rested a short time, he made ready to fly away. But before he left he begged the Bull's pardon for having used his horn for a resting place.
"You must be very glad to have me go now," he said.
"It's all the same to me," replied the Bull. "I did not even know you were there."
_We are often of greater importance in our own eyes than in the eyes of our neighbor._
_The smaller the mind the greater the conceit._
translated_paragraphs: 一只小蚊虫飞过草地，那么小个儿，嗡嗡起来倒挺响。他落在公牛的一只角尖上。歇了一小会儿，他准备飞走了。临走还向公牛赔礼，说自己把牛角借来当落脚处，多有打扰。
“我这就走，你一定很高兴吧。”他说。
“你走不走，对我都一样。”公牛回答，“我都不知道你在那儿。”
我们在自己眼中，往往比在旁人眼中重要得多。
心胸越小，自负越大。

source_paragraphs: Two Travellers, walking in the noonday sun, sought the shade of a widespreading tree to rest. As they lay looking up among the pleasant leaves, they saw that it was a Plane Tree.
"How useless is the Plane!" said one of them. "It bears no fruit whatever, and only serves to litter the ground with leaves."
"Ungrateful creatures!" said a voice from the Plane Tree. "You lie here in my cooling shade, and yet you say I am useless! Thus ungratefully, O Jupiter, do men receive their blessings!"
_Our best blessings are often the least appreciated._
translated_paragraphs: 两名旅人在正午的太阳下赶路，找了棵枝叶伸展的大树，到树荫底下歇脚。他们躺着仰望可爱的叶子，这才认出，原来是棵悬铃木。
“悬铃木可真没用啊！”其中一个说，“一点能吃的果子也不结，除了把叶子掉得满地乱糟糟，还会做什么？”
“两个忘恩负义的家伙！”悬铃木里传出个声音，“你们躺在我清凉的树荫里，还说我没用！哎，朱庇特啊，人们就是这么领受恩惠的！”
我们享有的最好的恩惠，往往最少得到珍惜。

source_paragraphs: A Stork of a very simple and trusting nature had been asked by a gay party of Cranes to visit a field that had been newly planted. But the party ended dismally with all the birds entangled in the meshes of the Farmer's net.
The Stork begged the Farmer to spare him.
"Please let me go," he pleaded. "I belong to the Stork family who you know are honest and birds of good character. Besides, I did not know the Cranes were going to steal."
"You may be a very good bird," answered the Farmer, "but I caught you with the thieving Cranes and you will have to share the same punishment with them."
_You are judged by the company you keep._
translated_paragraphs: 有只鹳天性单纯，容易相信人。一群兴高采烈的鹤请他去逛逛一块刚播了种的田。谁知这趟游玩收场十分惨淡，所有的鸟都被农夫的网眼缠住了。
鹳求农夫饶了他。
“请放了我吧，”他央求道，“您知道，鹳是老实可靠、品行端正的鸟。我又不知道，鹤来这里是要偷东西。”
“你也许确实是只好鸟，”农夫答道，“可是我捉到你的时候，你跟这群偷东西的鹤在一起。现在你也只好跟他们一起受罚了。”
别人会从你结交的伙伴来判断你的为人。

source_paragraphs: One day a shepherd discovered a fat Pig in the meadow where his Sheep were pastured. He very quickly captured the porker, which squealed at the top of its voice the moment the Shepherd laid his hands on it. You would have thought, to hear the loud squealing, that the Pig was being cruelly hurt. But in spite of its squeals and struggles to escape, the Shepherd tucked his prize under his arm and started off to the butcher's in the market place.
The Sheep in the pasture were much astonished and amused at the Pig's behavior, and followed the Shepherd and his charge to the pasture gate.

"What makes you squeal like that?" asked one of the Sheep. "The Shepherd often catches and carries off one of us. But we should feel very much ashamed to make such a terrible fuss about it like you do."
"That is all very well," replied the Pig, with a squeal and a frantic kick. "When he catches you he is only after your wool. But he wants my bacon! gree-ee-ee!"
_It is easy to be brave when there is no danger._
translated_paragraphs: 一天，牧羊人在自家羊群吃草的草地上发现一头胖猪。他手脚麻利地一把逮住，手刚碰上它，那猪就扯开嗓子大叫。光听这尖利的叫声，你准以为猪受了什么酷刑。猪叫个不停，拼命挣扎，可牧羊人把这件战利品往胳膊底下一夹，迈开步子就朝集市上的肉铺走去。
草场上的羊看着猪这副模样，既惊奇又好笑，就跟在牧羊人和猪身后，一路跟到草场门口。
“你叫得那么凶干什么？”一只羊问，“牧羊人也常从我们中间逮一只抱走。若是像你这样大惊小怪，我们可要羞死了。”
“你倒说得轻巧！”猪尖叫着，没命地踢了一脚，“他逮你们，不过想剪点儿羊毛。他看中的可是我的肉啊！叽——！”
没有危险的时候，谁都容易显得勇敢。

source_paragraphs: Two men were traveling in company along the road when one of them picked up a well-filled purse.
"How lucky I am!" he said. "I have found a purse. Judging by its weight it must be full of gold."
"Do not say '_I_ have found a purse,'" said his companion. "Say rather '_we_ have found a purse' and 'how lucky _we_ are.' Travelers ought to share alike the fortunes or misfortunes of the road."
"No, no," replied the other angrily. "_I_ found it and _I_ am going to keep it."
Just then they heard a shout of "Stop, thief!" and looking around, saw a mob of people armed with clubs coming down the road.
The man who had found the purse fell into a panic.
"We are lost if they find the purse on us," he cried.
"No, no," replied the other, "You would not say 'we' before, so now stick to your 'I'. Say '_I_ am lost.'"
_We cannot expect any one to share our misfortunes unless we are willing to share our good fortune also._
translated_paragraphs: 两个人正结伴赶路，其中一个捡到一只塞得鼓鼓的钱袋。
“我多走运！”他说，“我捡到一个钱袋。掂掂这分量，里头准装满了金币。”
“别说‘我捡到一个钱袋’，”同伴说，“你该说‘咱们捡到一个钱袋’，该说‘咱们多走运’。结伴出门，路上遇见好事也好，倒霉事也罢，都该一起分担。”
“不，不！”那人生气地答道，“是我捡到的，我要自己留着。”
正说着，身后传来一声喊：“抓贼！”两人回头一看，一群人拿着棍棒顺大路追来。
捡到钱袋的那个人慌了。
“他们要是在咱们身上找到那个钱袋，咱们就完啦！”他喊道。
“不，不，”同伴说，“刚才你不肯说‘咱们’，现在也请接着用你的‘我’吧。你得说‘我就完啦’。”
不肯把好运分给旁人，也别指望旁人和你分担霉运。

source_paragraphs: One day as the Lion walked proudly down a forest aisle, and the animals respectfully made way for him, an Ass brayed a scornful remark as he passed.
The Lion felt a flash of anger. But when he turned his head and saw who had spoken, he walked quietly on. He would not honor the fool with even so much as a stroke of his claws.
_Do not resent the remarks of a fool. Ignore them._
translated_paragraphs: 一天，狮子威风凛凛地沿林间小道走来，百兽恭恭敬敬地为他让开。偏有一头驴在他经过时，扯开嗓子叫了一句挖苦话。
狮子心头腾地蹿起一股怒火。但他回过头，看清说话的是谁，就不声不响往前走了。连赏这蠢货一爪子，他都嫌太抬举了他。
蠢人的闲话用不着往心里去。只管不理就是了。

sections.title_en: THE FROGS WHO WISHED FOR A KING
source_paragraphs: The Frogs were tired of governing themselves. They had so much freedom that it had spoiled them, and they did nothing but sit around croaking in a bored manner and wishing for a government that could entertain them with the pomp and display of royalty, and rule them in a way to make them know they were being ruled. No milk and water government for them, they declared. So they sent a petition to Jupiter asking for a king.

Jupiter saw what simple and foolish creatures they were, but to keep them quiet and make them think they had a king he threw down a huge log, which fell into the water with a great splash. The Frogs hid themselves among the reeds and grasses, thinking the new king to be some fearful giant. But they soon discovered how tame and peaceable King Log was. In a short time the younger Frogs were using him for a diving platform, while the older Frogs made him a meeting place, where they complained loudly to Jupiter about the government.

To teach the Frogs a lesson the ruler of the gods now sent a Crane to be king of Frogland. The Crane proved to be a very different sort of king from old King Log. He gobbled up the poor Frogs right and left and they soon saw what fools they had been. In mournful croaks they begged Jupiter to take away the cruel tyrant before they should all be destroyed.
"How now!" cried Jupiter "Are you not yet content? You have what you asked for and so you have only yourselves to blame for your misfortunes."
_Be sure you can better your condition before you seek to change._
translated_paragraphs: 青蛙们厌倦了自己管自己。他们自在惯了，反而被惯坏了，每天只知道坐着，无聊地呱呱叫，希望来个国王，一来让他们看看王家的排场，热闹热闹，二来也要使足威风，叫他们明明白白知道自己受人管束。他们宣称，软绵绵的治理可瞧不上眼。于是他们给朱庇特递上请求，请他赐位国王。
朱庇特看出他们又天真又糊涂。为了让他们安静下来，让他们觉得国王已经来了，他从天上扔下一根大木头。扑通一声，水花四溅。青蛙们以为新国王是个可怕的巨人，一下子躲进芦苇和水草里。可是没多久，他们就发现这位木头国王温顺极了，谁也不招惹。小青蛙把他当成跳水台，老青蛙把他当成议事场，坐在他身上，大声向朱庇特抱怨国王不称职。
众神之王想给青蛙们一个教训，这回派来一只鹤当蛙国国王。这位鹤王可跟老木头国王大不一样。他左一口右一口，把可怜的青蛙吞下肚去。青蛙这才看出自己当初有多傻。他们悲悲切切地呱呱叫，求朱庇特趁他们还没被吃光，快把这暴君弄走。
“怎么！”朱庇特喊道，“你们还不满意？你们自己要的，如今已经给了你们。碰上这样不幸的事，要怪也只能怪自己。”
想求改变，先弄清楚能不能叫自己的处境变好。

source_paragraphs: The Owl always takes her sleep during the day. Then after sundown, when the rosy light fades from the sky and the shadows rise slowly through the wood, out she comes ruffling and blinking from the old hollow tree. Now her weird "hoo-hoo-hoo-oo-oo" echoes through the quiet wood, and she begins her hunt for the bugs and beetles, frogs and mice she likes so well to eat.

Now there was a certain old Owl who had become very cross and hard to please as she grew older, especially if anything disturbed her daily slumbers. One warm summer afternoon as she dozed away in her den in the old oak tree, a Grasshopper nearby began a joyous but very raspy song. Out popped the old Owl's head from the opening in the tree that served her both for door and for window.
"Get away from here, sir," she said to the Grasshopper. "Have you no manners? You should at least respect my age and leave me to sleep in quiet!"
But the Grasshopper answered saucily that he had as much right to his place in the sun as the Owl had to her place in the old oak. Then he struck up a louder and still more rasping tune.

The wise old Owl knew quite well that it would do no good to argue with the Grasshopper, nor with anybody else for that matter. Besides, her eyes were not sharp enough by day to permit her to punish the Grasshopper as he deserved. So she laid aside all hard words and spoke very kindly to him.

"Well sir," she said, "if I must stay awake, I am going to settle right down to enjoy your singing. Now that I think of it, I have a wonderful wine here, sent me from Olympus, of which I am told Apollo drinks before he sings to the high gods. Please come up and taste this delicious drink with me. I know it will make you sing like Apollo himself."

The foolish Grasshopper was taken in by the Owl's flattering words. Up he jumped to the Owl's den, but as soon as he was near enough so the old Owl could see him clearly, she pounced upon him and ate him up.
_Flattery is not a proof of true admiration._
_Do not let flattery throw you off your guard against an enemy._
translated_paragraphs: 猫头鹰总是在白天睡觉。太阳沉下去，天边的玫瑰色褪尽，林间的影子慢慢升起，她才从那棵老树的洞里露出头来，一边抖着羽毛一边眨眼睛。这会儿，静静的林子里回响起她古怪的“呼——呼——呼呜呜”，她开始寻找自己最爱吃的虫子、甲虫、青蛙和老鼠。
有只老猫头鹰年纪越大，脾气越坏，也越难伺候，尤其讨厌别人搅了她白天的好梦。一天下午，夏日暖烘烘的，她正在老橡树的窝里打盹，附近一只蚂蚱忽然唱起一支欢快却格外刺耳的曲子。老猫头鹰的脑袋猛地从树洞里探出来，那洞既是她的门也是她的窗。
“这位先生，请走开！”她对蚂蚱说，“你懂不懂礼貌？至少也该敬一敬我这把年纪，让我安静睡会儿吧！”
蚂蚱却不客气地顶回去，说猫头鹰有权占着老橡树里的窝，他也同样有权占着太阳底下那块地。说罢他又唱起来，这一曲更响，也更加扎耳。
老猫头鹰很有见识，她明白跟蚂蚱争论不会有用。说起来，跟别人争论也好不到哪儿去。何况大白天她的眼睛不够敏锐，没法给蚂蚱一个应得的教训。于是她收起那些难听话，改用和和气气的口吻跟他说话。
“好吧，先生，”她说，“既然我睡不着，那就安安稳稳地欣赏你的歌声吧。我忽然想起来，我这儿有一坛从奥林匹斯山送来的美酒，听说阿波罗唱歌给天上诸神听之前，都会喝上一口。请你上来，跟我一道尝尝这美味。喝了以后，你准能唱得跟阿波罗本人一样动听。”
傻蚂蚱给这番恭维话哄住了。他一跳，跳到猫头鹰的洞口。蚂蚱一靠近，老猫头鹰看清了他，扑过去便把他吃了。
说得好听，未必是真心欣赏你。
面对敌人，别因几句奉承话就丢掉戒心。

source_paragraphs: A Wolf left his lair one evening in fine spirits and an excellent appetite. As he ran, the setting sun cast his shadow far out on the ground, and it looked as if the wolf were a hundred times bigger than he really was.
"Why," exclaimed the Wolf proudly, "see how big I am! Fancy _me_ running away from a puny Lion! I'll show him who is fit to be king, he or I."
Just then an immense shadow blotted him out entirely, and the next instant a Lion struck him down with a single blow.
_Do not let your fancy make you forget realities._
translated_paragraphs: 一天傍晚，狼精神抖擞地离开兽穴，胃口好极了。他一边跑，落日一边把他的影子远远投在地上。单看那影子，简直像是这头狼一下子长大了一百倍。
“嘿，”狼得意地叫道，“瞧我块头多大！想想看，我居然还躲着那么一丁点儿大的狮子跑！我得让他看看，到底他配当国王，还是我配。”
就在这一刻，一个巨大的影子把他整个儿罩住了。紧接着，一头狮子只一巴掌，就把他击倒在地。
别让想象遮住了眼前的实情。

source_paragraphs: A Giant Oak stood near a brook in which grew some slender Reeds. When the wind blew, the great Oak stood proudly upright with its hundred arms uplifted to the sky. But the Reeds bowed low in the wind and sang a sad and mournful song.

"You have reason to complain," said the Oak. "The slightest breeze that ruffles the surface of the water makes you bow your heads, while I, the mighty Oak, stand upright and firm before the howling tempest."

"Do not worry about us," replied the Reeds. "The winds do not harm us. We bow before them and so we do not break. You, in all your pride and strength, have so far resisted their blows. But the end is coming."

As the Reeds spoke a great hurricane rushed out of the north. The Oak stood proudly and fought against the storm, while the yielding Reeds bowed low. The wind redoubled in fury, and all at once the great tree fell, torn up by the roots, and lay among the pitying Reeds.
_Better to yield when it is folly to resist, than to resist stubbornly and be destroyed._
translated_paragraphs: 一棵巨大的橡树长在小溪边，溪里生着几株纤细的芦苇。风吹起来，大橡树傲然挺立，把上百条手臂高高举向天空。芦苇却向风低低弯腰，唱着悲伤哀婉的歌。
“你们抱怨得有道理，”橡树说，“只消一点点微风吹皱水面，你们就得低头。看看我这棵强壮的橡树，哪怕风暴在耳边怒吼，也能站得又直又稳。”
“不必为我们担心，”芦苇回答，“风伤不了我们。我们朝它弯一弯腰，就折不断。你凭着一身傲气和力气，至今都扛住了它的冲击，可到头的日子快来了。”
芦苇正在说话，一阵狂飙从北方呼啸而来。大橡树傲然挺着身子迎战，而柔韧的芦苇把腰弯得低低的。风一阵比一阵猛烈。猛然间，大树连根拔起，轰然倒下，躺在一丛为他惋惜的芦苇中间。
硬顶本是愚举的时候，肯弯一弯腰，总比死扛到底、落得粉身碎骨好。

source_paragraphs: A Rat was traveling along the King's highway. He was a very proud Rat, considering his small size and the bad reputation all Rats have. As Mr. Rat walked along--he kept mostly to the ditch--he noticed a great commotion up the road, and soon a grand procession came in view. It was the King and his retinue.

The King rode on a huge Elephant adorned with the most gorgeous trappings. With the King in his luxurious howdah were the royal Dog and Cat. A great crowd of people followed the procession. They were so taken up with admiration of the Elephant, that the Rat was not noticed. His pride was hurt.

"What fools!" he cried. "Look at me, and you will soon forget that clumsy Elephant! Is it his great size that makes your eyes pop out? Or is it his wrinkled hide? Why, I have eyes and ears and as many legs as he! I am of just as much importance, and"--
But just then the royal Cat spied him, and the next instant, the Rat knew he was _not_ quite so important as an Elephant.
_A resemblance to the great in some things does not make us great._
translated_paragraphs: 一只老鼠走在国王的大道上。想想他那么小的个头，再想想老鼠们普遍都没什么好名声，这位老鼠先生倒着实相当自负。他一路走着，大部分时间还是沿着路沟走，忽然发现前面闹哄哄的。很快，一支壮观的队伍出现在眼前，那是国王和他的随从。
国王骑在一头硕大的象上。大象全身披戴着无比华美的装饰，背上架着奢华的象轿。国王坐在轿中，身旁还有王宫的猫和狗。一大群百姓跟着队伍走，人人只顾仰慕大象，谁也没注意到老鼠。他的自尊心受伤了。
“一群傻子！”他叫道，“看看我，不消一会儿，你们就会把那头笨重的大象给忘了！是他那大块头叫你们眼珠子都要瞪出来了吗？还是他那层皱巴巴的皮？哼，我跟他一样有眼睛，有耳朵，连腿都一样多！我跟他一样要紧，而且——”
偏在这时候，王家的猫瞄到了他。紧接着，老鼠就知道，原来自己没有大象那么要紧。
有几样地方与了不起的人相似，并不能使我们也同样了不起。

source_paragraphs: Some Boys were playing one day at the edge of a pond in which lived a family of Frogs. The Boys amused themselves by throwing stones into the pond so as to make them skip on top of the water.
The stones were flying thick and fast and the Boys were enjoying themselves very much; but the poor Frogs in the pond were trembling with fear.
At last one of the Frogs, the oldest and bravest, put his head out of the water, and said, "Oh, please, dear children, stop your cruel play! Though it may be fun for you, it means death to us!"
_Always stop to think whether your fun may not be the cause of another's unhappiness._
translated_paragraphs: 池塘里住着青蛙一家。一天，几个男孩来到塘边玩，他们往池塘里扔石片，让石片贴着水面蹦跳，打起了水漂。
石片又快又密地飞来，男孩们玩得快活极了，可池塘里那些可怜的青蛙个个吓得发抖。
最后，他们当中年纪最大、胆子也最大的一只从水面探出头来：“啊，亲爱的孩子们，求你们别再玩这种残忍的游戏了吧！你们只是觉得好玩，对我们却会送命啊！”
尽兴的时候，记得停一停，想想自己的快乐会不会叫旁人遭殃。

source_paragraphs: In a spell of dry weather, when the Birds could find very little to drink, a thirsty Crow found a pitcher with a little water in it. But the pitcher was high and had a narrow neck, and no matter how he tried, the Crow could not reach the water. The poor thing felt as if he must die of thirst.

Then an idea came to him. Picking up some small pebbles, he dropped them into the pitcher one by one. With each pebble the water rose a little higher until at last it was near enough so he could drink.
_In a pinch a good use of our wits may help us out._
translated_paragraphs: 好久没下雨，鸟儿几乎找不到水喝。一只渴坏了的乌鸦找到一个水罐，里面还有一点水。可水罐高，罐口窄，乌鸦怎么试，嘴都够不到水。可怜的乌鸦觉得，自己非渴死不可了。
忽然，它有了主意。它捡起小石子，一颗一颗投进罐里。每放进去一颗，水就升高一点。最后，水面终于升到了它嘴边。乌鸦喝到水啦。
碰到难处，开动脑筋，也许就能找到办法。

source_paragraphs: One bright day in late autumn a family of Ants were bustling about in the warm sunshine, drying out the grain they had stored up during the summer, when a starving Grasshopper, his fiddle under his arm, came up and humbly begged for a bite to eat.
"What!" cried the Ants in surprise, "haven't you stored anything away for the winter? What in the world were you doing all last summer?"
"I didn't have time to store up any food," whined the Grasshopper; "I was so busy making music that before I knew it the summer was gone."
The Ants shrugged their shoulders in disgust.
"Making music, were you?" they cried. "Very well; now dance!" And they turned their backs on the Grasshopper and went on with their work.
_There's a time for work and a time for play._
translated_paragraphs: 深秋的一天，天朗气清，一窝蚂蚁在暖阳里来来往往，忙着晾晒夏天储下的粮食。一只快要饿死的蚂蚱胳膊底下夹着小提琴，走来低声下气地讨一口吃的。
“什么！”蚂蚁们惊讶地喊，“你一点过冬的粮食都没存下？整个夏天，你究竟干什么去了？”
“我没工夫存粮食呀，”蚂蚱哼哼着说，“我忙着奏乐呢，一不留神，夏天就过去了。”
蚂蚁们嫌弃地耸了耸肩膀。
“奏乐，是吗？”他们喊，“那好啊，现在跳舞去吧！”说完，他们把背转向蚂蚱，接着干自己的活儿了。
有玩乐的时候，也有该干活的时候。

source_paragraphs: A sacred Image was being carried to the temple. It was mounted on an Ass adorned with garlands and gorgeous trappings, and a grand procession of priests and pages followed it through the streets. As the Ass walked along, the people bowed their heads reverently or fell on their knees, and the Ass thought the honor was being paid to himself.

With his head full of this foolish idea, he became so puffed up with pride and vanity that he halted and started to bray loudly. But in the midst of his song, his driver guessed what the Ass had got into his head, and began to beat him unmercifully with a stick.
"Go along with you, you stupid Ass," he cried. "The honor is not meant for you but for the image you are carrying."
_Do not try to take the credit to yourself that is due to others._
translated_paragraphs: 有一尊神像正被送往神庙。它安放在驴背上，驴佩着花环和华美的鞍饰，后面跟着一队隆隆重重的祭司和侍童，一路穿街而过。驴走过时，人们或恭敬地低头，或屈膝跪拜。驴以为众人行的大礼都是给自己的。
这个荒唐念头占满了脑瓜，驴骄傲得不得了，索性停下脚步，高声嘶叫起来。他正唱到一半，赶驴人就猜到他心里打的什么主意，抡起棍子，毫不留情地揍他。
“往前走，你这头蠢驴！”赶驴人喊，“大家拜的是你驮着的神像，哪是在拜你！”
该归别人的功劳，别往自己身上揽。

source_paragraphs: A Raven, which you know is black as coal, was envious of the Swan, because her feathers were as white as the purest snow. The foolish bird got the idea that if he lived like the Swan, swimming and diving all day long and eating the weeds and plants that grow in the water, his feathers would turn white like the Swan's.

So he left his home in the woods and fields and flew down to live on the lakes and in the marshes. But though he washed and washed all day long, almost drowning himself at it, his feathers remained as black as ever. And as the water weeds he ate did not agree with him, he got thinner and thinner, and at last he died.
_A change of habits will not alter nature._
translated_paragraphs: 你知道，渡鸦浑身像煤一样黑。他很羡慕天鹅，因为她的羽毛跟最洁白的雪一般白。这只傻鸟有了个主意，以为只要像天鹅那样生活，整天游泳、潜水，吃生在水里的水草和植物，自己的羽毛也能像天鹅一般洁白。
于是他离开了林野里的家，飞到湖泊和沼泽中去住。可他整天洗呀洗呀，差点儿把自己淹死，羽毛还是跟从前一样黑。吃下去的水草又不合他的肠胃，他越来越瘦，最后死了。
换一种生活习惯，改变不了原来的天性。

source_paragraphs: Two Goats, frisking gayly on the rocky steeps of a mountain valley, chanced to meet, one on each side of a deep chasm through which poured a mighty mountain torrent. The trunk of a fallen tree formed the only means of crossing the chasm, and on this not even two squirrels could have passed each other in safety. The narrow path would have made the bravest tremble. Not so our Goats. Their pride would not permit either to stand aside for the other.
One set her foot on the log. The other did likewise. In the middle they met horn to horn. Neither would give way, and so they both fell, to be swept away by the roaring torrent below.
_It is better to yield than to come to misfortune through stubbornness._
translated_paragraphs: 山谷里，两只山羊在陡峭的岩坡上蹦蹦跳跳，正好隔着一道深沟打了照面。脚底下，是奔腾的山洪。一棵倒下的树横在上面，那是过沟的唯一一条路。树干窄得连两只松鼠都没法并肩错过去。再大胆的人走上去，也得腿软。两只山羊倒不怕。它们都太骄傲，谁也不肯往旁边站一站，让对方先过。
一只踏上去，另一只也踏上去。走到当中，羊角碰着了羊角。谁也不肯让。结果两只都跌了下去，叫底下轰隆隆的山洪冲走了。
肯退让一步，好过一味犟着，把自己送进险境。

sections.title_en: THE ASS AND THE LOAD OF SALT
source_paragraphs: A Merchant, driving his Ass homeward from the seashore with a heavy load of salt, came to a river crossed by a shallow ford. They had crossed this river many times before without accident, but this time the Ass slipped and fell when halfway over. And when the Merchant at last got him to his feet, much of the salt had melted away. Delighted to find how much lighter his burden had become, the Ass finished the journey very gayly.

Next day the Merchant went for another load of salt. On the way home the Ass, remembering what had happened at the ford, purposely let himself fall into the water, and again got rid of most of his burden.

The angry Merchant immediately turned about and drove the Ass back to the seashore, where he loaded him with two great baskets of sponges. At the ford the Ass again tumbled over; but when he had scrambled to his feet, it was a very disconsolate Ass that dragged himself homeward under a load ten times heavier than before.
_The same measures will not suit all circumstances._
translated_paragraphs: 一个商人从海边赶驴回家，驴背上驮着沉沉的盐。他们来到一条河，这里有处浅滩可以渡过去。从前他们在这儿过了许多趟，从没出过岔子，这回驴却在河心脚下一滑，摔倒了。等商人好不容易将他扶起来，盐已经化掉大半。驴发现背上轻了那么多，欢欢喜喜地走完了回家的路。
第二天，商人又去运了一驮盐。回来的时候，驴想起上次在浅滩发生的事，就故意往水里一倒，这回身上的重担又去了大半。
商人发起火来，立刻掉头把驴赶回海边，换了两大筐海绵让他驮着。来到浅滩，驴又往水里一躺。等他挣扎着站起来，担子比先前重了十倍。这回往家挪的，可是一头垂头丧气的驴。
同一个办法，未必适合所有情形。

source_paragraphs: "Away with you, vile insect!" said a Lion angrily to a Gnat that was buzzing around his head. But the Gnat was not in the least disturbed.
"Do you think," he said spitefully to the Lion, "that I am afraid of you because they call you king?"

The next instant he flew at the Lion and stung him sharply on the nose. Mad with rage, the Lion struck fiercely at the Gnat, but only succeeded in tearing himself with his claws. Again and again the Gnat stung the Lion, who now was roaring terribly. At last, worn out with rage and covered with wounds that his own teeth and claws had made, the Lion gave up the fight.

The Gnat buzzed away to tell the whole world about his victory, but instead he flew straight into a spider's web. And there, he who had defeated the King of beasts came to a miserable end, the prey of a little spider.
_The least of our enemies is often the most to be feared._
_Pride over a success should not throw us off our guard._
translated_paragraphs: “滚开，讨厌的虫子！”一只小蚊虫在狮子头边嗡嗡地飞，狮子生气地喝道。小蚊虫却半点也没被唬住。
“你以为，”他不客气地说，“大家管你叫国王，我就怕你不成？”
转眼间，他扑上去，在狮子的鼻尖上狠叮了一口。狮子气得发狂，猛挥爪子去打小蚊虫，却只在自己身上挠出了伤口。小蚊虫一次又一次叮他，狮子疼得吼声震天。终于，他气得精疲力尽，浑身都是被自己的牙齿和爪子弄出来的伤，只好认输了。
小蚊虫嗡嗡飞走，要向全世界宣告自己的胜利，谁知一头扎进了一张蛛网。在那儿，那个打败过百兽之王的胜利者，惨兮兮地败在一只小蜘蛛嘴下。
最不起眼的敌人，往往最值得防备。
一次得胜，再得意也不该放松警惕。

source_paragraphs: A certain man who visited foreign lands could talk of little when he returned to his home except the wonderful adventures he had met with and the great deeds he had done abroad.

One of the feats he told about was a leap he had made in a city Called Rhodes. That leap was so great, he said, that no other man could leap anywhere near the distance. A great many persons in Rhodes had seen him do it and would prove that what he told was true.
"No need of witnesses," said one of the hearers. "Suppose this city is Rhodes. Now show us how far you can jump."
_Deeds count, not boasting words._
translated_paragraphs: 有个人出国游历了一番。回家后，他几乎张口闭口都在说，自己在外头遇见了多少了不起的奇遇，做过多少了不起的事情。
他讲过这样一桩壮举：在罗得城里，他纵身一跃，跳出了惊人的距离。他说那一跳远极了，别人跳的距离连边都沾不上。罗得城里当时有好些人亲眼看见，个个都能作证他说的是真话。
“不用找人作证，”听众里有个人说，“就当咱们这个城就是罗得城。来，跳给大家瞧瞧，看你到底能跳多远。”
算数的是你做了什么，不是你吹了什么。

source_paragraphs: A Cock was busily scratching and scraping about to find something to eat for himself and his family, when he happened to turn up a precious jewel that had been lost by its owner.

"Aha!" said the Cock. "No doubt you are very costly and he who lost you would give a great deal to find you. But as for me, I would choose a single grain of barleycorn before all the jewels in the world."
_Precious things are without value to those who cannot prize them._
translated_paragraphs: 一只公鸡正忙着东扒西刨，要给自己和一家子找点吃的。他刨着刨着，翻出一颗名贵的宝石，是它的主人弄丢的。
“啊哈！”公鸡说，“你当然贵重得很，丢了你的人，说不定肯花好大一笔代价把你寻回来。可要我选，天下所有的珠宝加在一处，也比不过一粒大麦。”
对不懂得珍惜它的人，珍宝也毫无价值。

source_paragraphs: At a great celebration in honor of King Lion, the Monkey was asked to dance for the company. His dancing was very clever indeed, and the animals were all highly pleased with his grace and lightness.

The praise that was showered on the Monkey made the Camel envious. He was very sure that he could dance quite as well as the Monkey, if not better, so he pushed his way into the crowd that was gathered around the Monkey, and rising on his hind legs, began to dance. But the big hulking Camel made himself very ridiculous as he kicked out his knotty legs and twisted his long clumsy neck. Besides, the animals found it hard to keep their toes from under his heavy hoofs.
At last, when one of his huge feet came within an inch of King Lion's nose, the animals were so disgusted that they set upon the Camel in a rage and drove him out into the desert.
Shortly afterward, refreshments, consisting mostly of Camel's hump and ribs, were served to the company.
_Do not try to ape your betters._
translated_paragraphs: 大家为狮王举行了一场盛大的庆典，猴子受邀跳舞给宾客们看。他果真跳得很有本领，那身段既轻盈又漂亮，动物们个个都看得开心。
赞扬声纷纷落在猴子身上，惹得骆驼妒忌万分。他认定自己就算不比猴子跳得好，起码也一样好，于是硬往围着猴子的观众当中挤去，两条后腿一立，跳起舞来。他块头又大又笨，甩开骨节突出的长腿，扭着粗笨的长脖子，样子可笑极了。而且大家还得东躲西闪，生怕自己的脚趾头被他沉重的蹄子踩着。
后来，他一只大脚踢过去，只差一丁点儿就撞上狮王的鼻子。这一下，动物们再也受不了了，怒气冲冲一拥而上，把骆驼驱逐到沙漠去了。
过了不久，招待宾客的点心也端了上来，主要是骆驼的驼峰和肋排。
不要看见别人有本领，就硬去学他的样子卖弄。

sections.title_en: THE WILD BOAR AND THE FOX
source_paragraphs: A Wild Boar was sharpening his tusks busily against the stump of a tree, when a Fox happened by. Now the Fox was always looking for a chance to make fun of his neighbors. So he made a great show of looking anxiously about, as if in fear of some hidden enemy. But the Boar kept right on with his work.
"Why are you doing that?" asked the Fox at last with a grin. "There isn't any danger that I can see."
"True enough," replied the Boar, "but when danger does come there will not be time for such work as this. My weapons will have to be ready for use then, or I shall suffer for it."
_Preparedness for war is the best guarantee of peace._
translated_paragraphs: 野猪正对着一截树桩起劲地磨獠牙，一只狐狸恰巧经过。狐狸一向爱找机会取笑邻居。这会儿他装模作样，忧心忡忡地东张西望，仿佛担心什么敌人埋伏在旁边。可野猪照旧低头磨他的牙。
“你磨这个干吗？”狐狸终于咧嘴笑着问，“我可没看出有什么危险。”
“没错，”野猪回答，“可是危险当真来到，就没工夫干这个了。那时候我的武器得拿出来就能用，要不吃苦的就是我自己。”
平日做好应战的准备，才最有把握守住安宁。

sections.title_en: THE ASS, THE FOX, AND THE LION
source_paragraphs: An Ass and a Fox had become close comrades, and were constantly in each other's company. While the Ass cropped a fresh bit of greens, the Fox would devour a chicken from the neighboring farmyard or a bit of cheese filched from the dairy. One day the pair unexpectedly met a Lion. The Ass was very much frightened, but the Fox calmed his fears.
"I will talk to him," he said.
So the Fox walked boldly up to the Lion.

"Your highness," he said in an undertone, so the Ass could not hear him, "I've got a fine scheme in my head. If you promise not to hurt me, I will lead that foolish creature yonder into a pit where he can't get out, and you can feast at your pleasure."
The Lion agreed and the Fox returned to the Ass.
"I made him promise not to hurt us," said the Fox. "But come, I know a good place to hide till he is gone."
So the Fox led the Ass into a deep pit. But when the Lion saw that the Ass was his for the taking, he first of all struck down the traitor Fox.
_Traitors may expect treachery._
translated_paragraphs: 驴和狐狸成了亲密伙伴，常常形影不离。驴啃上一口鲜嫩的青草时，狐狸就在一旁吞吃从附近农家院叼来的鸡，或是从奶房里偷来的一块奶酪。一天，两个伙伴冷不防碰上一头狮子。驴怕得不得了，狐狸却让他放下心来。
“我去跟他说。”他说。
狐狸大着胆子走到狮子跟前。
“大王，”他放低声音，不叫驴听见，“我想到了一个好计策。您要是答应不伤害我，我就把那边那个蠢家伙引进深坑。等他爬不出来，您想怎么吃就怎么吃。”
狮子答应了，狐狸回到驴身旁。
“我已经让他答应不伤害我们，”狐狸说，“你跟我来，我知道个好地方，咱们躲一躲，等他过去。”
狐狸就这样把驴引进了深坑。可狮子一看，驴已经稳稳当当是他嘴里的肉了，头一件事就是一爪打倒出卖同伴的狐狸。
出卖别人的人，也别指望别人对他守信。

sections.title_en: THE BIRDS, THE BEASTS, AND THE BAT
source_paragraphs: The Birds and the Beasts declared war against each other. No compromise was possible, and so they went at it tooth and claw. It is said the quarrel grew out of the persecution the race of Geese suffered at the teeth of the Fox family. The Beasts, too, had cause for fight. The Eagle was constantly pouncing on the Hare, and the Owl dined daily on Mice.
It was a terrible battle. Many a Hare and many a Mouse died. Chickens and Geese fell by the score--and the victor always stopped for a feast.

Now the Bat family had not openly joined either side. They were a very politic race. So when they saw the Birds getting the better of it, they were Birds for all there was in it. But when the tide of battle turned, they immediately sided with the Beasts.

When the battle was over, the conduct of the Bats was discussed at the peace conference. Such deceit was unpardonable, and Birds and Beasts made common cause to drive out the Bats. And since then the Bat family hides in dark towers and deserted ruins, flying out only in the night.
_The deceitful have no friends._
translated_paragraphs: 飞鸟和走兽互相宣战。双方都不肯和解，便亮出尖牙利爪，大打出手。据说争执起于鹅族长期受狐狸一家欺压，吃尽了它们尖牙的苦头。走兽也有自己的开战理由。老鹰老是袭击野兔，猫头鹰天天拿老鼠当晚餐。
这一仗打得惨烈极了。死了好多野兔和老鼠，鸡和鹅也是一批批倒下。打赢的一方还总得停下来享顿大餐。
蝙蝠一族却没公开加入任何一方。他们精于盘算，见飞鸟占上风，立刻从头到脚都自认是鸟。一等战局逆转，他们又立刻站到了走兽那一边。
战事结束，双方在和谈会上议起蝙蝠的所作所为。这样的欺瞒实在不可原谅。飞鸟和走兽一致同意，把蝙蝠赶了出去。从那以后，蝙蝠一家就躲在昏暗的高塔和无人的废墟里，只有夜间才飞出来。
两面欺骗的人，交不到朋友。

sections.title_en: THE LION, THE BEAR, AND THE FOX
source_paragraphs: Just as a great Bear rushed to seize a stray kid, a Lion leaped from another direction upon the same prey. The two fought furiously for the prize until they had received so many wounds that both sank down unable to continue the battle.
Just then a Fox dashed up, and seizing the kid, made off with it as fast as he could go, while the Lion and the Bear looked on in helpless rage.
"How much better it would have been," they said, "to have shared in a friendly spirit."
_Those who have all the toil do not always get the profit._
translated_paragraphs: 一头大熊正要去捉一只走散的小山羊，偏有头狮子从另一边跳出来，扑向同一份猎物。为了争夺小山羊，两头猛兽拼命厮打，直到浑身伤痕累累，双双倒下，再也无力战斗。
正在这时，一只狐狸快步蹿来，一把叼起小山羊，使出最快的速度跑了。狮子和熊只能怒目而视，谁也奈何不了他。
“早知道，”他们说，“和和气气地分一分，该有多好。”
出力最多的，未必能得到好处。

source_paragraphs: A stray Lamb stood drinking early one morning on the bank of a woodland stream. That very same morning a hungry Wolf came by farther up the stream, hunting for something to eat. He soon got his eyes on the Lamb. As a rule Mr. Wolf snapped up such delicious morsels without making any bones about it, but this Lamb looked so very helpless and innocent that the Wolf felt he ought to have some kind of an excuse for taking its life.
"How dare you paddle around in my stream and stir up all the mud!" he shouted fiercely. "You deserve to be punished severely for your rashness!"
"But, your highness," replied the trembling Lamb, "do not be angry! I cannot possibly muddy the water you are drinking up there. Remember, you are upstream and I am downstream."
"You _do_ muddy it!" retorted the Wolf savagely. "And besides, I have heard that you told lies about me last year!"
"How could I have done so?" pleaded the Lamb. "I wasn't born until this year."
"If it wasn't you, it was your brother!"
"I have no brothers."
"Well, then," snarled the Wolf, "It was someone in your family anyway. But no matter who it was, I do not intend to be talked out of my breakfast."
And without more words the Wolf seized the poor Lamb and carried her off to the forest.
_The tyrant can always find an excuse for his tyranny._
_The unjust will not listen to the reasoning of the innocent._
translated_paragraphs: 一个清早，一只离群的小羊站在林间溪岸上喝水。就在这天早上，有只饿狼沿着溪流上游走来，正到处找东西吃。他很快盯上了小羊。往常狼先生碰到这种鲜嫩的小东西，总是二话不说，一口叼住。只是眼前的小羊显得那么无助、那么无辜，狼倒觉得，要取她性命，总该找个由头。
“你好大的胆子，在我的溪里乱踩，把泥全搅起来了！”他凶巴巴地喝道，“你这样放肆，就该受重罚！”
“可是，大王，”小羊发着抖回答，“请您别生气！您在那边喝的水，我怎么也搅不浑呀。您看，您在上游，我在下游。”
“我说是你搅浑的，就是你！”狼恶狠狠地顶回去，“再说，我听说你去年还造我的谣！”
“我怎么做得了那种事？”小羊央求道，“我今年才出生呢。”
“不是你，就是你的兄弟！”
“我没有兄弟呀。”
“哼，那总归是你们家谁干的。”狼龇着牙说，“不论是谁，你可别想用一张嘴把我的早饭说没了。”
他不再多说，一口攫住可怜的小羊，朝森林里叼去。
暴君总能为自己的暴行找到借口。
不讲公道的人，不肯听无辜者讲理。

source_paragraphs: A Wolf had been hurt in a fight with a Bear. He was unable to move and could not satisfy his hunger and thirst. A Sheep passed by near his hiding place, and the Wolf called to him.
"Please fetch me a drink of water," he begged, "that might give me strength enough so I can get me some solid food."
"Solid food!" said the Sheep. "That means me, I suppose. If I should bring you a drink, it would only serve to wash me down your throat. Don't talk to me about a drink!"
_A knave's hypocrisy is easily seen through._
translated_paragraphs: 狼在和熊搏斗时受了伤。他动弹不得，又饿又渴，没法弄到吃喝。一只绵羊从他藏身之处附近走过，狼出声喊他。
“请给我弄口水喝吧，”他恳求道，“喝点水，有力气了，我也许就能弄点实在的吃食了。”
“实在的吃食！”绵羊说，“你说的就是我喽。我要是给你水喝，无非帮你把我往喉咙里冲得更顺当些。少跟我提喝水的事！”
坏蛋惺惺作态，并不难识破。

source_paragraphs: Hares, as you know, are very timid. The least shadow, sends them scurrying in fright to a hiding place. Once they decided to die rather than live in such misery. But while they were debating how best to meet death, they thought they heard a noise and in a flash were scampering off to the warren. On the way they passed a pond where a family of Frogs was sitting among the reeds on the bank. In an instant the startled Frogs were seeking safety in the mud.
"Look," cried a Hare, "things are not so bad after all, for here are creatures who are even afraid of us!"
_However unfortunate we may think we are there is always someone worse off than ourselves._
translated_paragraphs: 你知道，野兔是很胆小的。连影子稍一晃动，都能吓得他们窜去躲藏。有一回，他们觉得日子过得这么苦，倒不如死了好。可就在大家商量怎么死才好时，仿佛听到一点动静，转眼间便都往兔窝里逃。途中经过池塘，有一家青蛙正在岸边芦苇丛里坐着。那些青蛙受到惊吓，刷的一下全钻到塘泥里避难去了。
“瞧！”一只兔子喊道，“咱们的日子原来也没那么糟，这里还有见了咱们都会害怕的动物呢！”
不论我们觉得自己多么不幸，总有人处境比我们更糟。

source_paragraphs: The Fox one day thought of a plan to amuse himself at the expense of the Stork, at whose odd appearance he was always laughing.

"You must come and dine with me today," he said to the Stork, smiling to himself at the trick he was going to play. The Stork gladly accepted the invitation and arrived in good time and with a very good appetite.

For dinner the Fox served soup. But it was set out in a very shallow dish, and all the Stork could do was to wet the very tip of his bill. Not a drop of soup could he get. But the Fox lapped it up easily, and, to increase the disappointment of the Stork, made a great show of enjoyment.

The hungry Stork was much displeased at the trick, but he was a calm, even-tempered fellow and saw no good in flying into a rage. Instead, not long afterward, he invited the Fox to dine with him in turn. The Fox arrived promptly at the time that had been set, and the Stork served a fish dinner that had a very appetizing smell. But it was served in a tall jar with a very narrow neck. The Stork could easily get at the food with his long bill, but all the Fox could do was to lick the outside of the jar, and sniff at the delicious odor. And when the Fox lost his temper, the Stork said calmly:
_Do not play tricks on your neighbors unless you can stand the same treatment yourself._
translated_paragraphs: 有一天，狐狸想出个拿鹳开心的花招。平常他就老爱嘲笑鹳的怪模样。
“今天你可一定得来我家用餐，”他对鹳说，一想起自己的诡计就暗暗发笑。鹳高兴地答应，早早到了狐狸家，胃口也好极了。
狐狸端上来的是汤，却盛在一个浅得不能再浅的盘子里。鹳最多只能把尖尖的嘴尖沾湿，一滴汤也喝不进肚。狐狸倒舔得毫不费力，还故意咂嘴，装作享受得不得了，好让鹳更失望。
鹳空着肚子，被这样捉弄，心里十分不悦。不过他平静温和，看不出大发雷霆能有什么好处。过了不久，他反过来请狐狸吃饭。狐狸准时到了，鹳端上一道香气扑鼻的鱼。可鱼却装在一只又高又深、颈口极细的长罐里。鹳有长嘴，取鱼来吃轻而易举。狐狸只能舔到罐子外面，干闻闻好香的气味。等狐狸发起脾气，鹳平静地开口了。
“如果你自己受不了同样的招待，就不要用这个法子捉弄邻居。”

source_paragraphs: Two Travelers were walking along the seashore. Far out they saw something riding on the waves.
"Look," said one, "a great ship rides in from distant lands, bearing rich treasures!"
The object they saw came ever nearer the shore.
"No," said the other, "that is not a treasure ship. That is some fisherman's skiff, with the day's catch of savoury fish."
Still nearer came the object. The waves washed it up on shore.
"It is a chest of gold lost from some wreck," they cried. Both Travelers rushed to the beach, but there they found nothing but a water-soaked log.
_Do not let your hopes carry you away from reality._
translated_paragraphs: 两个旅人正沿着海岸散步，远远看见一个东西在浪头上起伏。
“看！”一个人说，“一艘大船从远方的国度开过来啦，满载珍宝呢！”
那个东西离岸越来越近。
“不对，”另一个人说，“那不是运宝船，是哪位渔夫的小艇，载着今天捕到的鲜鱼。”
那东西又漂近了些。海浪把它冲上岸来。
“是沉船上丢的一箱金子！”两个人喊着，一起奔向沙滩。可是到了近前，那里只有一截被海水浸透的木头。
别任由心里的盼望把你从眼前的实情带开。

source_paragraphs: A Wolf had stolen a Lamb and was carrying it off to his lair to eat it. But his plans were very much changed when he met a Lion, who, without making any excuses, took the Lamb away from him.
The Wolf made off to a safe distance, and then said in a much injured tone:
"You have no right to take my property like that!"
The Lion looked back, but as the Wolf was too far away to be taught a lesson without too much inconvenience, he said:
"Your property? Did you buy it, or did the Shepherd make you a gift of it? Pray tell me, how did you get it?"
_What is evil won is evil lost._
translated_paragraphs: 狼偷来一只小羊，正要叼回窝里吃掉。迎面遇上一头狮子，事情就跟他原先打算的大不一样了。狮子连个理由都没给，就把小羊从他嘴里夺走了。
狼撤到一个安全距离，才用好生委屈的口气说：
“你没权利这样拿走我的东西！”
狮子回过头。狼已经躲得太远，再跑去教训他一回，未免太费事，于是狮子说道：
“你的东西？你买下来的？还是牧羊人亲手送给你的？劳驾，告诉我，你是怎么弄到手的？”
以不正当的手段得来的，也会被不正当地夺走。

source_paragraphs: A Stag, drinking from a crystal spring, saw himself mirrored in the clear water. He greatly admired the graceful arch of his antlers, but he was very much ashamed of his spindling legs.
"How can it be," he sighed, "that I should be cursed with such legs when I have so magnificent a crown."

At that moment he scented a panther and in an instant was bounding away through the forest. But as he ran his wide-spreading antlers caught in the branches of the trees, and soon the Panther overtook him. Then the Stag perceived that the legs of which he was so ashamed would have saved him had it not been for the useless ornaments on his head.
_We often make much of the ornamental and despise the useful._
translated_paragraphs: 雄鹿到一泓晶亮的泉水边饮水，看见清水中映出了自己的模样。他非常欣赏那副弯曲得漂亮的鹿角，看见细瘦的腿，却害臊起来。
“我头上戴着这样堂皇的一顶王冠，”他叹道，“怎么偏偏摊上了这么几条难看的腿？”
恰在这时，他嗅到一只豹的气息，转瞬间便腾跃着往林子里逃。可是跑着跑着，那对向两边张开的鹿角被树枝绊住。豹很快追上了他。雄鹿这才明白，要不是头上这副不顶用的摆设，自己最瞧不上的那几条腿原本是能救他一命的。
我们常常看重装饰，轻看真正管用的东西。

source_paragraphs: The Peacock, they say, did not at first have the beautiful feathers in which he now takes so much pride. These, Juno, whose favorite he was, granted to him one day when he begged her for a train of feathers to distinguish him from the other birds. Then, decked in his finery, gleaming with emerald, gold, purple, and azure, he strutted proudly among the birds. All regarded him with envy. Even the most beautiful pheasant could see that his beauty was surpassed.

Presently the Peacock saw an Eagle soaring high up in the blue sky and felt a desire to fly, as he had been accustomed to do. Lifting his wings he tried to rise from the ground. But the weight of his magnificent train held him down. Instead of flying up to greet the first rays of the morning sun or to bathe in the rosy light among the floating clouds at sunset, he would have to walk the ground more encumbered and oppressed than any common barnyard fowl.
_Do not sacrifice your freedom for the sake of pomp and show._
translated_paragraphs: 据说，孔雀起初并没有如今这身引以为傲的美丽羽毛。有一天，他求女神朱诺赐他一袭长尾，好跟别的鸟儿区别开来。女神偏爱他，便答应了。从此，他披一身华服，闪着翡翠、金黄、紫色和蔚蓝的光彩，在群鸟间昂首阔步。大家无不羡慕，就连最漂亮的野鸡，也看得出自己已经被他比了下去。
不久，孔雀望见一只鹰在碧空高处翱翔，也想像从前那样飞一飞。他扬起翅膀，要从地上腾起，可那条华丽的长尾重得把他拴在了地上。他再也不能飞起来迎接清晨的第一缕阳光，不能在暮色浮云间沐浴玫瑰色的晚霞，只得在地上走着，比农家院里任何一只寻常家禽都要沉重、拘束。
别为了排场和炫耀，牺牲自己的自由。

source_paragraphs: The Weasels and the Mice were always up in arms against each other. In every battle the Weasels carried off the victory, as well as a large number of the Mice, which they ate for dinner next day. In despair the Mice called a council, and there it was decided that the Mouse army was always beaten because it had no leaders. So a large number of generals and commanders were appointed from among the most eminent Mice.

To distinguish themselves from the soldiers in the ranks, the new leaders proudly bound on their heads lofty crests and ornaments of feathers or straw. Then after long preparation of the Mouse army in all the arts of war, they sent a challenge to the Weasels.

The Weasels accepted the challenge with eagerness, for they were always ready for a fight when a meal was in sight. They immediately attacked the Mouse army in large numbers. Soon the Mouse line gave way before the attack and the whole army fled for cover. The privates easily slipped into their holes, but the Mouse leaders could not squeeze through the narrow openings because of their head-dresses. Not one escaped the teeth of the hungry Weasels.
_Greatness has its penalties._
translated_paragraphs: 黄鼠狼和老鼠总在打仗。场场都是黄鼠狼获胜，他们还会带走一大群老鼠，好充作第二天的饭食。老鼠们绝望地召开会议，最后认定鼠军总吃败仗，是因为没有带头的统帅。于是，他们在最出名的老鼠里挑了许多，委任为将军和指挥官。
新上任的首领为了显出与普通士兵的区别，都骄傲地在头上绑起高高的冠饰，有的插羽毛，有的插稻草。等全体鼠军长久地操练过各种战法，他们便向黄鼠狼下了战书。
黄鼠狼们兴致勃勃地应战了。只要眼看有一顿饭可吃，他们一向乐意打仗。大批黄鼠狼立刻扑向鼠军。很快，老鼠的战线撑不住了，全军四散奔逃。小兵们轻轻松松溜进洞去，鼠军首领却因为顶着头饰，挤不进那狭窄的洞口。饿着肚皮的黄鼠狼，一个首领都没放过。
显赫的地位，也有它的代价。

sections.title_en: THE WOLF AND THE LEAN DOG
source_paragraphs: A Wolf prowling near a village one evening met a Dog. It happened to be a very lean and bony Dog, and Master Wolf would have turned up his nose at such meager fare had he not been more hungry than usual. So he began to edge toward the Dog, while the Dog backed away.

"Let me remind your lordship," said the Dog, his words interrupted now and then as he dodged a snap of the Wolf's teeth, "how unpleasant it would be to eat me now. Look at my ribs. I am nothing but skin and bone. But let me tell you something in private. In a few days my master will give a wedding feast for his only daughter. You can guess how fine and fat I will grow on the scraps from the table. _Then_ is the time to eat me."
The Wolf could not help thinking how nice it would be to have a fine fat Dog to eat instead of the scrawny object before him. So he went away pulling in his belt and promising to return.
Some days later the Wolf came back for the promised feast. He found the Dog in his master's yard, and asked him to come out and be eaten.
"Sir," said the Dog, with a grin, "I shall be delighted to have you eat me. I'll be out as soon as the porter opens the door."
But the "porter" was a huge Dog whom the Wolf knew by painful experience to be very unkind toward wolves. So he decided not to wait and made off as fast as his legs could carry him.
_Do not depend on the promises of those whose interest it is to deceive you._
_Take what you can get when you can get it._
translated_paragraphs: 一天傍晚，狼在村子附近转悠，碰见一条狗。这狗实在瘦得够呛，一把骨头。要不是狼大爷今天比平常更饿，才瞧不上眼前这点寒酸的饭食呢。他朝狗一点一点挨过去，狗就一步一步往后退。
“大王，请容我提醒您一句，”狗一边说，一边得时不时躲一躲狼咬过来的牙，“这会儿吃我可真不划算。瞧我这排肋骨，我只剩下皮包骨啦。不过我悄悄告诉您一件事，过不了几天，主人要给独生女儿办喜宴。您不妨猜猜，桌上那么多剩下来的好东西，会把我养得多肥多壮。到那个时候，再来吃我才好。”
狼不由得想，把眼前这把干瘦的骨头换作一条肥嘟嘟的狗，那该多美呀。于是他紧了紧腰带，答应改日再来，转身走了。
过了几天，狼回来赴这场说好的盛宴。看见狗待在主人院里，他便请狗出来给自己吃。
“先生，”狗咧嘴笑道，“能让您吃我，我高兴极了。等守门人一开门，我马上出来。”
那位“守门人”却是一条大得惊人的狗。狼吃过他的苦头，深知他对狼向来很不客气。于是，狼决定不等了，拔腿就跑，有多快跑多快。
骗人能得利的人，他许下的诺言靠不住。
能拿到手的东西，趁拿得到的时候拿住。

source_paragraphs: A very young Fox, who had never before seen a Lion, happened to meet one in the forest. A single look was enough to send the Fox off at top speed for the nearest hiding place.

The second time the Fox saw the Lion he stopped behind a tree to look at him a moment before slinking away. But the third time, the Fox went boldly up to the Lion and, without turning a hair, said, "Hello, there, old top."
_Familiarity breeds contempt._
_Acquaintance with evil blinds us to its dangers._
translated_paragraphs: 一只很年轻的狐狸从来没见过狮子，有一回碰巧在树林里撞见一头。只看了一眼，狐狸就使足了劲，直奔最近的藏身处。
第二次看见狮子，狐狸先在一棵树后停了一阵，打量了他两眼，才悄悄溜走。可到了第三回，狐狸大模大样走到狮子跟前，面不改色地招呼：“哟，老兄，你好啊。”
过于熟悉，容易心生轻慢。
跟危险的事物处惯了，就容易看不见其中的凶险。

source_paragraphs: A Lion and an Ass agreed to go hunting together. In their search for game the hunters saw a number of Wild Goats run into a cave, and laid plans to catch them. The Ass was to go into the cave and drive the Goats out, while the Lion would stand at the entrance to strike them down.

The plan worked beautifully. The Ass made such a frightful din in the cave, kicking and braying with all his might, that the Goats came running out in a panic of fear, only to fall victim to the Lion.
The Ass came proudly out of the cave.
"Did you see how I made them run?" he said.
"Yes, indeed," answered the Lion, "and if I had not known you and your kind I should certainly have run, too."
_The loud-mouthed boaster does not impress nor frighten those who know him._
translated_paragraphs: 狮子和驴商量好一起去打猎。他们寻找猎物时，看见一群野山羊奔进一处山洞，就定下了捕羊的计策。驴进洞把山羊往外赶，狮子守在洞口，出来一只打倒一只。
计策十分奏效。驴在洞里拼尽全力又踢又叫，闹得可怕极了。山羊们吓得慌慌张张往外逃，结果一只只都落到了狮子爪下。
驴得意扬扬地走出洞来。
“看见我怎么把他们吓跑了吗？”他问。
“当然看见了，”狮子答道，“要不是我认得你，又晓得驴是怎么回事，连我也准得跑。”
大嗓门的吹牛者，既打动不了熟悉他的人，也吓不倒他们。

sections.title_en: THE DOG AND HIS MASTER'S DINNER
source_paragraphs: A Dog had learned to carry his master's dinner to him every day. He was very faithful to his duty, though the smell of the good things in the basket tempted him.
The Dogs in the neighborhood noticed him carrying the basket and soon discovered what was in it. They made several attempts to steal it from him. But he always guarded it faithfully.
Then one day all the Dogs in the neighborhood got together and met him on his way with the basket. The Dog tried to run away from them. But at last he stopped to argue.
That was his mistake. They soon made him feel so ridiculous that he dropped the basket and seized a large piece of roast meat intended for his master's dinner.
"Very well," he said, "you divide the rest."
_Do not stop to argue with temptation._
translated_paragraphs: 有条狗学会了每天给主人送饭。篮子里的好东西闻起来实在诱人，他却一直忠实地守着自己的差事。
附近的狗见他提着篮子来来往往，很快就弄明白里面装的是什么。他们好几回试图从他那里偷吃。可他每次都尽责地护住了篮子。
后来有一天，附近的狗全凑到一起，在他提篮送饭的路上堵住了他。他起先想从他们中间逃开，最后还是停住了，跟他们争起理来。
错就错在这里。没多久，那群狗就把他说得觉得自己好可笑。他放下篮子，一口叼起原本留给主人午饭吃的一大块烤肉。
“好吧，”他说，“剩下的归你们分。”
面对诱惑，别停下来同它争辩。

sections.title_en: THE VAIN JACKDAW AND HIS BORROWED FEATHERS
source_paragraphs: A Jackdaw chanced to fly over the garden of the King's palace. There he saw with much wonder and envy a flock of royal Peacocks in all the glory of their splendid plumage.

Now the black Jackdaw was not a very handsome bird, nor very refined in manner. Yet he imagined that all he needed to make himself fit for the society of the Peacocks was a dress like theirs. So he picked up some castoff feathers of the Peacocks and stuck them among his own black plumes.

Dressed in his borrowed finery he strutted loftily among the birds of his own kind. Then he flew down into the garden among the Peacocks. But they soon saw who he was. Angry at the cheat, they flew at him, plucking away the borrowed feathers and also some of his own.

The poor Jackdaw returned sadly to his former companions. There another unpleasant surprise awaited him. They had not forgotten his superior airs toward them, and, to punish him, they drove him away with a rain of pecks and jeers.
_Borrowed feathers do not make fine birds._
translated_paragraphs: 一只寒鸦偶然飞过王宫的花园，看见一群王家饲养的孔雀，那一身身绚丽的羽衣，叫他既惊叹又羡慕。
这只黑寒鸦长得谈不上好看，举止也算不上文雅。可是他总以为，自己要挤进孔雀的圈子，只差一身跟他们一样的衣裳。于是他捡来几根孔雀掉落的羽毛，插在自己的黑羽毛中间。
穿上借来的盛装，他先在同类当中昂着头走来走去，然后飞进花园，落在孔雀群里。可孔雀们很快就认出他是谁。他们恼怒他竟敢冒充孔雀，一齐扑过来，不但拔去了那些借来的羽毛，还顺便拔掉他自己身上的好几根。
可怜的寒鸦只得伤心地回到原先的伙伴中间。可这儿另有一件叫他意想不到的不愉快事在等着。他们可没忘记他先前那副高人一等的派头，为了惩罚他，又啄又嘲，把他从同伴中间赶走了。
借来的羽毛，装扮不出真正的美鸟。

source_paragraphs: It happened once upon a time that a certain Greek ship bound for Athens was wrecked off the coast close to Piraeus, the port of Athens. Had it not been for the Dolphins, who at that time were very friendly toward mankind and especially toward Athenians, all would have perished. But the Dolphins took the shipwrecked people on their backs and swam with them to shore.

Now it was the custom among the Greeks to take their pet monkeys and dogs with them whenever they went on a voyage. So when one of the Dolphins saw a Monkey struggling in the water, he thought it was a man, and made the Monkey climb up on his back. Then off he swam with him toward the shore.
The Monkey sat up, grave and dignified, on the Dolphin's back.
"You are a citizen of illustrious Athens, are you not?" asked the Dolphin politely.
"Yes," answered the Monkey, proudly. "My family is one of the noblest in the city."
"Indeed," said the Dolphin. "Then of course you often visit Piraeus."
"Yes, yes," replied the Monkey. "Indeed, I do. I am with him constantly. Piraeus is my very best friend."

This answer took the Dolphin by surprise, and, turning his head, he now saw what it was he was carrying. Without more ado, he dived and left the foolish Monkey to take care of himself, while he swam off in search of some human being to save.
_One falsehood leads to another._
translated_paragraphs: 从前有艘希腊船驶向雅典，在雅典的港口比雷埃夫斯附近触礁失事了。当时海豚和人类非常友好，尤其亲近雅典人。要不是有海豚帮忙，船上所有的人都会丧命。海豚让遇难的人骑到背上，驮着他们往岸边游去。
那时候，希腊人远航，总爱带上自己养的猴子和狗。有头海豚瞧见一只猴子在水里挣扎，以为也是个人，就叫猴子爬到自己背上，然后驮着他向岸边游去。
猴子在海豚背上坐得端端正正，神情好不庄重。
“您是赫赫有名的雅典城的公民，对吗？”海豚客气地问。
“是的，”猴子自豪地答道，“我的家族是城里最高贵的家族之一。”
“果然如此，”海豚说，“那您一定常去比雷埃夫斯吧。”
“是呀，是呀，”猴子答道，“当然常去。我跟他整天在一块儿。比雷埃夫斯是我最要好的朋友。”
这个回答让海豚大吃一惊。他一回头，方才看清自己驮的到底是什么。他二话不说，一头扎进水底，让傻猴子自己照顾自己。海豚游走了，去找真正需要援救的人。
撒了一个谎，就得再撒一个。

source_paragraphs: An Ass was feeding in a pasture near a wood when he saw a Wolf lurking in the shadows along the hedge. He easily guessed what the Wolf had in mind, and thought of a plan to save himself. So he pretended he was lame, and began to hobble painfully.
When the Wolf came up, he asked the Ass what had made him lame, and the Ass replied that he had stepped on a sharp thorn.
"Please pull it out," he pleaded, groaning as if in pain. "If you do not, it might stick in your throat when you eat me."

The Wolf saw the wisdom of the advice, for he wanted to enjoy his meal without any danger of choking. So the Ass lifted up his foot and the Wolf began to search very closely and carefully for the thorn.
Just then the Ass kicked out with all his might, tumbling the Wolf a dozen paces away. And while the Wolf was getting very slowly and painfully to his feet, the Ass galloped away in safety.
"Serves me right," growled the Wolf as he crept into the bushes. "I'm a butcher by trade, not a doctor."
_Stick to your trade._
translated_paragraphs: 驴正在林旁草场吃草，看见一头狼躲在树篱的阴影里。他不难猜到狼在打什么主意，便想了个自救的办法。他假装瘸了，一瘸一拐，走得很是痛苦。
狼一过来就问，驴怎么瘸成了这样。驴回答说，一脚踩中了一根尖刺。
“求你替我拔出来吧，”他哼哼着，像是疼得厉害，“你要是不拔，等你吃我的时候，那刺可能会卡在你喉咙里。”
狼觉得这个主意高明。他很想痛痛快快吃顿饭，又不想担被刺噎住的风险。于是驴抬起蹄子，狼凑得很近，认认真真地找起刺来。
就在这时，驴使出全身力气猛踢一脚，把狼踹出十来步远。狼疼得好半天才慢慢站起来，驴早已飞奔而去，脱离了险境。
“活该！”狼龇着牙往灌木丛里爬，“我干的本来是屠夫的行当，充什么大夫！”
守住自己的本行。

source_paragraphs: Once upon a time a Cat and a Monkey lived as pets in the same house. They were great friends and were constantly in all sorts of mischief together. What they seemed to think of more than anything else was to get something to eat, and it did not matter much to them how they got it.
One day they were sitting by the fire, watching some chestnuts roasting on the hearth. How to get them was the question.
"I would gladly get them," said the cunning Monkey, "but you are much more skillful at such things than I am. Pull them out and I'll divide them between us."

Pussy stretched out her paw very carefully, pushed aside some of the cinders, and drew back her paw very quickly. Then she tried it again, this time pulling a chestnut half out of the fire. A third time and she drew out the chestnut. This performance she went through several times, each time singeing her paw severely. As fast as she pulled the chestnuts out of the fire, the Monkey ate them up.

Now the master came in, and away scampered the rascals, Mistress Cat with a burnt paw and no chestnuts. From that time on, they say, she contented herself with mice and rats and had little to do with Sir Monkey.
_The flatterer seeks some benefit at your expense._
translated_paragraphs: 从前，猫和猴子同住一家，都是主人养的宠物。他俩很要好，总爱结伴惹出各种乱子。看来他们最惦记的是弄点好吃的，至于东西是怎么弄来的，两位全不在乎。
有一天，他们坐在炉火旁，看着炉膛里正在烤的几颗栗子。问题是，怎么才能拿出来呢？
“我倒很乐意去拿，”狡猾的猴子说，“可是这种事，你比我高明多了。你把它们扒出来，我来给咱俩分。”
猫儿小心翼翼地伸出爪子，把几块余烬拨到一边，赶快缩回爪子。她又试了一下，这回把一颗栗子从火里扒出一半。第三回，她总算扒出整颗栗子。她照样试了好几次，回回爪子都被烫得厉害。她从火里扒出一颗，猴子就吃掉一颗。
这会儿主人进来了，两个小坏蛋拔腿就逃。猫儿小姐烫坏一只爪，一颗栗子也没吃到。据说从那以后，她安下心来吃大老鼠和小耗子，不大再跟猴子先生往来了。
奉承你的人，常想让你付出代价，好叫他自己得利。

source_paragraphs: Some Dogs found the skin of a Lion and furiously began to tear it with their teeth. A Fox chanced to see them and laughed scornfully.
"If that Lion had been alive," he said, "it would have been a very different story. He would have made you feel how much sharper his claws are than your teeth."
_It is easy and also contemptible to kick a man that is down._
translated_paragraphs: 几条狗找到一张狮子皮，龇着牙凶狠狠地撕咬起来。狐狸恰好瞧见，不屑地笑了。
“那头狮子要是还活着，”他说，“可就完全是另一回事啦。他准会叫你们领教领教，他的爪子比你们的牙锋利多少。”
对倒下的人补上一脚，很容易，也很卑鄙。

source_paragraphs: Some hungry Dogs saw a number of hides at the bottom of a stream where the Tanner had put them to soak. A fine hide makes an excellent meal for a hungry Dog, but the water was deep and the Dogs could not reach the hides from the bank. So they held a council and decided that the very best thing to do was to drink up the river.

All fell to lapping up the water as fast as they could. But though they drank and drank until, one after another, all of them had burst with drinking, still, for all their effort, the water in the river remained as high as ever.
_Do not try to do impossible things._
translated_paragraphs: 几条饿狗望见溪底泡着好几张兽皮，是制革匠放在那里浸的。对饿狗来说，一张好皮就是一顿好饭。可是水深，狗站在岸边够不着。他们开了个会，决定最好的办法莫过于把这条河喝干。
所有的狗都伸出舌头，能舔多快就舔多快。他们喝了又喝，一条接着一条，肚皮全都撑破了。可下了那么大工夫，溪水还是跟先前一样高。
不要硬做办不到的事。

sections.title_en: THE RABBIT, THE WEASEL, AND THE CAT
source_paragraphs: A Rabbit left his home one day for a dinner of clover. But he forgot to latch the door of his house and while he was gone a Weasel walked in and calmly made himself at home. When the Rabbit returned, there was the Weasel's nose sticking out of the Rabbit's own doorway, sniffing the fine air.
The Rabbit was quite angry--for a Rabbit--, and requested the Weasel to move out. But the Weasel was perfectly content. He was settled down for good.
A wise old Cat heard the dispute and offered to settle it.
"Come close to me," said the Cat, "I am very deaf. Put your mouths close to my ears while you tell me the facts."
The unsuspecting pair did as they were told and in an instant the Cat had them both under her claws. No one could deny that the dispute had been definitely settled.
_The strong are apt to settle questions to their own advantage._
translated_paragraphs: 一天，兔子出门去吃一餐三叶草，却忘了闩上家门。趁他不在，黄鼠狼大摇大摆走进去，安安稳稳当成了自己的家。兔子回来，只见自家门洞里伸出黄鼠狼的鼻子，正闻着外头的好空气。
兔子很生气——就兔子的脾气而言，已经相当生气了——便请黄鼠狼立刻搬走。可黄鼠狼住得再称心不过了。他打定主意，要在这里住到底。
一只有见识的老猫听到了争执，自告奋勇替他们解决。
“凑到我跟前来，”猫说，“我的耳朵很背。你们把嘴贴近我的耳朵，好好说说事情的来龙去脉。”
两位毫不起疑，照着做了。转眼间，他们双双落在猫爪底下。这场争执算是彻底解决了，谁也没法否认这一点。
强者裁决争端，常会裁得对自己最有利。

source_paragraphs: A Bear roaming the woods in search of berries happened on a fallen tree in which a swarm of Bees had stored their honey. The Bear began to nose around the log very carefully to find out if the Bees were at home. Just then one of the swarm came home from the clover field with a load of sweets. Guessing what the Bear was after, the Bee flew at him, stung him sharply and then disappeared into the hollow log.

The Bear lost his temper in an instant, and sprang upon the log tooth and claw, to destroy the nest. But this only brought out the whole swarm. The poor Bear had to take to his heels, and he was able to save himself only by diving into a pool of water.
_It is wiser to bear a single injury in silence than to provoke a thousand by flying into a rage._
translated_paragraphs: 熊在林中转悠，想找几颗浆果吃，偶然发现一棵倒树，树干里存着一群蜜蜂酿的蜜。熊小心翼翼地围着树干东嗅西嗅，想弄清蜜蜂在不在家。恰巧一只蜜蜂采足了花蜜，从三叶草地飞回来。他猜到熊在找什么，扑过去狠狠蜇了熊一下，随即消失在空树干里。
熊当即大发脾气，对着树干又撕又咬，非要捣毁蜂窝不可。这样一来，蜂群整个儿涌了出来。可怜的熊只得拔腿就逃，最后一头扎进池水里，才保住了命。
挨了一下，安静地忍过去，比大发雷霆招来一千下更明智。

source_paragraphs: A Fox and a Leopard, resting lazily after a generous dinner, amused themselves by disputing about their good looks. The Leopard was very proud of his glossy, spotted coat and made disdainful remarks about the Fox, whose appearance he declared was quite ordinary.
