The Fox prided himself on his fine bushy tail with its tip of white, but he was wise enough to see that he could not rival the Leopard in looks. Still he kept up a flow of sarcastic talk, just to exercise his wits and to have the fun of disputing. The Leopard was about to lose his temper when the Fox got up, yawning lazily.

"You may have a very smart coat," he said, "but you would be a great deal better off if you had a little more smartness inside your head and less on your ribs, the way I am. That's what I call real beauty."
_A fine coat is not always an indication of an attractive mind._
translated_paragraphs: 狐狸和豹子吃罢一顿丰盛的饭，懒洋洋地歇着，闲来争论谁长得好看，权当消遣。豹子对自己那身油亮的斑点外套十分自豪，把狐狸奚落了一番，说他不过是寻寻常常的长相。
狐狸一向对自己的蓬松大尾巴和雪白的尾巴尖很自豪，不过他很聪明，看得出要比外貌，自己赢不了豹子。可他还是满口俏皮的挖苦话，接连不断，既想练练脑筋，也想享受斗嘴的趣味。豹子眼看要发火，狐狸才懒懒地打着呵欠站起来。
“你那身外套，的确神气，”他说，“可要是你像我一样，把身上的神气减一点，把脑袋里的灵气加一点，你的境况会好得多。我管那叫真正的美。”
好看的外衣，未必藏着有趣的头脑。

source_paragraphs: A Heron was walking sedately along the bank of a stream, his eyes on the clear water, and his long neck and pointed bill ready to snap up a likely morsel for his breakfast. The clear water swarmed with fish, but Master Heron was hard to please that morning.
"No small fry for me," he said. "Such scanty fare is not fit for a Heron."
Now a fine young Perch swam near.
"No indeed," said the Heron. "I wouldn't even trouble to open my beak for anything like that!"

As the sun rose, the fish left the shallow water near the shore and swam below into the cool depths toward the middle. The Heron saw no more fish, and very glad was he at last to breakfast on a tiny Snail.
_Do not be too hard to suit or you may have to be content with the worst or with nothing at all._
translated_paragraphs: 一只苍鹭沿着溪岸迈着从容的步子，眼睛盯住清水，伸着长脖子和尖嘴，随时准备叼起一份称心的早餐。清水里鱼群游来游去，可这天早上，苍鹭先生格外难伺候。
“小鱼苗我可不要，”他说，“这点寒酸的食物，哪配给苍鹭吃。”
这时，一尾漂亮的小鲈鱼游到了近旁。
“不，才不要，”苍鹭说，“为了那样的东西，我连嘴都懒得张！”
太阳升高了，鱼离开岸边的浅水，往河中央凉爽的深处游去。苍鹭再也看不见一条鱼。到最后，能拿一只细小的水蜗牛当早餐，他已经高兴得很了。
别挑剔过头，否则只能将就最差的，或是什么也落不着。

source_paragraphs: One bright evening as the sun was sinking on a glorious world a wise old Cock flew into a tree to roost. Before he composed himself to rest, he flapped his wings three times and crowed loudly. But just as he was about to put his head under his wing, his beady eyes caught a flash of red and a glimpse of a long pointed nose, and there just below him stood Master Fox.
"Have you heard the wonderful news?" cried the Fox in a very joyful and excited manner.
"What news?" asked the Cock very calmly. But he had a queer, fluttery feeling inside him, for, you know, he was very much afraid of the Fox.

"Your family and mine and all other animals have agreed to forget their differences and live in peace and friendship from now on forever. Just think of it! I simply cannot wait to embrace you! Do come down, dear friend, and let us celebrate the joyful event."
"How grand!" said the Cock. "I certainly am delighted at the news." But he spoke in an absent way, and stretching up on tiptoes, seemed to be looking at something afar off.
"What is it you see?" asked the Fox a little anxiously.
"Why, it looks to me like a couple of Dogs coming this way. They must have heard the good news and--"
But the Fox did not wait to hear more. Off he started on a run.
"Wait," cried the Cock. "Why do you run? The Dogs are friends of yours now!"
"Yes," answered the Fox. "But they might not have heard the news. Besides, I have a very important errand that I had almost forgotten about."
The Cock smiled as he buried his head in his feathers and went to sleep, for he had succeeded in outwitting a very crafty enemy.
_The trickster is easily tricked._
translated_paragraphs: 一个晴朗的傍晚，夕阳正照着美丽的大地。一只聪明的老公鸡飞到树上准备过夜。他先拍了三下翅膀，扯开嗓子啼了一声，才打算把头埋进翅膀里。这时，那双珠子般的眼睛忽然瞥见一道红影，又瞥见一个又长又尖的鼻头。狐狸先生就站在他身子正下方。
“你听到那个了不得的好消息了吗？”狐狸喊道，显得欢喜又激动。
“什么消息？”公鸡十分平静地问。其实他心里有点七上八下，要知道，他怕狐狸怕得厉害。
“你们一家和我们一家，还有其他所有动物，都已经同意把分歧一笔勾销，从此和和气气，永远做朋友。你想想看！我恨不得立刻拥抱你！下来吧，好朋友，咱们一起庆祝这件大喜事。”
“太好啦！”公鸡说，“这消息可真叫我高兴。”可是他说得有点心不在焉，又踮起脚尖，伸长脖子，仿佛在望远处什么东西。
“你看见什么了？”狐狸有点不安地问。
“哎，我看着像两条狗，正往这边过来呢。他们一定也听见了好消息，所以——”
狐狸没等他说完，早跑开了。
“等等，”公鸡高喊，“你跑什么？狗如今也是你的朋友啦！”
“是啊，”狐狸答道，“不过，他们没准还没听见这消息呢。再说，我差点忘了，我还有件很要紧的差事要办。”
公鸡微微一笑，把脑袋埋进羽毛，安心睡去。他已经用计胜过了一个十分狡猾的敌人。
爱耍花招的人，也容易中了旁人的花招。

source_paragraphs: A Dog asleep in a manger filled with hay, was awakened by the Cattle, which came in tired and hungry from working in the field. But the Dog would not let them get near the manger, and snarled and snapped as if it were filled with the best of meat and bones, all for himself.
The Cattle looked at the Dog in disgust. "How selfish he is!" said one. "He cannot eat the hay and yet he will not let us eat it who are so hungry for it!"
Now the farmer came in. When he saw how the Dog was acting, he seized a stick and drove him out of the stable with many a blow for his selfish behavior.
_Do not grudge others what you cannot enjoy yourself._
translated_paragraphs: 一条狗睡在装满干草的饲料槽里。几头牛在田里干活归来，又饿又累，惊醒了他。狗硬不让牛靠近，一边低吼一边乱咬，好像那槽里装的全是最好的肉和骨头，样样都归他似的。
牛们厌恶地看着狗。“多自私呀！”一头牛说，“干草他自己又吃不了，偏不让我们这些饿得想吃草的来吃！”
这时农夫进来了。看见狗这副做派，就抓起一根棍子，一连打了他好几下，为他这自私的举动把他赶出了牲口棚。
自己享用不了的东西，别眼红他人享用。

source_paragraphs: A hungry Wolf spied a Goat browsing at the top of a steep cliff where he could not possibly get at her.

"That is a very dangerous place for you," he called out, pretending to be very anxious about the Goat's safety. "What if you should fall! Please listen to me and come down! Here you can get all you want of the finest, tenderest grass in the country."
The Goat looked over the edge of the cliff.
"How very, very anxious you are about me," she said, "and how generous you are with your grass! But I know you! It's your _own_ appetite you are thinking of, not mine!"
_An invitation prompted by selfishness is not to be accepted._
translated_paragraphs: 一头饿狼瞧见一只山羊在陡崖顶端吃草。她待在那里，他怎么也够不到。
“你那个地方太危险了，”他大声喊道，装作十分挂念山羊的安危，“要是摔下来可怎么办！听我一句劝，请下来吧！这边有这一带最嫩最好的草，要多少有多少。”
山羊从悬崖边探出头来。
“你还真是十分、十分地挂念我呀，”她说，“对你的青草又真慷慨！可是我认得你！你挂念的是你自己的胃口，才不是我的呢！”
一心为自己打算的人发出的邀请，不该接受。

source_paragraphs: One day as an Ass was walking in the pasture, he found some Grasshoppers chirping merrily in a grassy corner of the field.
He listened with a great deal of admiration to the song of the Grasshoppers. It was such a joyful song that his pleasure-loving heart was filled with a wish to sing as they did.
"What is it?" he asked very respectfully, "that has given you such beautiful voices? Is there any special food you eat, or is it some divine nectar that makes you sing so wonderfully?"
"Yes," said the Grasshoppers, who were very fond of a joke; "it is the dew we drink! Try some and see."
So thereafter the Ass would eat nothing and drink nothing but dew.
Naturally, the poor foolish Ass soon died.
_The laws of nature are unchangeable._
translated_paragraphs: 一天，驴走过草场，在田角一块青草丛里，发现几只蚂蚱正欢快地唧唧歌唱。
他满心赞叹地听着蚂蚱们的歌。那歌声那样快活，听得他那颗爱乐子的心只想做一件事：像他们一样唱歌。
“请问，”他十分恭敬地问，“是什么给了你们这样美妙的嗓子？是你们吃了哪样特别的食物，还是喝过天上的琼浆，才唱得这么动听？”
“正是，”爱开玩笑的蚂蚱们说，“秘诀就在我们喝的露水里！你也尝尝看。”
从此，除了露水，那头驴什么也不肯吃，什么也不肯喝。
可想而知，这头可怜的傻驴没多久就死了。
自然的规律改不了。

source_paragraphs: A Mule had had a long rest and much good feeding. He was feeling very vigorous indeed, and pranced around loftily, holding his head high.
"My father certainly was a full-blooded racer," he said. "I can feel that distinctly."
Next day he was put into harness again and that evening he was very downhearted indeed.
"I was mistaken," he said. "My father was an Ass after all."
_Be sure of your pedigree before you boast of it._
translated_paragraphs: 骡子歇了好长一阵子，好饲料也吃得足足的。这会儿他觉得浑身力气使不完，昂着头，神气活现地踢踏跳步。
“我爸爸准是匹纯种赛马，”他说，“我可是感觉得一清二楚。”
第二天，他又被套上挽具去干活。到那天晚上，他委实有些垂头丧气。
“我弄错啦，”他说，“我爸爸说到底还是一头驴。”
夸耀家世之前，先把来历弄明白。

source_paragraphs: A Fox fell into a well, and though it was not very deep, he found that he could not get out again. After he had been in the well a long time, a thirsty Goat came by. The Goat thought the Fox had gone down to drink, and so he asked if the water was good.
"The finest in the whole country," said the crafty Fox, "jump in and try it. There is more than enough for both of us."
The thirsty Goat immediately jumped in and began to drink. The Fox just as quickly jumped on the Goat's back and leaped from the tip of the Goat's horns out of the well.
The foolish Goat now saw what a plight he had got into, and begged the Fox to help him out. But the Fox was already on his way to the woods.
"If you had as much sense as you have beard, old fellow," he said as he ran, "you would have been more cautious about finding a way to get out again before you jumped in."
_Look before you leap._
translated_paragraphs: 狐狸掉进一口井里。井虽说不算很深，他却发现自己爬不出去。他在里面待了好久，才碰见一只口渴的山羊路过。山羊以为狐狸主动下井喝水，就问水好不好喝。
“走遍全国，你也找不出比这更好的水！”狡猾的狐狸说，“跳下来尝尝。咱俩喝都绰绰有余。”
口渴的山羊立即跳进井里，喝了起来。狐狸也同样麻利地蹿上山羊背，踩着山羊的角尖，一跃跳出了井。
傻山羊这才明白自己落到了什么境地，央求狐狸帮他出去。狐狸却已经动身往林子里去了。
“老兄，你脑子里的见识要是有下巴上的胡子那么多，”他一边跑一边说，“起跳之前，总该多留个心，先找好能爬出去的路。”
往下跳之前，先看清楚。

sections.title_en: THE CAT, THE COCK, AND THE YOUNG MOUSE
source_paragraphs: A very young Mouse, who had never seen anything of the world, almost came to grief the very first time he ventured out. And this is the story he told his mother about his adventures.

"I was strolling along very peaceably when, just as I turned the corner into the next yard, I saw two strange creatures. One of them had a very kind and gracious look, but the other was the most fearful monster you can imagine. You should have seen him.

"On top of his head and in front of his neck hung pieces of raw red meat. He walked about restlessly, tearing up the ground with his toes, and beating his arms savagely against his sides. The moment he caught sight of me he opened his pointed mouth as if to swallow me, and then he let out a piercing roar that frightened me almost to death."
Can you guess who it was that our young Mouse was trying to describe to his mother? It was nobody but the Barnyard Cock and the first one the little Mouse had ever seen.

"If it had not been for that terrible monster," the Mouse went on, "I should have made the acquaintance of the pretty creature, who looked so good and gentle. He had thick, velvety fur, a meek face, and a look that was very modest, though his eyes were bright and shining. As he looked at me he waved his fine long tail and smiled.
"I am sure he was just about to speak to me when the monster I have told you about let out a screaming yell, and I ran for my life."

"My son," said the Mother Mouse, "that gentle creature you saw was none other than the Cat. Under his kindly appearance, he bears a grudge against every one of us. The other was nothing but a bird who wouldn't harm you in the least. As for the Cat, he eats us. So be thankful, my child, that you escaped with your life, and, as long as you live, never judge people by their looks."
_Do not trust alone to outward appearances._
translated_paragraphs: 有只极小极小的老鼠，从来没出门见过世面。头一回冒险出门，就差点出事。这是他回家告诉妈妈的历险经过。
“我本来在安安静静地散步。刚绕过拐角进了隔壁的院子，就见到两只奇怪的动物。一只看上去温和亲切，另一只呢，是你能想到的最可怕的怪物。你要是能看看他的样子就好了。
“他头顶上和脖子前头，挂着好几块生生的红肉。他走来走去总不安分，用脚趾把地面刨得乱七八糟，还挥动两条胳膊，凶猛地拍打两边身子。他一看见我就张开尖尖的嘴，像要把我吞下去似的，接着发出一声尖利的怒吼，差点儿把我吓死。”
你猜，小老鼠费了这么大劲想讲给妈妈听的究竟是谁？不过是农家院里的一只公鸡，恰好是小老鼠有生以来看见的第一只。
“要不是那个可怕的怪物，”老鼠接着说，“我准能跟那个漂亮的家伙交上朋友。他看起来善良又温柔，长着厚厚的绒毛，像天鹅绒一样，一副驯服的面孔。眼睛虽然又亮又闪，看我的神情却腼腆极了。他对我摇摇那条漂亮的长尾巴，还微笑呢。
“他准是正要开口跟我说话。偏在这时候，刚才说的那只怪物尖叫一声，吓得我只顾逃命。”
“我的孩子，”鼠妈妈说，“你见到的那个温顺家伙，正是猫啊。别看他模样和善，他对咱们个个都不安好心。另一位倒只是一只鸟，半点也不会伤害你。可是猫要吃我们。孩子呀，庆幸你能活着回来吧。只要你还活在世上，就千万别凭模样判断人。”
光看外表，是靠不住的。

source_paragraphs: A Wolf had been prowling around a flock of Sheep for a long time, and the Shepherd watched very anxiously to prevent him from carrying off a Lamb. But the Wolf did not try to do any harm. Instead he seemed to be helping the Shepherd take care of the Sheep. At last the Shepherd got so used to seeing the Wolf about that he forgot how wicked he could be.

One day he even went so far as to leave his flock in the Wolf's care while he went on an errand. But when he came back and saw how many of the flock had been killed and carried off, he knew how foolish to trust a Wolf.
_Once a wolf, always a wolf._
translated_paragraphs: 有只狼在羊群附近徘徊好久了。牧人戒备地盯着他，唯恐他叼走一只羊羔。可狼一次也没加害羊群。相反，他看起来倒像在帮牧人照看羊。到头来，牧人经常见到狼在旁边，见惯了，就把狼能有多坏给忘了。
有一天，他甚至放心把羊群交给狼看守，自己出门办事去了。等他回来，看见那么多羊被咬死拖走，这才明白相信一只狼是多么愚蠢。
狼终究是狼。

source_paragraphs: A Peacock, puffed up with vanity, met a Crane one day, and to impress him spread his gorgeous tail in the Sun.
"Look," he said. "What have you to compare with this? I am dressed in all the glory of the rainbow, while your feathers are gray as dust!"
The Crane spread his broad wings and flew up toward the sun.
"Follow me if you can," he said. But the Peacock stood where he was among the birds of the barnyard, while the Crane soared in freedom far up into the blue sky.
_The useful is of much more importance and value, than the ornamental._
translated_paragraphs: 有一天，自命不凡的孔雀遇见了鹤。他想在鹤面前显一显，就迎着日光打开那面华丽的尾屏。
“瞧！”他说，“你有什么能跟这个比？我身上穿着彩虹的全部光彩，你那层羽毛呢，灰得像尘土！”
鹤舒展开宽大的双翅，迎着太阳向高处飞去。
“你要是能，就跟我来吧。”他说。孔雀依然留在原地，站在农家院的一群家禽当中。鹤却越飞越高，向遥远的蓝天自在翱翔而去。
真正有用的东西，远比纯作装饰的东西重要，也更有价值。

source_paragraphs: Some Cranes saw a farmer plowing a large field. When the work of plowing was done, they patiently watched him sow the seed. It was their feast, they thought.
So, as soon as the Farmer had finished planting and had gone home, down they flew to the field, and began to eat as fast as they could.

The Farmer, of course, knew the Cranes and their ways. He had had experience with such birds before. He soon returned to the field with a sling. But he did not bring any stones with him. He expected to scare the Cranes just by swinging the sling in the air, and shouting loudly at them.

At first the Cranes flew away in great terror. But they soon began to see that none of them ever got hurt. They did not even hear the noise of stones whizzing through the air, and as for words, they would kill nobody. At last they paid no attention whatever to the Farmer.

The Farmer saw that he would have to take other measures. He wanted to save at least some of his grain. So he loaded his sling with stones and killed several of the Cranes. This had the effect the Farmer wanted, for from that day the Cranes visited his field no more.
_Bluff and threatening words are of little value with rascals._
_Bluff is no proof that hard fists are lacking._
translated_paragraphs: 几只鹤看见农夫正在翻耕一大片田地。他耕完，鹤便耐心地看着他播种。它们心里想，这是在给我们预备宴席呢。
所以农夫种完地刚一回家，它们便飞落田间，尽可能快地啄起种子来。
农夫当然认得鹤，也知道它们的习性。以前他就跟这种鸟打过交道。很快，他拿了投石索回到地里，可他一块石子也没带，只盼着在空中把投石索抡得呼呼转，再高声吆喝，就能把鹤吓走。
开头鹤群很害怕，纷纷逃走。不过没多久，它们就发觉，大家一次也没受过伤，连石子嗖嗖飞过的声音也没听到。至于喝骂嘛，那可打不死人。到后来，它们根本不把农夫当回事了。
农夫明白，得想个别的办法了，好歹也要保住几把谷种。他在投石索里装进石子，打死了好几只鹤。这才起了他想要的效果。从那天起，鹤群再没光顾过他的田。
遇上无赖，光靠虚张声势、出言恫吓，没多少用处。
可是一个人先前虚张声势，也不能证明他的拳头真的不硬。

source_paragraphs: A rich old farmer, who felt that he had not many more days to live, called his sons to his bedside.

"My sons," he said, "heed what I have to say to you. Do not on any account part with the estate that has belonged to our family for so many generations. Somewhere on it is hidden a rich treasure. I do not know the exact spot, but it is there, and you will surely find it. Spare no energy and leave no spot unturned in your search."

The father died, and no sooner was he in his grave than the sons set to work digging with all their might, turning up every foot of ground with their spades, and going over the whole farm two or three times.

No hidden gold did they find; but at harvest time when they had settled their accounts and had pocketed a rich profit far greater than that of any of their neighbors, they understood that the treasure their father had told them about was the wealth of a bountiful crop, and that in their industry had they found the treasure.
_Industry is itself a treasure._
translated_paragraphs: 有个富裕的老农，感觉自己活不了多少日子了，就把儿子们喊到床前。
“孩子们，”他说，“把我的话记在心里。不论什么缘故，也不要把咱家世世代代传下来的土地卖掉。那里有个地方，埋藏着一份厚实的宝贝。我说不出确切的地点，可它就在那里，你们一定能找到。找的时候别吝惜力气，一寸土地也别放过。”
父亲死了。等他一入土，儿子们便动手拼命挖掘。每一尺地都用铁锹翻过了，整座农场从头到尾，翻了两三遍。
他们没找到什么埋藏的金子，可到了收获季节，等他们算清了账，把远远超过所有邻居的一大笔进项装进口袋，终于明白过来，父亲告诉他们的宝贝，就是丰收所得的财富。他们从自己的勤劳中，找到了那份宝贝。
勤劳本身就是一份宝藏。

source_paragraphs: Two Pots, one of brass and the other of clay, stood together on the hearthstone. One day the Brass Pot proposed to the Earthen Pot that they go out into the world together. But the Earthen Pot excused himself, saying that it would be wiser for him to stay in the corner by the fire.
"It would take so little to break me," he said. "You know how fragile I am. The least shock is sure to shatter me!"
"Don't let that keep you at home," urged the Brass Pot. "I shall take very good care of you. If we should happen to meet anything hard I will step between and save you."
So the Earthen Pot at last consented, and the two set out side by side, jolting along on three stubby legs first to this side, then to that, and bumping into each other at every step.
The Earthen Pot could not survive that sort of companionship very long. They had not gone ten paces before the Earthen Pot cracked, and at the next jolt he flew into a thousand pieces.
_Equals make the best friends._
translated_paragraphs: 炉床上并排站着两只罐子，一只黄铜打成，另一只用泥烧成。一天，铜罐提议和陶罐一块儿出门闯天下。陶罐婉言谢绝，说自己还是留在炉火旁的角落里更妥当。
“稍不小心我就会碎的，”他说，“你知道我有多脆，只消轻轻一撞，我准会裂开！”
“别为这点儿事留在家里，”铜罐劝道，“我会好好照顾你的。万一遇到硬东西，我就上前挡在中间，保准让你平安无事。”
陶罐终于答应了。两只罐子肩并肩出发，分别挪动三条又粗又短的腿，一会儿颠向这边，一会儿晃向那边，走一步，两只就撞一下。
这样的伙伴关系，陶罐哪能维持多久？十步还没走到，罐上就裂开了一条缝，再一颠，他摔成了千百个碎片。
彼此相当的人，最适合做朋友。

sections.title_en: THE GOOSE AND THE GOLDEN EGG
source_paragraphs: There was once a Countryman who possessed the most wonderful Goose you can imagine, for every day when he visited the nest, the Goose had laid a beautiful, glittering, golden egg.

The Countryman took the eggs to market and soon began to get rich. But it was not long before he grew impatient with the Goose because she gave him only a single golden egg a day. He was not getting rich fast enough.

Then one day, after he had finished counting his money, the idea came to him that he could get all the golden eggs at once by killing the Goose and cutting it open. But when the deed was done, not a single golden egg did he find, and his precious Goose was dead.
_Those who have plenty want more and so lose all they have._
translated_paragraphs: 从前有个乡下人，养着一只你能想象到的最神奇的鹅。每天去窝里看时，那里总有一枚新下的金蛋，漂亮，耀眼，闪闪发光。
乡下人把金蛋拿去集市，不久就富了起来。可是没过多久，他对鹅渐渐不耐烦起来，因为鹅一天只给他下一个金蛋。他嫌自己发财发得太慢了。
一天，数完了钱，他想到，只要把鹅杀了，剖开肚皮，就能一次把所有金蛋全都拿到。可是事情做完了，他连一个金蛋也没找到，宝贵的鹅也死了。
已经有了许多，还一味贪图更多，到头来连原有的也会失去。

sections.title_en: THE FIGHTING BULLS AND THE FROG
source_paragraphs: Two Bulls were fighting furiously in a field, at one side of which was a marsh. An old Frog living in the marsh, trembled as he watched the fierce battle.
"What are _you_ afraid of?" asked a young Frog.
"Do you not see," replied the old Frog, "that the Bull who is beaten, will be driven away from the good forage up there to the reeds of this marsh, and we shall all be trampled into the mud?"
It turned out as the Frog had said. The beaten Bull was driven to the marsh, where his great hoofs crushed the Frogs to death.
_When the great fall out, the weak must suffer for it._
translated_paragraphs: 两头公牛在田里凶狠地搏斗。田的一侧是片沼泽，住在那里的一只老青蛙望着这场恶斗，吓得直发抖。
“你怕什么？”一只小青蛙问。
“你没看出来吗？”老青蛙回答，“落败的公牛准要被赶出上面水草肥美的地方，到这片沼泽的芦苇里来。我们全要叫他踩进泥里了！”
事情果真像青蛙预料的那样。打输了的公牛被赶进沼泽，用大蹄子把青蛙们踩死了。
强者相争，往往要弱者受苦。

source_paragraphs: A little hungry Mouse found his way one day into a basket of corn. He had to squeeze himself a good deal to get through the narrow opening between the strips of the basket. But the corn was tempting and the Mouse was determined to get in. When at last he had succeeded, he gorged himself to bursting. Indeed he became about three times as big around the middle as he was when he went in.

At last he felt satisfied and dragged himself to the opening to get out again. But the best he could do was to get his head out. So there he sat groaning and moaning, both from the discomfort inside him and his anxiety to escape from the basket.
Just then a Weasel came by. He understood the situation quickly.

"My friend," he said, "I know what you've been doing. You've been stuffing. That's what you get. You will have to stay there till you feel just like you did when you went in. Good night, and good enough for you."
And that was all the sympathy the poor Mouse got.
_Greediness leads to misfortune._
translated_paragraphs: 一天，一只饥肠辘辘的小老鼠找到个办法，能钻进一篮谷物。编篮子的篾条之间空隙狭小，他须把身子挤了又挤，才钻得进去。可那谷物实在诱人，老鼠铁了心要进去。他最后终于成功，便放开肚皮猛吃，一直撑得快要爆开。其实他的腰围足有进去时的三倍粗了。
终于吃够了，他拖着身子来到原先的洞缝，想从那儿出去。他用尽力气也只钻得出一个脑袋。于是他坐在那里，哼哼唧唧，一半因为肚里撑得难受，一半因为急着逃出篮子。
恰巧一只黄鼠狼从旁经过，一眼就把情形看明白了。
“朋友，”他说，“我知道你干了什么。你光顾着往肚子里塞，这就是你的下场。你只好老老实实待着，等肚子瘪得和进来时一样再说。晚安，你这也算自找的。”
可怜的老鼠得到的同情，一共就这么多。
贪吃会招来不幸。

source_paragraphs: A Farmer walked through his field one cold winter morning. On the ground lay a Snake, stiff and frozen with the cold. The Farmer knew how deadly the Snake could be, and yet he picked it up and put it in his bosom to warm it back to life.

The Snake soon revived, and when it had enough strength, bit the man who had been so kind to it. The bite was deadly and the Farmer felt that he must die. As he drew his last breath, he said to those standing around:
_Learn from my fate not to take pity on a scoundrel._
translated_paragraphs: 一个寒冷的冬日早晨，农夫走过自家的田地。地上躺着一条蛇，冻得僵硬，一动不动。农夫知道这蛇要起人命来有多厉害，还是把它拾了起来，放在怀里，想把它暖活过来。
蛇很快苏醒了。它刚有了足够的力气，就咬了这个好心待它的人。这一口是致命的，农夫知道自己要死了。咽下最后一口气时，他对围在身旁的人说：
“请记取我的下场，别去怜惜恶棍。”

source_paragraphs: A Stag had fallen sick. He had just strength enough to gather some food and find a quiet clearing in the woods, where he lay down to wait until his strength should return. The Animals heard about the Stag's illness and came to ask after his health. Of course, they were all hungry, and helped themselves freely to the Stag's food; and as you would expect, the Stag soon starved to death.
_Good will is worth nothing unless it is accompanied by good acts._
translated_paragraphs: 一只雄鹿生病了。他仅剩的力气，只够搜集一点食物，在林子里寻得一块僻静的空地，躺在那里等体力慢慢恢复。动物们听说雄鹿病了，纷纷前来探问他的病情。当然，它们个个都饿着肚子，便毫不见外地吃起雄鹿的口粮。接下来的事，你准猜到了，雄鹿不久就饿死了。
好意若没有善行来相配，也就值不了什么。

sections.title_en: THE GOATHERD AND THE WILD GOATS
source_paragraphs: One cold stormy day a Goatherd drove his Goats for shelter into a cave, where a number of Wild Goats had also found their way. The Shepherd wanted to make the Wild Goats part of his flock; so he fed them well. But to his own flock, he gave only just enough food to keep them alive. When the weather cleared, and the Shepherd led the Goats out to feed, the Wild Goats scampered off to the hills.
"Is that the thanks I get for feeding you and treating you so well?" complained the Shepherd.
"Do not expect us to join your flock," replied one of the Wild Goats. "We know how you would treat us later on, if some strangers should come as we did."
_It is unwise to treat old friends badly for the sake of new ones._
translated_paragraphs: 一个风雨交加的寒冷日子，牧羊人赶着山羊进山洞躲避，洞里也来了一群野山羊。牧羊人希望它们加入自己的羊群，便给它们好吃好喝，对自己养的山羊却只给那么一点点食物，勉强够活命。天放晴，他把山羊赶出去吃草，野山羊们撒开蹄子，朝山里跑去了。
“我喂饱了你们，又对你们这么好，你们就这样谢我？”牧羊人抱怨。
“别指望我们加入你的羊群，”一只野山羊答道，“等以后又有陌生的客人像我们一样上门，你会怎么对待我们，我们已经知道啦。”
为讨新朋友欢心而亏待老朋友，不是明智的做法。

source_paragraphs: A young fellow, who was very popular among his boon companions as a good spender, quickly wasted his fortune trying to live up to his reputation. Then one fine day in early spring he found himself with not a penny left, and no property save the clothes he wore.

He was to meet some jolly young men that morning, and he was at his wits' end how to get enough money to keep up appearances. Just then a Swallow flew by, twittering merrily, and the young man, thinking summer had come, hastened off to a clothes dealer, to whom he sold all the clothes he wore down to his very tunic.

A few days later a change in weather brought a severe frost; and the poor swallow and that foolish young man in his light tunic, and with his arms and knees bare, could scarcely keep life in their shivering bodies.
_One swallow does not make a summer._
translated_paragraphs: 有个青年在一帮酒肉朋友里很受欢迎，只因花钱一向大方。他为保全这个名声，飞快地把家产挥霍一空。初春的一个晴天，他发现自己分文不剩，除了身上穿的衣服，一点儿东西也没有了。
那天早晨，他约好了要见几个爱玩乐的年轻人。上哪儿找钱维持体面呢？他愁得毫无办法。恰在此时，一只燕子吱吱啾啾，欢快地飞过。青年以为夏天已经来了，赶紧跑去找旧衣商，把身上能卖的衣服全卖了，只剩一件贴身短衣。
几天后天气突变，降了一场严霜。可怜的燕子，还有那个穿着单薄短衣、两臂和膝头全露在外头的糊涂青年，都冻得浑身发抖，几乎保不住性命。
飞来一只燕子，并不等于夏天到了。

source_paragraphs: A Cat was growing very thin. As you have guessed, he did not get enough to eat. One day he heard that some Birds in the neighborhood were ailing and needed a doctor. So he put on a pair of spectacles, and with a leather box in his hand, knocked at the door of the Bird's home.
The Birds peeped out, and Dr. Cat, with much solicitude, asked how they were. He would be very happy to give them some medicine.
"Tweet, tweet," laughed the Birds. "Very smart, aren't you? We are very well, thank you, and more so, if _you_ only keep away from here."
_Be wise and shun the quack._
translated_paragraphs: 一只猫日渐消瘦。你想得到，这是没吃饱。一天，他听说附近有几只鸟生了病，需要医生。于是他架上一副眼镜，手里提着一个皮箱，敲响了鸟儿的家门。
鸟儿偷偷往外瞧。这位猫大夫殷勤地打听他们的病情，表示自己很愿意给他们开点药。
“啾啾，啾啾，”鸟儿们笑道，“你真够机灵的呀！谢谢，我们身体好着呢。只要你离这地方远一点，我们还会更好。”
放聪明些，避开冒牌大夫。

source_paragraphs: There was once a Dog who was very fond of eggs. He visited the hen house very often and at last got so greedy that he would swallow the eggs whole.
One day the Dog wandered down to the seashore. There he spied an Oyster. In a twinkling the Oyster was resting in the Dog's stomach, shell and all.
It pained the Dog a good deal, as you can guess.
"I've learned that all round things are not eggs," he said groaning.
_Act in haste and repent at leisure--and often in pain._
translated_paragraphs: 从前有一条非常爱吃蛋的狗。他三天两头往鸡窝里跑，到后来越来越馋，捞到一只蛋，就整只往下吞。
有一天，狗一路溜达到海边，发现一只牡蛎。转眼之间，牡蛎已经进了狗肚子，连壳一起。
你想得到，那家伙可把狗硌得够痛。
“这回我知道啦，”他呻吟着说，“圆乎乎的东西，不见得个个都是蛋。”
做事太急，后悔起来时间却很长，而且常常还伴着疼痛。

source_paragraphs: A man who lived a long time ago believed that he could read the future in the stars. He called himself an Astrologer, and spent his time at night gazing at the sky.

One evening he was walking along the open road outside the village. His eyes were fixed on the stars. He thought he saw there that the end of the world was at hand, when all at once, down he went into a hole full of mud and water.
There he stood up to his ears, in the muddy water, and madly clawing at the slippery sides of the hole in his effort to climb out.
His cries for help soon brought the villagers running. As they pulled him out of the mud, one of them said:

"You pretend to read the future in the stars, and yet you fail to see what is at your feet! This may teach you to pay more attention to what is right in front of you, and let the future take care of itself."
"What use is it," said another, "to read the stars, when you can't see what's right here on the earth?"
_Take care of the little things and the big things will take care of themselves._
translated_paragraphs: 很久以前，有个人相信自己能从星星上读出未来。他自称占星人，整夜整夜抬头望天。
一天傍晚，他沿着村外的旷野大路散步，眼睛紧紧盯着星辰。他以为自己从中看见了世界末日将临的征兆。突然，扑通一声，他掉进了一个满是泥浆和水的坑。
他站在坑里，泥水一直淹到了耳朵，两只手发狂地抠着滑溜溜的坑壁，想爬上去。
村里人很快听见他的求救，跑来帮忙。一人边把他从泥里往外拉，边说：
“你号称能从星星里看出未来，却看不见就在脚下的东西！吃了这一回教训，往后多留心眼前，至于未来，让未来自己去操心吧。”
“眼前地上的东西你都看不见，”另一个人说，“读星星有什么用？”
把小事照顾好，大事自然会各得其所。

source_paragraphs: A Lion had been watching three Bullocks feeding in an open field. He had tried to attack them several times, but they had kept together, and helped each other to drive him off. The Lion had little hope of eating them, for he was no match for three strong Bullocks with their sharp horns and hoofs. But he could not keep away from that field, for it is hard to resist watching a good meal, even when there is little chance of getting it.

Then one day the Bullocks had a quarrel, and when the hungry Lion came to look at them and lick his chops as he was accustomed to do, he found them in separate corners of the field, as far away from one another as they could get.
It was now an easy matter for the Lion to attack them one at a time, and this he proceeded to do with the greatest satisfaction and relish.
_In unity is strength._
translated_paragraphs: 狮子一直在盯着三头在旷地里吃草的小公牛。他试过好几回，要扑过去袭击，可它们始终待在一起，互相帮忙，把他赶走。狮子已经不大指望能吃到它们，毕竟三头健壮公牛都有尖角和硬蹄，他不是它们的对手。可他又舍不得离开那片田。明明有顿好饭放在眼前，哪怕吃到的指望不大，也很难忍住不去看看。
后来有一天，小公牛们吵了一场。饥饿的狮子照例想来看两眼，舔舔嘴巴，这回却发现三头牛各站在田地一角，彼此能离多远就离多远。
现在，要把他们一头一头分开袭击，可就轻松多了。狮子立刻动手，吃得称心如意，津津有味。
合在一起，才有力量。

source_paragraphs: A poor Woodman was cutting down a tree near the edge of a deep pool in the forest. It was late in the day and the Woodman was tired. He had been working since sunrise and his strokes were not so sure as they had been early that morning. Thus it happened that the axe slipped and flew out of his hands into the pool.

The Woodman was in despair. The axe was all he possessed with which to make a living, and he had not money enough to buy a new one. As he stood wringing his hands and weeping, the god Mercury suddenly appeared and asked what the trouble was. The Woodman told what had happened, and straightway the kind Mercury dived into the pool. When he came up again he held a wonderful golden axe.
"Is this your axe?" Mercury asked the Woodman.
"No," answered the honest Woodman, "that is not my axe."

Mercury laid the golden axe on the bank and sprang back into the pool. This time he brought up an axe of silver, but the Woodman declared again that his axe was just an ordinary one with a wooden handle.
Mercury dived down for the third time, and when he came up again he had the very axe that had been lost.
The poor Woodman was very glad that his axe had been found and could not thank the kind god enough. Mercury was greatly pleased with the Woodman's honesty.
"I admire your honesty," he said, "and as a reward you may have all three axes, the gold and the silver as well as your own."

The happy Woodman returned to his home with his treasures, and soon the story of his good fortune was known to everybody in the village. Now there were several Woodmen in the village who believed that they could easily win the same good fortune. They hurried out into the woods, one here, one there, and hiding their axes in the bushes, pretended they had lost them. Then they wept and wailed and called on Mercury to help them.

And indeed, Mercury did appear, first to this one, then to that. To each one he showed an axe of gold, and each one eagerly claimed it to be the one he had lost. But Mercury did not give them the golden axe. Oh no! Instead he gave them each a hard whack over the head with it and sent them home. And when they returned next day to look for their own axes, they were nowhere to be found.
_Honesty is the best policy._
translated_paragraphs: 一个穷樵夫在林间一处深潭边伐树。时候已晚，他累坏了。他从日出就动手干活，现在落斧，已经不如清早那么准了。因此手一滑，斧子脱手飞出，落进水潭。
樵夫绝望极了。靠这把斧子，他才能谋生，他又没有足够的钱另买一把。他绞着双手流泪，神使墨丘利忽然出现，问他出了什么事。樵夫把事情经过说了一遍。好心的墨丘利立刻潜进潭里，等他再浮上来，手里拿着一把美妙的金斧头。
“这是你的斧头吗？”墨丘利问樵夫。
“不，”诚实的樵夫回答，“那不是我的斧头。”
墨丘利把金斧放到岸边，再次跳进水潭。这回，他拿上来一把银斧头。樵夫却再一次说明，他的斧头只是把带木把儿的普通斧头。
墨丘利第三次潜下去，等他浮出水面，这回拿着的正是那把丢失的斧子。
失物找回，穷樵夫高兴极了，怎么感谢这位好心的神也觉得不够。墨丘利对他的诚实非常满意。
“我很欣赏你的诚实，”他说，“作为奖赏，三把斧子都给你吧。除了你自己的，那金的和银的也一并送你。”
樵夫高高兴兴带着宝贝们回了家。很快，全村都听说了他走运的事。村里有几位樵夫觉得，要得到同样的好运很容易。他们匆匆到树林里去，这里一个那里一个，把各自的斧子藏进灌木丛，假装斧子丢了。随后他们又哭又号，呼唤墨丘利来帮忙。
果然，墨丘利出现了。他先见这个，又去见那个，给每个人看一把金斧头。人人都迫不及待地认领，说那就是自己丢失的斧子。但墨丘利没有把金斧送给他们。哦，才没有呢！他反而拿着金斧，在每人头上重重敲了一下，叫他们回家去。次日，他们回来寻找原来的斧子，却已经怎么也找不到了。
为人诚实，最是上策。

source_paragraphs: A young Mouse in search of adventure was running along the bank of a pond where lived a Frog. When the Frog saw the Mouse, he swam to the bank and croaked:
"Won't you pay me a visit? I can promise you a good time if you do."
The Mouse did not need much coaxing, for he was very anxious to see the world and everything in it. But though he could swim a little, he did not dare risk going into the pond without some help.
The Frog had a plan. He tied the Mouse's leg to his own with a tough reed. Then into the pond he jumped, dragging his foolish companion with him.

The Mouse soon had enough of it and wanted to return to shore; but the treacherous Frog had other plans. He pulled the Mouse down under the water and drowned him. But before he could untie the reed that bound him to the dead Mouse, a Hawk came sailing over the pond. Seeing the body of the Mouse floating on the water, the Hawk swooped down, seized the Mouse and carried it off, with the Frog dangling from its leg. Thus at one swoop he had caught both meat and fish for his dinner.
_Those who seek to harm others often come to harm themselves through their own deceit._
translated_paragraphs: 一只年轻的小老鼠想找些新奇的经历，正沿池塘岸边跑。那里住着一只青蛙。青蛙看见老鼠，游到岸边，呱呱叫道：
“你不来做个客吗？只要你来，我保证叫你好好快活一场。”
老鼠用不着怎么劝，因为他正渴望去看看世界，看看世界上的一切。可是他尽管会游那么一小会儿，没有谁帮忙，却不敢贸然进塘。
青蛙有个办法。他用一根结实的芦苇，把老鼠的腿和自己的腿拴在一起。接着纵身往塘里一跳，拖着糊涂的伙伴一起下了水。
老鼠没过多久就玩够了，想返回岸上，奸诈的青蛙却另有打算。他拉着老鼠沉到水下，把老鼠淹死了。可是还没等解开把自己拴在死老鼠身上的芦苇，一只鹰从池塘上空滑翔而过。看见鼠尸浮在水面，鹰俯冲下来，抓起老鼠飞走了。青蛙还在老鼠腿下头吊着呢。鹰这一扑，晚餐的鱼啊肉啊，便一齐到手了。
存心害人的，常被自己的诡计害了。

source_paragraphs: A Crab one day grew disgusted with the sands in which he lived. He decided to take a stroll to the meadow not far inland. There he would find better fare than briny water and sand mites. So off he crawled to the meadow. But there a hungry Fox spied him, and in a twinkling, ate him up, both shell and claw.
_Be content with your lot._
translated_paragraphs: 一天，螃蟹嫌住腻了沙滩，决定爬到离海不远的草地上逛逛。那一定能吃到比咸海水和小沙虫更好的东西。他就这样爬进了草地。可一只饿狐狸瞄见他，转眼之间，连壳带钳把他吃得干干净净。
要懂得对自己的境遇知足。

source_paragraphs: A Serpent had succeeded in surprising an Eagle and had wrapped himself around the Eagle's neck. The Eagle could not reach the Serpent, neither with beak nor claws. Far into the sky he soared trying to shake off his enemy. But the Serpent's hold only tightened, and slowly the Eagle sank back to earth, gasping for breath.
A Countryman chanced to see the unequal combat. In pity for the noble Eagle he rushed up and soon had loosened the coiling Serpent and freed the Eagle.
The Serpent was furious. He had no chance to bite the watchful Countryman. Instead he struck at the drinking horn, hanging at the Countryman's belt, and into it let fly the poison of his fangs.

The Countryman now went on toward home. Becoming thirsty on the way, he filled his horn at a spring, and was about to drink. There was a sudden rush of great wings. Sweeping down, the Eagle seized the poisoned horn from out his savior's hands, and flew away with it to hide it where it could never be found.
_An act of kindness is well repaid._
translated_paragraphs: 一条蛇出其不意袭击了一只鹰，缠住了鹰的脖子。鹰用尖嘴够不着它，用利爪也抓不着。鹰飞向高空，想甩掉敌人，可蛇反而缠得更紧。鹰喘不过气来，一点点跌回了地面。
一个乡下人恰好看见了这场力量悬殊的搏斗。他可怜那只英武的鹰，赶上前去，很快解开盘缠的蛇，救出了鹰。
蛇愤怒极了。乡下人十分警觉，不给它下口的机会。它转而咬住挂在那人腰带上的牛角杯，把毒牙里的汁液射进杯中。
乡下人随后继续往家走。半路上口渴了，他在泉眼里接满一杯水，正想喝，忽听巨翼破空之声。鹰俯冲下来，从恩人手里抓走了带毒的角杯，远远地飞去，把它藏在再也没人找得到的地方。
行善待人，自有善意相报。

source_paragraphs: A certain Wolf could not get enough to eat because of the watchfulness of the Shepherds. But one night he found a sheep skin that had been cast aside and forgotten. The next day, dressed in the skin, the Wolf strolled into the pasture with the Sheep. Soon a little Lamb was following him about and was quickly led away to slaughter.

That evening the Wolf entered the fold with the flock. But it happened that the Shepherd took a fancy for mutton broth that very evening, and, picking up a knife, went to the fold. There the first he laid hands on and killed was the Wolf.
_The evil doer often comes to harm through his own deceit._
translated_paragraphs: 牧羊人们处处提防，有只狼总弄不够吃的。一天夜里，他找到一张被丢在一旁、已经叫人遗忘的羊皮。第二天，狼披上羊皮，混在羊群里，悠悠然进了草场。没过多久，一只羊羔跟在他身后，很快就被他引到别处杀害了。
那天傍晚，狼随着羊群进了羊圈。不巧，牧人偏在这天晚上想喝羊肉汤，提把刀进了羊圈。他头一个捉住、下刀宰杀的，就是这头狼。
作恶的人，常被自己设下的骗局害苦。

source_paragraphs: A Bull once escaped from a Lion by entering a cave which the Goatherds used to house their flocks in stormy weather and at night. It happened that one of the Goats had been left behind, and the Bull had no sooner got inside than this Goat lowered his head and made a rush at him, butting him with his horns. As the Lion was still prowling outside the entrance to the cave, the Bull had to submit to the insult.
"Do not think," he said, "that I submit to your cowardly treatment because I am afraid of you. When that Lion leaves, I'll teach you a lesson you won't forget."
_It is wicked to take advantage of another's distress._
translated_paragraphs: 有一回，公牛为躲避狮子，钻进一个山洞。刮风下雨的时候，或者夜里，牧人们都把羊群赶进这洞里栖身。这天刚巧有一只山羊落了单，留在里面。公牛刚一进洞，山羊就低下脑袋，猛冲上去，用犄角顶他。狮子还徘徊在洞口，公牛只好忍下这番欺侮。
“别以为我忍着你这懦夫的欺侮，是因为我怕你，”公牛说，“那头狮子一走，我就给你一个忘不了的教训。”
趁别人遭难的时候欺负人，是种恶行。

source_paragraphs: A Beetle once begged the Eagle to spare a Hare which had run to her for protection. But the Eagle pounced upon her prey, the sweep of her great wings tumbling the Beetle a dozen feet away. Furious at the disrespect shown her, the Beetle flew to the Eagle's nest and rolled out the eggs. Not one did she spare. The Eagle's grief and anger knew no bounds, but who had done the cruel deed she did not know.

Next year the Eagle built her nest far up on a mountain crag; but the Beetle found it and again destroyed the eggs. In despair the Eagle now implored great Jupiter to let her place her eggs in his lap. There none would dare harm them. But the Beetle buzzed about Jupiter's head, and made him rise to drive her away; and the eggs rolled from his lap.

Now the Beetle told the reason for her action, and Jupiter had to acknowledge the justice of her cause. And they say that ever after, while the Eagle's eggs lie in the nest in spring, the Beetle still sleeps in the ground. For so Jupiter commanded.
_Even the weakest may find means to avenge a wrong._
translated_paragraphs: 有只野兔跑来，求甲虫保护。甲虫恳求鹰饶过野兔，可鹰一把就攫住了猎物，巨大的翅膀扫过去，把甲虫掀出十来英尺远。甲虫受了这番轻侮，勃然大怒，飞到鹰巢里，把巢里的蛋一个个推出去，一个也没留下。鹰的悲伤和愤怒简直没有边际，却不知道究竟是谁做下了这件残忍的事。
第二年，鹰在高山峭壁上筑了窝。甲虫还是找到了，再一次毁掉了鹰蛋。走投无路的鹰这回恳求伟大的朱庇特，容她把蛋放在他的膝上。放在那里，谁也不敢动它们。可甲虫偏在朱庇特脑袋边嗡嗡打转，惹得他站起身来赶她，鹰蛋就从他膝上滚了下去。
这时候，甲虫才道出自己这么做的缘故。朱庇特也只好承认，她的申诉有道理。据说，自此以后，每逢春天，鹰蛋安放在巢中的时候，甲虫还在地下睡觉。这正是朱庇特下的命令。
最弱小的生灵，受了欺负，也可能找到报复的办法。

sections.title_en: THE OLD LION AND THE FOX
source_paragraphs: An old Lion, whose teeth and claws were so worn that it was not so easy for him to get food as in his younger days, pretended that he was sick. He took care to let all his neighbors know about it, and then lay down in his cave to wait for visitors. And when they came to offer him their sympathy, he ate them up one by one.

The Fox came too, but he was very cautious about it. Standing at a safe distance from the cave, he inquired politely after the Lion's health. The Lion replied that he was very ill indeed, and asked the Fox to step in for a moment. But Master Fox very wisely stayed outside, thanking the Lion very kindly for the invitation.

"I should be glad to do as you ask," he added, "but I have noticed that there are many footprints leading into your cave and none coming out. Pray tell me, how do your visitors find their way out again?"
_Take warning from the misfortunes of others._
translated_paragraphs: 老狮子的牙齿和爪子都磨钝了，要弄到吃的，不再像年轻时那样容易。他便装起病来，特意让四邻全都知道，随后卧在洞里，等着客人上门。来探病、表示慰问的动物，他一个接一个地吃掉了。
狐狸也来了，不过他十分谨慎。他站在离洞口安全的地方，彬彬有礼地问候狮子的身体。狮子答道，自己的病着实很重，请狐狸进洞坐一会儿。狐狸先生却聪明地留在外头，只和和气气地谢了他的邀请。
“我很愿意照您的意思做，”他补充道，“只是我留意到，进洞的脚印倒是很多，出洞的却一个都没有。请问，您的客人是从哪条路再出去的呢？”
从旁人的不幸中记取警告。

source_paragraphs: A Lion and a Man chanced to travel in company through the forest. They soon began to quarrel, for each of them boasted that he and his kind were far superior to the other both in strength and mind.
Now they reached a clearing in the forest and there stood a statue. It was a representation of Heracles in the act of tearing the jaws of the Nemean Lion.
"See," said the man, "that's how strong _we_ are! The King of Beasts is like wax in our hands!"
"Ho!" laughed the Lion, "a Man made that statue. It would have been quite a different scene had a Lion made it!"
_It all depends on the point of view, and who tells the story._
translated_paragraphs: 有个人碰巧和一头狮子结伴穿过森林。没过多久，两位就争吵起来，因为他们各自夸口，说自家一族无论力气还是头脑，都远远超过对方。
他们走到林中一片空地，那里立着一尊雕像，刻的是大力士赫拉克勒斯正用双手扳开涅墨亚猛狮的上下颚。
“看，”那人说，“这才是我们人类的力量！百兽之王落在我们手里，跟一团软蜡差不多。”
“哈！”狮子笑了，“那雕像可是人做的。倘若是狮子动手雕，你看到的怕是完全不同的一幕！”
这得看从哪个角度瞧，还得看讲故事的是谁。

sections.title_en: THE ASS AND THE LAP DOG
source_paragraphs: There was once an Ass whose Master also owned a Lap Dog. This Dog was a favorite and received many a pat and kind word from his Master, as well as choice bits from his plate. Every day the Dog would run to meet the Master, frisking playfully about and leaping up to lick his hands and face.
All this the Ass saw with much discontent. Though he was well fed, he had much work to do; besides, the Master hardly ever took any notice of him.
Now the jealous Ass got it into his silly head that all he had to do to win his Master's favor was to act like the Dog. So one day he left his stable and clattered eagerly into the house.

Finding his Master seated at the dinner table, he kicked up his heels and, with a loud bray, pranced giddily around the table, upsetting it as he did so. Then he planted his forefeet on his Master's knees and rolled out his tongue to lick the Master's face, as he had seen the Dog do. But his weight upset the chair, and Ass and man rolled over together in the pile of broken dishes from the table.

The Master was much alarmed at the strange behavior of the Ass, and calling for help, soon attracted the attention of the servants. When they saw the danger the Master was in from the clumsy beast, they set upon the Ass and drove him with kicks and blows back to the stable. There they left him to mourn the foolishness that had brought him nothing but a sound beating.
_Behavior that is regarded as agreeable in one is very rude and impertinent in another._
_Do not try to gain favor by acting in a way that is contrary to your own nature and character._
translated_paragraphs: 从前有一头驴，主人还养了一只小哈巴狗。小狗是主人的心头好，常得到他的爱抚、温存的话，还有他从自己盘子里拣出的可口食物。每天，狗都跑去迎接主人，在他身旁撒欢跳跃，蹿起来舔他的手和脸。
这一切，驴看在眼里，很是不服。虽说他的口粮不薄，可要干的活儿很多，而且主人几乎看也不看他一眼。
眼红的驴心里冒出个傻念头。要想讨主人的喜欢，只须学小狗的样就好了。于是一天，他走出驴棚，满心欢喜，踢踢踏踏一路走进屋去。
他见主人坐在饭桌边，便扬起后蹄，大叫一声，围着桌子胡蹦乱跳，顺势把桌子掀翻了。接着他照从前看见小狗做的那样，把两只前蹄往主人膝盖上一搭，吐出舌头要舔主人的脸。可驴的分量一下子把椅子压倒，他和主人一起滚进满地从桌上摔下的碗碟碎片里。
主人被驴的怪相吓坏了，大喊救命，很快把仆人们引了过来。他们一见这蠢笨的牲口让主人陷入险境，一齐上前，拳脚齐下，把驴撵回牲口棚。随后他们就把驴留在那儿，任他独自哀叹，自己犯傻，只换来一顿痛打。
同样的举动，出自一个人显得可爱，换一个人做，却可能粗鲁冒失。
别为了讨人欢心，硬做与自己天性和性情相违的事。

source_paragraphs: A Milkmaid had been out to milk the cows and was returning from the field with the shining milk pail balanced nicely on her head. As she walked along, her pretty head was busy with plans for the days to come.

"This good, rich milk," she mused, "will give me plenty of cream to churn. The butter I make I will take to market, and with the money I get for it I will buy a lot of eggs for hatching. How nice it will be when they are all hatched and the yard is full of fine young chicks. Then when May day comes I will sell them, and with the money I'll buy a lovely new dress to wear to the fair. All the young men will look at me. They will come and try to make love to me,--but I shall very quickly send them about their business!"

As she thought of how she would settle that matter, she tossed her head scornfully, and down fell the pail of milk to the ground. And all the milk flowed out, and with it vanished butter and eggs and chicks and new dress and all the milkmaid's pride.
_Do not count your chickens before they are hatched._
translated_paragraphs: 挤奶姑娘出门给奶牛挤完奶，从田里往回走。那只亮闪闪的奶桶，稳稳当当地顶在头上。她边走，漂亮的小脑瓜边忙着打算以后的日子。
“这样又浓又好的奶，”她想着，“可以撇下好多奶油来搅黄油。做好黄油，我就拿到集市去卖，用赚的钱买一大堆鸡蛋来孵。等蛋都孵出来，满院子尽是健壮的小鸡，那多好！到了五月节，我就把鸡卖掉，用钱买一条漂亮的新裙子，穿去赶集。所有小伙子都会朝我看！他们会围过来，想向我献殷勤。哼，我立刻就能把他们打发走！”
她正想着要怎样打发人家，轻蔑地一扬脑袋，一整桶牛奶扑通落到地上。所有的牛奶流光了，跟着一道消失的，还有黄油、鸡蛋、小鸡、新裙子，以及挤奶姑娘满心的得意。
鸡雏还没孵出壳，别急着数有几只。

source_paragraphs: A Wolf, lurking near the Shepherd's hut, saw the Shepherd and his family feasting on a roasted lamb.
"Aha!" he muttered. "What a great shouting and running about there would have been, had they caught me at just the very thing they are doing with so much enjoyment!"
_Men often condemn others for what they see no wrong in doing themselves._
translated_paragraphs: 狼潜伏在牧人的小屋附近，看见牧人一家正津津有味地大吃烤羊羔。
“哼！”他低声嘟囔，“他们自己做这件事，吃得多开心呀！要是逮着我做一模一样的事，还不知道会有多少人一边大喊大叫，一边到处追赶呢！”
同样的事，自己做来觉得没错，却常拿来指责旁人。

source_paragraphs: A Goat strayed away from the flock, tempted by a patch of clover. The Goatherd tried to call it back, but in vain. It would not obey him. Then he picked up a stone and threw it, breaking the Goat's horn.
The Goatherd was frightened.
"Do not tell the master," he begged the Goat.
"No," said the Goat, "that broken horn can speak for itself!"
_Wicked deeds will not stay hid._
translated_paragraphs: 一只山羊被一片三叶草吸引，离开了羊群。牧人试图把它唤回来，怎么唤也没用，它不肯听话。牧人就捡起一块石头扔过去，把山羊一只犄角打断了。
牧人吓坏了。
“别告诉主人。”他求山羊。
“不必我说，”山羊回答，“这只断角自己会开口！”
坏事是藏不住的。

source_paragraphs: A Miser had buried his gold in a secret place in his garden. Every day he went to the spot, dug up the treasure and counted it piece by piece to make sure it was all there. He made so many trips that a Thief, who had been observing him, guessed what it was the Miser had hidden, and one night quietly dug up the treasure and made off with it.
When the Miser discovered his loss, he was overcome with grief and despair. He groaned and cried and tore his hair.
A passerby heard his cries and asked what had happened.
"My gold! O my gold!" cried the Miser, wildly, "someone has robbed me!"
"Your gold! There in that hole? Why did you put it there? Why did you not keep it in the house where you could easily get it when you had to buy things?"
"Buy!" screamed the Miser angrily. "Why, I never touched the gold. I couldn't think of spending any of it."
The stranger picked up a large stone and threw it into the hole.
"If that is the case," he said, "cover up that stone. It is worth just as much to you as the treasure you lost!"
_A possession is worth no more than the use we make of it._
translated_paragraphs: 一个守财奴把自己的黄金埋在花园里一处隐秘的地方。他每天到那儿，把宝贝挖出来，一块块地数过，确定一块也不少。他来来回回次数实在太多，一个一直盯着他的小偷便猜着了那里埋着什么。一晚，小偷悄悄挖出金子，带着它们逃走了。
守财奴发现金子没了，悲痛欲绝，陷入绝望。他一会儿呻吟，一会儿大哭，揪扯着自己的头发。
一位路人听见哭声，来问出了什么事。
“我的金子！哎，我的金子啊！”守财奴发疯似的喊，“我的金子叫人抢走啦！”
“你的金子？原先搁在这个坑里？怎么放在那儿呢？怎么不收在屋里？要买什么的时候，伸手就够得着。”
“买！”守财奴生气地尖叫，“我可是从来不动那些金子的。要叫我花掉哪怕一块，想都别想！”
陌生人捡起一块大石头，扔进坑里。
“既然如此，”他说，“把这块石头埋起来吧。对你而言，它和你失去的宝贝一模一样值钱！”
一件财物有多大价值，要看我们能拿它做多少用处。

sections.title_en: THE WOLF AND THE HOUSE DOG
source_paragraphs: There was once a Wolf who got very little to eat because the Dogs of the village were so wide awake and watchful. He was really nothing but skin and bones, and it made him very downhearted to think of it.

One night this Wolf happened to fall in with a fine fat House Dog who had wandered a little too far from home. The Wolf would gladly have eaten him then and there, but the House Dog looked strong enough to leave his marks should he try it. So the Wolf spoke very humbly to the Dog, complimenting him on his fine appearance.

"You can be as well-fed as I am if you want to," replied the Dog. "Leave the woods; there you live miserably. Why, you have to fight hard for every bite you get. Follow my example and you will get along beautifully."
"What must I do?" asked the Wolf.

"Hardly anything," answered the House Dog. "Chase people who carry canes, bark at beggars, and fawn on the people of the house. In return you will get tidbits of every kind, chicken bones, choice bits of meat, sugar, cake, and much more beside, not to speak of kind words and caresses."
The Wolf had such a beautiful vision of his coming happiness that he almost wept. But just then he noticed that the hair on the Dog's neck was worn and the skin was chafed.
"What is that on your neck?"
"Nothing at all," replied the Dog.
"What! nothing!"
"Oh, just a trifle!"
"But please tell me."
"Perhaps you see the mark of the collar to which my chain is fastened."
"What! A chain!" cried the Wolf. "Don't you go wherever you please?"
"Not always! But what's the difference?" replied the Dog.
"All the difference in the world! I don't care a rap for your feasts and I wouldn't take all the tender young lambs in the world at that price." And away ran the Wolf to the woods.
_There is nothing worth so much as liberty._
translated_paragraphs: 从前，有头狼很难弄够吃的，因为村里的狗个个机警，严加防范。狼简直只剩下皮和骨头，每回想到自己的境况，就好生伤心。
一天夜里，他碰巧遇上一条油光水滑、养得胖胖的家犬。狗不留神走得离家远了些。狼巴不得当场就把他吃下去，可家犬十分强壮，看那模样，狼要真敢动手，身上准得留下几道伤痕。于是狼很谦卑地跟狗说话，称赞他模样长得好。
“只要你愿意，你也能吃得像我一样好，”狗回答，“离开树林吧，在那儿你过得这么苦。每吃上一口，都得拼命去抢。照我的样子做，日子就快活了。”
“我得干什么？”狼问。
“几乎什么也不用干，”家犬回答，“追赶拄棍子的人，朝乞丐汪汪几声，讨好家里的人。作为回报，你会吃到各式各样的小美味，鸡骨头，上好的碎肉，糖，蛋糕，好多好多别的东西。更别提好听的话和轻轻的抚摸啦。”
狼把即将得到的幸福想得那么美，差点感动得流下泪来。偏在这时，他注意到狗脖子上的毛已磨秃，连皮肤都擦破了。
“你脖子上那是什么？”
“什么也没有。”狗答道。
“什么？什么都没有？”
“哎，无非一点小事！”
“还是请你告诉我吧。”
“也许你看到的是项圈留下的印子。我的链子就系在项圈上。”
“什么！链子！”狼喊道，“难道你不能爱去哪儿就去哪儿？”
“有时候不能，这又有什么区别呢？”狗答道。
“天底下最大的区别就在这儿！你那些好吃的，我连稀罕也不稀罕。就算拿天下所有细嫩的小羊羔来换，我也不肯出这个价钱！”说罢，狼奔回树林里去了。
再没有什么，比自由更值钱。

source_paragraphs: A Fox, swimming across a river, was barely able to reach the bank, where he lay bruised and exhausted from his struggle with the swift current. Soon a swarm of blood-sucking flies settled on him; but he lay quietly, still too weak to run away from them.
A Hedgehog happened by. "Let me drive the flies away," he said kindly.
"No, no!" exclaimed the Fox, "do not disturb them! They have taken all they can hold. If you drive them away, another greedy swarm will come and take the little blood I have left."
_Better to bear a lesser evil than to risk a greater in removing it._
translated_paragraphs: 一只狐狸游泳渡河，好不容易才到达岸边。他在急流中苦苦挣扎，已满身青肿，精疲力尽，只能躺在那里。很快，一群吸血的苍蝇落在他身上。他还是静静躺着，实在没力气跑开了。
一只刺猬刚巧路过，好心地说：“让我替你赶走这些苍蝇吧。”
“不，不！”狐狸叫道，“别去惊动它们！它们已经喝得再也装不下了。你要是赶走它们，会另来一群贪嘴的，把我剩下的一点儿血都吸干。”
与其为摆脱一桩小害，冒招来大害的险，不如暂且忍一忍。

source_paragraphs: A Bat blundered into the nest of a Weasel, who ran up to catch and eat him. The Bat begged for his life, but the Weasel would not listen.
"You are a Mouse," he said, "and I am a sworn enemy of Mice. Every Mouse I catch, I am going to eat!"
"But I am not a Mouse!" cried the Bat. "Look at my wings. Can Mice fly? Why, I am only a Bird! Please let me go!"

The Weasel had to admit that the Bat was not a Mouse, so he let him go. But a few days later, the foolish Bat went blindly into the nest of another Weasel. This Weasel happened to be a bitter enemy of Birds, and he soon had the Bat under his claws, ready to eat him.
"You are a Bird," he said, "and I am going to eat you!"
"What," cried the Bat, "I, a Bird! Why, all Birds have feathers! I am nothing but a Mouse. 'Down with all Cats,' is _my_ motto!"
And so the Bat escaped with his life a second time.
_Set your sails with the wind._
translated_paragraphs: 一只蝙蝠误闯进黄鼠狼的窝，黄鼠狼跑上来，要逮住他吃掉。蝙蝠苦苦求饶，黄鼠狼不肯听。
“你是老鼠，”他说，“我跟老鼠誓不两立。我逮到一只，就要吃一只！”
“可我不是老鼠呀！”蝙蝠叫道，“看看我的翅膀。老鼠会飞吗？我只是一只鸟啊！请放我走吧！”
黄鼠狼只好承认，蝙蝠不是老鼠，于是放他走了。可没过几天，糊涂的蝙蝠又冒冒失失走进另一只黄鼠狼的窝。这一位偏是鸟儿的死对头，他很快把蝙蝠按在爪底下，准备把他吃了。
“你是一只鸟，”他说，“我要吃了你！”
“什么！”蝙蝠大叫，“我，是鸟？可是鸟全都有羽毛啊！我就是一只老鼠。‘打倒天下所有的猫’，这才是我的口号！”
蝙蝠就这样第二次捡回一条命。
看准风向，调整船帆。

source_paragraphs: An old Toad once informed all his neighbors that he was a learned doctor. In fact he could cure anything. The Fox heard the news and hurried to see the Toad. He looked the Toad over very carefully.

"Mr. Toad," he said, "I've been told that you cure anything! But just take a look at yourself, and then try some of your own medicine. If you can cure yourself of that blotchy skin and that rheumatic gait, someone might believe you. Otherwise, I should advise you to try some other profession."
_Those who would mend others, should first mend themselves._
translated_paragraphs: 有一次，一只老癞蛤蟆通知所有邻居，说自己是个学问很深的大夫。照他自己的说法，什么病都包治。狐狸听到消息，急忙赶去见他，把癞蛤蟆从上到下仔细打量了一遍。
“癞蛤蟆先生，”他说，“听讲您什么都能治！不过，还是请您瞧瞧自己，再吃上一剂自己的药。要是能治好您那斑斑驳驳的皮肤，还有那害风湿似的步子，兴许会有人相信您。否则，我劝您还是换个行当试试。”
要替别人医治毛病，先治治自己。

source_paragraphs: A Fox that had been caught in a trap, succeeded at last, after much painful tugging, in getting away. But he had to leave his beautiful bushy tail behind him.

For a long time he kept away from the other Foxes, for he knew well enough that they would all make fun of him and crack jokes and laugh behind his back. But it was hard for him to live alone, and at last he thought of a plan that would perhaps help him out of his trouble.
He called a meeting of all the Foxes, saying that he had something of great importance to tell the tribe.
When they were all gathered together, the Fox Without a Tail got up and made a long speech about those Foxes who had come to harm because of their tails.

This one had been caught by hounds when his tail had become entangled in the hedge. That one had not been able to run fast enough because of the weight of his brush. Besides, it was well known, he said, that men hunt Foxes simply for their tails, which they cut off as prizes of the hunt. With such proof of the danger and uselessness of having a tail, said Master Fox, he would advise every Fox to cut it off, if he valued life and safety.
When he had finished talking, an old Fox arose, and said, smiling:
"Master Fox, kindly turn around for a moment, and you shall have your answer."
When the poor Fox Without a Tail turned around, there arose such a storm of jeers and hooting, that he saw how useless it was to try any longer to persuade the Foxes to part with their tails.
_Do not listen to the advice of him who seeks to lower you to his own level._
translated_paragraphs: 狐狸落入捕兽夹，吃尽痛苦，拼命拉扯，终于逃了出来。不过，他那条漂亮的蓬松大尾巴却留在了夹子里。
好长一段日子，他躲着别的狐狸。他很清楚，它们准会拿他打趣，在背后说俏皮话，偷偷笑他。可是独自过日子实在不好受。到后来，他想出个办法，也许能解脱自己的窘境。
他把所有狐狸召来开会，说有一桩很要紧的事要向全族宣布。
大伙儿到齐以后，无尾狐狸站起来，滔滔不绝地演说，专讲那些受尾巴拖累、吃过苦头的狐狸。
这一个，因为尾巴绊在树篱上，叫猎狗捉住了；那一个，因为大尾巴沉重，跑得不够快。他说，更何况人人都知道，人类猎狐，就是为了割下狐狸尾巴，当作狩猎的奖品。关于尾巴既危险又不中用，他已经给出了这么多证据。这位狐狸先生说，哪一位若珍惜生命和安全，他就劝哪一位把尾巴砍掉。
等他讲完，一只老狐狸起身，微笑着说：
“狐狸先生，劳烦你转过身来一会儿，大伙儿自会给你回答。”
可怜的无尾狐狸一转过身，四下里嘘声、哄笑声如风暴般响起。他这才看明白，再想劝大家舍弃尾巴，是多么徒劳。
有人想把你拉低到他自己的境地，这样的人出的主意，不要听。

source_paragraphs: There was once a Dog who was so ill-natured and mischievous that his Master had to fasten a heavy wooden clog about his neck to keep him from annoying visitors and neighbors. But the Dog seemed to be very proud of the clog and dragged it about noisily as if he wished to attract everybody's attention. He was not able to impress anyone.
"You would be wiser," said an old acquaintance, "to keep quietly out of sight with that clog. Do you want everybody to know what a disgraceful and ill-natured Dog you are?"
_Notoriety is not fame._
translated_paragraphs: 从前有条狗，性子恶劣，又爱闯祸。为了不让他骚扰来客和邻居，主人不得不在他脖子上系了一块沉重的木头。可狗对那块木头似乎颇为得意，拖着它到处撞得哐啷响，仿佛故意要招来所有人的目光。没有谁因此对他另眼相看。
一位老相识说：“你要是聪明些，就该带着那木头静静躲到人家看不见的地方。你想叫所有人都知道，你是条多么丢脸、脾气多么坏的狗吗？”
臭名远扬，不等于享有美名。

source_paragraphs: A Butterfly once fell in love with a beautiful Rose. The Rose was not indifferent, for the Butterfly's wings were powdered in a charming pattern of gold and silver. And so, when he fluttered near and told how he loved her, she blushed rosily and said yes. After much pretty love-making and many whispered vows of constancy, the Butterfly took a tender leave of his sweetheart.
But alas! It was a long time before he came back to her.

"Is this your constancy?" she exclaimed tearfully. "It is ages since you went away, and all the time, you have been carrying on with all sorts of flowers. I saw you kiss Miss Geranium, and you fluttered around Miss Mignonette until Honey Bee chased you away. I wish he had stung you!"

"Constancy!" laughed the Butterfly. "I had no sooner left you than I saw Zephyr kissing you. You carried on scandalously with Mr. Bumble Bee and you made eyes at every single Bug you could see. You can't expect any constancy from me!"
_Do not expect constancy in others if you have none yourself._
translated_paragraphs: 蝴蝶爱上了一朵美丽的玫瑰。玫瑰也不是全无心意，因为蝴蝶的翅膀撒着金银色的细粉，花纹动人。因此，他翩翩飞近，诉说他多爱她时，她的脸染上一层玫瑰红，答应了他。两位说了许多甜蜜话，在彼此耳边许下无数永不变心的誓言，蝴蝶这才温柔地向心上人告别。
可是，唉！他去了好久才回到她身边。
“这就是你说的忠贞吗？”她含着眼泪喊道，“你走了有一辈子那么久，这期间，却一直在跟各式各样的花儿谈情说爱！我亲眼看见你亲吻天竺葵小姐，又绕着木犀草小姐飞个不停，直到蜜蜂把你撵走。我真希望他当时蜇了你！”
“忠贞！”蝴蝶笑起来，“我刚离开你，就看见西风在吻你。你跟熊蜂先生亲热得不像话，又朝每一只看得见的小虫子送秋波。你可不能指望我对你一心一意！”
自己做不到专一，就别指望别人始终不变心。

source_paragraphs: Once a Cat and a Fox were traveling together. As they went along, picking up provisions on the way--a stray mouse here, a fat chicken there--they began an argument to while away the time between bites. And, as usually happens when comrades argue, the talk began to get personal.
"You think you are extremely clever, don't you?" said the Fox. "Do you pretend to know more than I? Why, I know a whole sackful of tricks!"
"Well," retorted the Cat, "I admit I know one trick only, but that one, let me tell you, is worth a thousand of yours!"
Just then, close by, they heard a hunter's horn and the yelping of a pack of hounds. In an instant the Cat was up a tree, hiding among the leaves.
"This is my trick," he called to the Fox. "Now let me see what yours are worth."

But the Fox had so many plans for escape he could not decide which one to try first. He dodged here and there with the hounds at his heels. He doubled on his tracks, he ran at top speed, he entered a dozen burrows,--but all in vain. The hounds caught him, and soon put an end to the boaster and all his tricks.
_Common sense is always worth more than cunning._
translated_paragraphs: 有一回，猫和狐狸结伴赶路。他们一路张罗口粮，这里一只离群的老鼠，那里一只肥鸡，吃东西的间歇就斗起嘴来，权当消磨时光。伙伴之间拌嘴常常这样，说着说着，话锋就冲着对方本人去了。
“你自以为机灵透顶，对不对？”狐狸说，“你敢说你懂得比我多？嘿，我的妙计足足能装一整口袋！”
“好吧，”猫回嘴道，“我承认我只懂一个法子。不过我告诉你，我这一个顶得过你那样的一千个！”
就在这时，近处响起了猎人的号角和一群猎犬的吠声。猫一转眼就已经上了树，藏进枝叶之间。
“这就是我的法子，”他向狐狸喊，“现在让我看看，你的那些能顶多大用场。”
可狐狸的逃生办法太多，拿不定主意先试哪一个。猎犬紧追脚后，他左躲右闪。他沿原路折返，他撒腿飞奔，他一连钻进十来个洞穴，全都没用。猎犬抓住了他，爱吹牛的狐狸和他那一袋子妙计，很快一并完蛋了。
踏实的见识总比耍小聪明更管用。

source_paragraphs: A Boy, stung by a Nettle, ran home crying, to get his mother to blow on the hurt and kiss it.
"Son," said the Boy's mother, when she had comforted him, "the next time you come near a Nettle, grasp it firmly, and it will be as soft as silk."
_Whatever you do, do with all your might._
translated_paragraphs: 男孩被荨麻蜇了，哭着跑回家，要妈妈给疼的地方吹一吹，亲一亲。
妈妈安慰过他，说：“孩子，下回你再碰到荨麻，就一把攥牢它。那样它就会像丝绸一样柔软了。”
无论做什么，都要尽力去做。

source_paragraphs: A Lion had grown very old. His teeth were worn away. His limbs could no longer bear him, and the King of Beasts was very pitiful indeed as he lay gasping on the ground, about to die.
Where now his strength and his former graceful beauty?

Now a Boar spied him, and rushing at him, gored him with his yellow tusk. A Bull trampled him with his heavy hoofs. Even a contemptible Ass let fly his heels and brayed his insults in the face of the Lion.
_It is cowardly to attack the defenseless, though he be an enemy._
translated_paragraphs: 有一头狮子很老很老了。他的牙齿已经磨尽，四肢再也撑不起身子。这位百兽之王躺在地上喘息，眼看就要死去，那样子实在可怜。
他的力量，还有从前优雅美丽的风姿，如今到哪儿去了呢？
一头野猪瞧见了，冲上前用黄色的獠牙刺他。公牛抬起沉重的蹄子踩他。连一头叫人看不起的驴也飞起后蹄踹他几脚，还对着狮子的脸高声嘶叫，尽情辱骂。
对方哪怕是敌人，欺负一个无力自卫的，也实在懦弱。

source_paragraphs: One moonlight evening as Master Fox was taking his usual stroll in the woods, he saw a number of Pheasants perched quite out of his reach on a limb of a tall old tree. The sly Fox soon found a bright patch of moonlight, where the Pheasants could see him clearly; there he raised himself up on his hind legs, and began a wild dance. First he whirled 'round and 'round like a top, then he hopped up and down, cutting all sorts of strange capers. The Pheasants stared giddily. They hardly dared blink for fear of losing him out of their sight a single instant.

Now the Fox made as if to climb a tree, now he fell over and lay still, playing dead, and the next instant he was hopping on all fours, his back in the air, and his bushy tail shaking so that it seemed to throw out silver sparks in the moonlight.

By this time the poor birds' heads were in a whirl. And when the Fox began his performance all over again, so dazed did they become, that they lost their hold on the limb, and fell down one by one to the Fox.
_Too much attention to danger may cause us to fall victims to it._
translated_paragraphs: 一个月色皎洁的夜晚，狐狸先生照例在林中散步，看见几只野鸡栖在一棵高大老树的枝头，他根本够不着。狡猾的狐狸立刻找到一块月光照得透亮的地方，让野鸡们清楚地看见他。他用两条后腿站起来，狂舞起来。先是像陀螺那样转啊转，接着蹦上蹦下，跳出千奇百怪的花样。野鸡们盯得眼睛都花了，连眼也不敢眨，生怕有一瞬间看不见他。
一会儿，狐狸摆出架势要爬树。一会儿，他又一头倒下去，躺着不动，假装死了。转眼之间，他又拱起背，用四条腿一起蹦起来，蓬松的大尾巴抖动得那样厉害，在月光底下仿佛放射出银色的火星。
这时候，可怜的鸟儿们已经看得头晕目眩。等狐狸把刚才那套戏法从头来过，他们更给晃得晕晕乎乎，爪子没抓牢树枝，一只接一只跌落下来，都落到了狐狸面前。
目不转睛盯着危险，有时反倒叫我们落入它手里。

source_paragraphs: Two Men were traveling in company through a forest, when, all at once, a huge Bear crashed out of the brush near them.
One of the Men, thinking of his own safety, climbed a tree.
The other, unable to fight the savage beast alone, threw himself on the ground and lay still, as if he were dead. He had heard that a Bear will not touch a dead body.
It must have been true, for the Bear snuffed at the Man's head awhile, and then, seeming to be satisfied that he was dead, walked away.
The Man in the tree climbed down.
"It looked just as if that Bear whispered in your ear," he said. "What did he tell you?"
"He said," answered the other, "that it was not at all wise to keep company with a fellow who would desert his friend in a moment of danger."
_Misfortune is the test of true friendship._
translated_paragraphs: 两个人结伴穿越森林。突然，一头巨大的熊撞开近旁的灌木，闯了出来。
其中一个一心顾着自己的安全，爬上了一棵树。
另一个没法独自对付这凶猛的野兽，扑倒在地，一动不动地躺着，仿佛已经死了。他听说熊不会碰死人的身体。
在这则故事里，这话倒像是应验了。熊在那人的脑袋边嗅了一阵，好像已经认定他死了，便走开了。
树上的人爬了下来。
“刚才那头熊好像在你耳朵边上说悄悄话呢，”他说，“它跟你讲了什么？”
“它说，”另一个人回答，“跟一个遇到危险就会丢下朋友不顾的人作伴，可不怎么明智。”
遇到患难，才知是不是真朋友。

source_paragraphs: A Porcupine was looking for a good home. At last he found a little sheltered cave, where lived a family of Snakes. He asked them to let him share the cave with them, and the Snakes kindly consented.
The Snakes soon wished they had not given him permission to stay. His sharp quills pricked them at every turn, and at last they politely asked him to leave.

"I am very well satisfied, thank you," said the Porcupine. "I intend to stay right here." And with that, he politely escorted the Snakes out of doors. And to save their skins, the Snakes had to look for another home.
_Give a finger and lose a hand._
translated_paragraphs: 豪猪想找一个好住处，最后发现一处避风的小洞，里面住着一家蛇。他请求搭个伙，一起住洞。蛇一家好心地同意了。
很快，蛇就后悔不该答应留客了。每转一个身，豪猪身上的尖刺都扎着它们。到了最后，它们客客气气地请他搬走。
“我很满意呀，谢谢，”豪猪说，“我就打算住在这儿。”他说着，客客气气地把蛇送出大门。为了保全自己的一身皮，蛇一家子只好去另找个家。
让出一根指头，结果丢掉了整只手。

source_paragraphs: At a great meeting of the Animals, who had gathered to elect a new ruler, the Monkey was asked to dance. This he did so well, with a thousand funny capers and grimaces, that the Animals were carried entirely off their feet with enthusiasm, and then and there, elected him their king.
The Fox did not vote for the Monkey and was much disgusted with the Animals for electing so unworthy a ruler.
One day he found a trap with a bit of meat in it. Hurrying to King Monkey, he told him he had found a rich treasure, which he had not touched because it belonged by right to his majesty the Monkey.
The greedy Monkey followed the Fox to the trap. As soon as he saw the meat he grasped eagerly for it, only to find himself held fast in the trap. The Fox stood off and laughed.
"You pretend to be our king," he said, "and cannot even take care of yourself!"
Shortly after that, another election among the Animals was held.
_The true leader proves himself by his qualities._
translated_paragraphs: 动物们齐聚一堂，要选出一位新首领。大家请猴子跳舞。他跳得真好，翻出千百种可笑的花样，扮出无数张鬼脸，动物们热烈欢呼，个个叫他迷住了，当场便选他做了自己的王。
狐狸没有把票投给猴子。他对动物们十分反感，居然选了个这么不称职的首领。
有一天，狐狸发现一个夹子，里头放着一块肉。他赶去见猴王，禀报说自己发现了一份贵重的宝贝，没敢伸手，因为照理那该归猴王陛下所有。
贪心的猴子跟着狐狸来到夹子边。一见那块肉，他就迫不及待伸手去抓，结果把自己牢牢夹住了。狐狸远远站着，笑了起来。
“你还充当我们的王，”他说，“连你自己都照顾不了呢！”
不久，动物们便又举行了一次选举。
配得上带领大家的人，要拿自己的本领和品行来证明。

source_paragraphs: Early one morning a hungry Wolf was prowling around a cottage at the edge of a village, when he heard a child crying in the house. Then he heard the Mother's voice say:
"Hush, child, hush! Stop your crying, or I will give you to the Wolf!"

Surprised but delighted at the prospect of so delicious a meal, the Wolf settled down under an open window, expecting every moment to have the child handed out to him. But though the little one continued to fret, the Wolf waited all day in vain. Then, toward nightfall, he heard the Mother's voice again as she sat down near the window to sing and rock her baby to sleep.
"There, child, there! The Wolf shall not get you. No, no! Daddy is watching and Daddy will kill him if he should come near!"
Just then the Father came within sight of the home, and the Wolf was barely able to save himself from the Dogs by a clever bit of running.
_Do not believe everything you hear._
translated_paragraphs: 有一天清早，一头饿狼在村边的一间茅舍外徘徊，听见屋里有个孩子在哭。随后他听到母亲的声音：
“乖，孩子，别哭了，安静点儿！再哭，我就把你交给狼去！”
听说将有这么可口的一餐，狼又惊又喜。他在一扇打开的窗户底下安顿下来，随时盼着有人把孩子递出来。可是孩子尽管一直哼哼唧唧，狼也白等了一整天。临近黄昏，他又听见那位母亲的声音。她坐到了窗边，一边唱歌，一边摇着宝宝睡觉。
“好了，孩子，好了！狼捉不到你的。不，不！爸爸看着呢，他要敢靠近，爸爸就会把他杀掉！”
正说着，父亲已经走到能望见家门的地方。狼全靠跑得机灵，才勉强从狗嘴底下逃脱。
听来的话，不能句句都信。

source_paragraphs: A jar of honey was upset and the sticky sweetness flowed out on the table. The sweet smell of the honey soon brought a large number of Flies buzzing around. They did not wait for an invitation. No, indeed; they settled right down, feet and all, to gorge themselves. The Flies were quickly smeared from head to foot with honey. Their wings stuck together. They could not pull their feet out of the sticky mass. And so they died, giving their lives for the sake of a taste of sweetness.
_Be not greedy for a little passing pleasure. It may destroy you._
translated_paragraphs: 一罐蜂蜜翻倒了，甜甜黏黏的蜜流了一桌子。蜂蜜的甜香很快招来一大群苍蝇，嗡嗡飞个不停。它们也没等谁招呼，当然不等！连脚带身，整只落了下去，只管大吃特吃。很快，苍蝇们从头到脚全糊满了蜜。两片翅膀粘在一起，脚也拔不出那片黏糊糊的蜜汁。就这样，它们死去了，为尝一口甜头，付出了自己的性命。
别贪图转瞬即逝的小小快活，它可能要了你的命。

source_paragraphs: An Eagle sat high in the branches of a great Oak. She seemed very sad and drooping for an Eagle. A Kite saw her.
"Why do you look so woebegone?" asked the Kite.
"I want to get married," replied the Eagle, "and I can't find a mate who can provide for me as I should like."
"Take me," said the Kite; "I am very strong, stronger even than you!"
"Do you really think you can provide for me?" asked the Eagle eagerly.
"Why, of course," replied the Kite. "That would be a very simple matter. I am so strong I can carry away an Ostrich in my talons as if it were a feather!"
The Eagle accepted the Kite immediately. But after the wedding, when the Kite flew away to find something to eat for his bride, all he had when he returned, was a tiny Mouse.
"Is that the Ostrich you talked about?" said the Eagle in disgust.
"To win you I would have said and promised anything," replied the Kite.
_Everything is fair in love._
translated_paragraphs: 一只鹰坐在一棵大橡树高高的枝头。对鹰而言，她的样子实在太忧伤、太无精打采了。一只鸢看见了她。
“你怎么一副愁眉苦脸的样子？”鸢问。
“我想结婚，”鹰答道，“但是找不到一个伴儿，能像我盼的那样供养我。”
“嫁给我吧，”鸢说，“我强壮极了，比你还强壮呢！”
“你当真觉得养得起我？”鹰热切地问。
“当然，”鸢回答，“那还不容易。我力气大得很，用爪子拎走一只鸵鸟，就跟拎片羽毛似的！”
鹰当即答应了鸢的求婚。可是婚礼过后，鸢飞出去为新娘找吃的，等他回来，手里却只有一只小得不能再小的老鼠。
“这就是你说的鸵鸟？”鹰很嫌弃地说。
“为了让你嫁给我，”鸢回答，“什么话我都说得出，什么诺我都肯许。”
在情场上，什么手段都算数。

sections.title_en: THE STAG, THE SHEEP, AND THE WOLF
source_paragraphs: One day a Stag came to a Sheep and asked her to lend him a measure of wheat. The Sheep knew him for a very swift runner, who could easily take himself out of reach, were he so inclined. So she asked him if he knew someone who would answer for him.
"Yes, yes," answered the Stag confidently, "the Wolf has promised to be my surety."

"The Wolf!" exclaimed the Sheep indignantly. "Do you think I would trust you on such security? I know the Wolf! He takes what he wants and runs off with it without paying. As for you, you can use your legs so well that I should have little chance of collecting the debt if I had to catch you for it!"
_Two blacks do not make a white._
translated_paragraphs: 一天，雄鹿来找绵羊，请她借给他一斗小麦。绵羊知道他跑得很快，要是他愿意，随时能跑得叫人再也追不上。于是她问他，认不认识愿意为他作保的。
“有，有！”雄鹿胸有成竹地答道，“狼已经答应给我做担保啦。”
“狼！”绵羊气愤地喊，“你以为有这样的担保，我就会相信你？我可知道狼的德行！他看中什么就拿了跑，从来不给钱。至于你，跑得又那么快，万一还得我来追你才能讨债，哪里能讨得到！”
两块黑的加在一起，也变不成白的。

source_paragraphs: Once upon a time a severe plague raged among the animals. Many died, and those who lived were so ill, that they cared for neither food nor drink, and dragged themselves about listlessly. No longer could a fat young hen tempt Master Fox to dinner, nor a tender lamb rouse greedy Sir Wolf's appetite.
At last the Lion decided to call a council. When all the animals were gathered together he arose and said:

"Dear friends, I believe the gods have sent this plague upon us as a punishment for our sins. Therefore, the most guilty one of us must be offered in sacrifice. Perhaps we may thus obtain forgiveness and cure for all.

"I will confess all _my_ sins first. I admit that I have been very greedy and have devoured many sheep. They had done me no harm. I have eaten goats and bulls and stags. To tell the truth, I even ate up a shepherd now and then.
"Now, if I am the most guilty, I am ready to be sacrificed. But I think it best that each one confess his sins as I have done. Then we can decide in all justice who is the most guilty."
"Your majesty," said the Fox, "you are too good. Can it be a crime to eat sheep, such stupid mutton heads? No, no, your majesty. You have done them great honor by eating them up.
"And so far as shepherds are concerned, we all know they belong to that puny race that pretends to be our masters."

All the animals applauded the Fox loudly. Then, though the Tiger, the Bear, the Wolf, and all the savage beasts recited the most wicked deeds, all were excused and made to appear very saint-like and innocent.
It was now the Ass's turn to confess.

"I remember," he said guiltily, "that one day as I was passing a field belonging to some priests, I was so tempted by the tender grass and my hunger, that I could not resist nibbling a bit of it. I had no right to do it, I admit--"

A great uproar among the beasts interrupted him. Here was the culprit who had brought misfortune on all of them! What a horrible crime it was to eat grass that belonged to someone else! It was enough to hang anyone for, much more an Ass.
Immediately they all fell upon him, the Wolf in the lead, and soon had made an end to him, sacrificing him to the gods then and there, and without the formality of an altar.
_The weak are made to suffer for the misdeeds of the powerful._
translated_paragraphs: 从前，动物中间暴发了一场严重的瘟疫。许多动物死了，活着的也病得厉害，吃喝都没兴致，拖着身子，无精打采地四处挪动。哪怕一只年轻肥嫩的母鸡，也引不起狐狸先生开饭的兴致，哪怕一只细皮嫩肉的小羊，也勾不动贪婪的狼大爷的胃口。
狮子终于决定召开会议。等所有动物齐集，他起身说道：
“亲爱的朋友们，我相信，众神降下这场瘟疫，是为了惩罚我们的罪过。因此，我们必须把其中罪过最大的那一个献作祭品。也许大家就能得到宽恕，也能一起得救。
“我先把我的罪过全坦白出来。我承认，我贪婪透顶，吃掉了许许多多绵羊。它们对我毫无伤害；我还吃过山羊、公牛和雄鹿。说老实话，隔三岔五，我甚至连牧羊人也吃。
“如果我罪最重，我愿意做祭品。不过我认为最好每位都像我这样认一认自己的罪。这样，咱们才好公公道道地裁决，究竟谁的罪最重。”
“大王，”狐狸说，“您实在太善良了。把绵羊那样一群蠢羊头吃掉，有什么罪可言？没有，没有啊，大王。能叫您吃进肚里，那可是给它们添了莫大的光彩。
“至于牧羊人嘛，大家都晓得，他们属于那个渺小却妄想做我们主人的族类。”
动物们为狐狸大声鼓掌。接下来，老虎、熊、狼以及各种凶猛的野兽，一个个供述了极其残暴的恶行，也全得到了开脱，显得跟圣徒似的，清清白白。
现在该驴认罪了。
“我记得，”他心怀愧疚地说，“有一天经过几位祭司的一块田，我肚子饿得慌，那些草又嫩得叫人忍不住，就偷偷啃了一点。我承认，那草我无权动——”
兽群一片喧嚣，打断了他的话。可算抓到把灾祸带给大家的罪魁祸首啦！吃属于别人的草，这是何等可怕的罪过！就凭这一条，无论谁都够上绞架了，何况还是一头驴。
狼打头阵，动物们一起扑上去，很快要了驴的命。也不用劳烦搭祭坛了，它们就地将他献给了神。
强者犯下的恶事，却叫弱者受苦抵偿。

source_paragraphs: A Shepherd, counting his Sheep one day, discovered that a number of them were missing.

Much irritated, he very loudly and boastfully declared that he would catch the thief and punish him as he deserved. The Shepherd suspected a Wolf of the deed and so set out toward a rocky region among the hills, where there were caves infested by Wolves. But before starting out he made a vow to Jupiter that if he would help him find the thief he would offer a fat Calf as a sacrifice.

The Shepherd searched a long time without finding any Wolves, but just as he was passing near a large cave on the mountain side, a huge Lion stalked out, carrying a Sheep. In great terror the Shepherd fell on his knees.
"Alas, O Jupiter, man does not know what he asks! To find the thief I offered to sacrifice a fat Calf. Now I promise you a full-grown Bull, if you but make the thief go away!"
_We are often not so eager for what we seek, after we have found it._
_Do not foolishly ask for things that would bring ruin if they were granted._
translated_paragraphs: 一天，牧人在清点自己的羊时，发现有好几只不见了。
他气恼极了，放声夸口，说自己非捉住那个贼不可，还要给他应得的惩罚。牧人怀疑是狼干的，就往山间多岩石的地方去寻。那里的山洞经常有狼出没。动身之前，他向朱庇特许了一个愿：若能得到神的帮助，找到偷羊贼，他便献一头肥牛犊作祭品。
牧人找了好久，一只狼也没看见。他正从山腰的一个大洞旁边经过，一头硕大的狮子叼着羊，大踏步走了出来。牧人吓得魂飞魄散，双膝跪倒。
“唉，朱庇特啊，人可真不懂自己求的究竟是什么！为了找到贼，我说献一头肥牛犊。现在，我答应献上一头成年的大公牛，只求您让这贼离开吧！”
苦苦寻觅的东西，一旦找到了，我们往往就没那么想要了。
要是愿望实现反而会带来毁灭，就别糊里糊涂地去求。

source_paragraphs: A Dog, to whom the butcher had thrown a bone, was hurrying home with his prize as fast as he could go. As he crossed a narrow footbridge, he happened to look down and saw himself reflected in the quiet water as if in a mirror. But the greedy Dog thought he saw a real Dog carrying a bone much bigger than his own.

If he had stopped to think he would have known better. But instead of thinking, he dropped his bone and sprang at the Dog in the river, only to find himself swimming for dear life to reach the shore. At last he managed to scramble out, and as he stood sadly thinking about the good bone he had lost, he realized what a stupid Dog he had been.
_It is very foolish to be greedy._
translated_paragraphs: 肉贩扔给狗一根骨头。狗叼着这件宝贝，以最快的脚步往家里赶。经过一座窄窄的人行桥时，他无意间低头一看。水面平静得像镜子，把他的模样映得清清楚楚。可贪心的狗以为水里真有一条狗，还叼着根比自己这根大得多的骨头。
要是他肯停一下想想，就会知道自己看错了。但他连想也不想，松嘴扔下骨头，腾身扑向河里的狗，结果只好在水里拼命游，设法保住性命，游到岸边。终于，他挣扎着爬了上来，伤心地想起自己丢掉的那根好骨头，这才明白自己做了一条多傻的狗。
贪心实在愚蠢。

source_paragraphs: A Hare was making fun of the Tortoise one day for being so slow.
"Do you ever get anywhere?" he asked with a mocking laugh.
"Yes," replied the Tortoise, "and I get there sooner than you think. I'll run you a race and prove it."

The Hare was much amused at the idea of running a race with the Tortoise, but for the fun of the thing he agreed. So the Fox, who had consented to act as judge, marked the distance and started the runners off.

The Hare was soon far out of sight, and to make the Tortoise feel very deeply how ridiculous it was for him to try a race with a Hare, he lay down beside the course to take a nap until the Tortoise should catch up.

The Tortoise meanwhile kept going slowly but steadily, and, after a time, passed the place where the Hare was sleeping. But the Hare slept on very peacefully; and when at last he did wake up, the Tortoise was near the goal. The Hare now ran his swiftest, but he could not overtake the Tortoise in time.
_The race is not always to the swift._
translated_paragraphs: 一天，野兔取笑乌龟走得慢。“照你这么走，能走得到什么地方呀？”野兔讥笑道。
“走得到呀，”乌龟说，“比你想的还快呢。来赛一场，你就知道了。”
跟乌龟赛跑，这念头把野兔逗乐了。为了好玩，它答应了。狐狸同意当裁判，划好赛程，让两位选手出发。
野兔一下子就跑得没影了。为了叫乌龟好好领教，跟野兔赛跑有多可笑，它干脆在赛道旁躺下来，打算睡上一觉，等乌龟追上来。
乌龟一步一步，虽慢，却一直在向前走。过了一阵，它经过了野兔睡觉的地方。野兔睡得真香啊！等它终于醒来，乌龟已经快到终点了。野兔使出最快的速度去追，到底还是没赶上。
赢得比赛的，不一定是跑得最快的那个。

sections.title_en: THE BEES AND WASPS, AND THE HORNET
source_paragraphs: A store of honey had been found in a hollow tree, and the Wasps declared positively that it belonged to them. The Bees were just as sure that the treasure was theirs. The argument grew very pointed, and it looked as if the affair could not be settled without a battle, when at last, with much good sense, they _agreed_ to let a judge decide the matter. So they brought the case before the Hornet, justice of the peace in that part of the woods.

When the Judge called the case, witnesses declared that they had seen certain winged creatures in the neighborhood of the hollow tree, who hummed loudly, and whose bodies were striped, yellow and black, like Bees.
Counsel for the Wasps immediately insisted that this description fitted his clients exactly.

Such evidence did not help Judge Hornet to any decision, so he adjourned court for six weeks to give him time to think it over. When the case came up again, both sides had a large number of witnesses. An Ant was first to take the stand, and was about to be cross-examined, when a wise old Bee addressed the Court.

"Your honor," he said, "the case has now been pending for six weeks. If it is not decided soon, the honey will not be fit for anything. I move that the Bees and the Wasps be both instructed to build a honey comb. Then we shall soon see to whom the honey really belongs."
The Wasps protested loudly. Wise Judge Hornet quickly understood why they did so: They knew they could not build a honey comb and fill it with honey.
"It is clear," said the Judge, "who made the comb and who could not have made it. The honey belongs to the Bees."
_Ability proves itself by deeds._
translated_paragraphs: 有人在一棵空心树里发现了一批蜂蜜。黄蜂斩钉截铁地声称，蜜归它们。蜜蜂同样坚持，这份宝藏是自己的。双方争论得越来越尖锐，眼看非打上一仗才能了结。好在最后它们总算做了件明白事，一致同意请法官裁决。它们把这桩案子告到了胡蜂那里，他是这片林子的治安法官。
法官开庭审理时，证人们纷纷作证，说看见过一些带翅膀的生物在空心树旁出没。这些生物嗡嗡声很大，身上黄黑两色相间，有一道道条纹，像是蜜蜂。
黄蜂一方的辩护人立刻坚持说，这些描述跟他的当事人也丝毫不差。
这样的证据帮不了胡蜂法官下判断，他便宣布休庭六个星期，好留出时间仔细琢磨。等到再次开庭，双方都带来大批证人。一只蚂蚁头一个作证，正要接受双方询问，一只聪明的老蜜蜂向法庭开口了。
“法官大人，”他说，“这桩案子已经拖了六个星期。再不快些判明，那些蜂蜜就什么用也没有了。我提议，请命蜜蜂和黄蜂各建一个蜂巢。到时候大家马上就会明白，蜂蜜究竟归谁。”
黄蜂们顿时高声抗议。聪明的胡蜂法官立刻明白，它们为什么抗议：它们自己知道，自己造不出那样的蜜巢，更没法把它装满蜂蜜。
“谁造了那个蜂巢，谁绝不可能造得出来，现在清楚了，”法官说，“蜂蜜归蜜蜂所有。”
真本事要用做出来的事证明。

sections.title_en: THE LARK AND HER YOUNG ONES
source_paragraphs: A Lark made her nest in a field of young wheat. As the days passed, the wheat stalks grew tall and the young birds, too, grew in strength. Then one day, when the ripe golden grain waved in the breeze, the Farmer and his son came into the field.
"This wheat is now ready for reaping," said the Farmer. "We must call in our neighbors and friends to help us harvest it."

The young Larks in their nest close by were much frightened, for they knew they would be in great danger if they did not leave the nest before the reapers came. When the Mother Lark returned with food for them, they told her what they had heard.
"Do not be frightened, children," said the Mother Lark. "If the Farmer said he would call in his neighbors and friends to help him do his work, this wheat will not be reaped for a while yet."
A few days later, the wheat was so ripe, that when the wind shook the stalks, a hail of wheat grains came rustling down on the young Larks' heads.
"If this wheat is not harvested at once," said the Farmer, "we shall lose half the crop. We cannot wait any longer for help from our friends. Tomorrow we must set to work, ourselves."
When the young Larks told their mother what they had heard that day, she said:
"Then we must be off at once. When a man decides to do his own work and not depend on any one else, then you may be sure there will be no more delay."
There was much fluttering and trying out of wings that afternoon, and at sunrise next day, when the Farmer and his son cut down the grain, they found an empty nest.
_Self-help is the best help._
translated_paragraphs: 云雀在一块青苗麦田里做了窝。一天天过去，麦秆长高了，雏鸟也渐渐结实起来。一天，麦粒熟了，金色的麦浪随微风摇荡。农夫带着儿子来到田里。
“麦子已经可以割了，”农夫说，“我们得喊来邻居朋友帮忙收割。”
窝就在旁边，小云雀们听了怕得很。它们明白，要是等割麦人来了还没来得及离窝，处境就会很危险。等妈妈带着吃的回来，它们便把听到的话告诉了她。
“不用怕，孩子们，”云雀妈妈说，“如果农夫说要叫来邻居朋友帮他干活，这麦子一时半会儿还割不了。”
几天后，麦子实在熟透了。风一摇麦秆，一阵冰雹似的麦粒便沙沙落下来，砸在小云雀们的头上。
“这麦子再不赶紧收割，”农夫说，“我们会损失半数收成。不能再等朋友来帮忙了。明天我们得自己动手。”
小云雀们把当天听到的话告诉妈妈。她说：
“那我们马上就得走。等一个人决定自己动手做自己的事，再也不靠旁人的时候，你就知道他不会再拖延了。”
那天下午，窝里好一阵扑棱拍动、练习飞翔。第二天太阳升起，农夫和儿子割起麦子时，他们找到的已是个空巢。
最管用的帮手是自己。

sections.title_en: THE CAT AND THE OLD RAT
source_paragraphs: There was once a Cat who was so watchful, that a Mouse hardly dared show the tip of his whiskers for fear of being eaten alive. That Cat seemed to be everywhere at once with his claws all ready for a pounce. At last the Mice kept so closely to their dens, that the Cat saw he would have to use his wits well to catch one. So one day he climbed up on a shelf and hung from it, head downward, as if he were dead, holding himself up by clinging to some ropes with one paw.

When the Mice peeped out and saw him in that position, they thought he had been hung up there in punishment for some misdeed. Very timidly at first they stuck out their heads and sniffed about carefully. But as nothing stirred, all trooped joyfully out to celebrate the death of the Cat.
Just then the Cat let go his hold, and before the Mice recovered from their surprise, he had made an end of three or four.

Now the Mice kept more strictly at home than ever. But the Cat, who was still hungry for Mice, knew more tricks than one. Rolling himself in flour until he was covered completely, he lay down in the flour bin, with one eye open for the Mice.

Sure enough, the Mice soon began to come out. To the Cat it was almost as if he already had a plump young Mouse under his claws, when an old Rat, who had had much experience with Cats and traps, and had even lost a part of his tail to pay for it, sat up at a safe distance from a hole in the wall where he lived.
"Take care!" he cried. "That may be a heap of meal, but it looks to me very much like the Cat. Whatever it is, it is wisest to keep at a safe distance."
_The wise do not let themselves be tricked a second time._
translated_paragraphs: 从前有一只猫看守得太严，老鼠连胡须尖都几乎不敢露出来，生怕被活活吃掉。那猫仿佛能同时出现在各处，两爪随时准备出击。到后来，老鼠们紧守着各自的洞穴，猫看出来，想逮到一只非得好好动点脑筋不可。有一天，他爬上架子，一只爪勾牢几条绳子，头朝下倒挂着，好像已经死了。
老鼠们往外偷看，见他那样悬着，以为他做了什么坏事受罚，被吊死在那儿。起初，他们怯生生地把头探出来，小心地四处闻一闻。见始终一点动静也没有，大家便高高兴兴一队队跑出洞来，庆祝猫的死讯。
就在这一刻，猫松开了爪子。老鼠们还来不及从惊愕中回过神，他已经解决了三四只。
从此，老鼠们比从前更严地守在家里。可是猫还馋老鼠肉，而且他的花招可不止一个。他在面粉里打滚，直到全身上下盖得严严实实，随后躺进面粉箱，留一只眼睛守着老鼠。
果然没多久，老鼠们开始从洞里出来。猫几乎已经感觉爪底按住了一只肥嫩的小老鼠。偏在这时，一只老鼠长者在离猫很远的墙洞附近直起身来。那个洞是他的住处。他跟猫和捕鼠夹打过不少交道，为了这些经验，甚至还赔进了一截尾巴。
“小心！”他喊道，“那也许是一堆面粉，可我瞅着更像那只猫。不管是个什么，还是离得远些最明智。”
有见识的人，不肯上第二回当。
