source_paragraphs: One bright morning as the Fox was following his sharp nose through the wood in search of a bite to eat, he saw a Crow on the limb of a tree overhead. This was by no means the first Crow the Fox had ever seen. What caught his attention this time and made him stop for a second look, was that the lucky Crow held a bit of cheese in her beak.
"No need to search any farther," thought sly Master Fox. "Here is a dainty bite for my breakfast."
Up he trotted to the foot of the tree in which the Crow was sitting, and looking up admiringly, he cried, "Good-morning, beautiful creature!"
The Crow, her head cocked on one side, watched the Fox suspiciously. But she kept her beak tightly closed on the cheese and did not return his greeting.

"What a charming creature she is!" said the Fox. "How her feathers shine! What a beautiful form and what splendid wings! Such a wonderful Bird should have a very lovely voice, since everything else about her is so perfect. Could she sing just one song, I know I should hail her Queen of Birds."
Listening to these flattering words, the Crow forgot all her suspicion, and also her breakfast. She wanted very much to be called Queen of Birds.
So she opened her beak wide to utter her loudest caw, and down fell the cheese straight into the Fox's open mouth.
"Thank you," said Master Fox sweetly, as he walked off. "Though it is cracked, you have a voice sure enough. But where are your wits?"
_The flatterer lives at the expense of those who will listen to him._
translated_paragraphs: 一个明亮的早晨，狐狸循着灵敏的鼻子在林子里转悠，想弄点吃的。他看见头顶树枝上站着一只乌鸦。这当然不是狐狸生来头一次看见乌鸦。叫他停下脚步、再看一眼的是，这只好运气的乌鸦嘴里叼着块奶酪。
“不必再往前找了，”狡猾的狐狸先生想，“这就有一份精致可口的早餐。”
他一路小跑，来到乌鸦歇脚的树底下，仰着脸，满怀仰慕地喊：“早上好啊，美丽的小鸟！”
乌鸦偏着头，警惕地打量狐狸。她紧紧用嘴衔住奶酪，没有回他的招呼。
“多么迷人的小鸟！”狐狸说，“她的羽毛多么有光泽！多么漂亮的身段，何等辉煌的翅膀！这么美妙的一只鸟，别的地方样样完美，准有副很好听的嗓子。要是她肯唱上一首，我准会尊她为百鸟之后。”
听着这一番奉承，乌鸦把满心的怀疑忘光了，也把自己的早餐忘光了。她一心想着受封为百鸟之后。
她猛地张开嘴，拼命大叫了一声“哇”。奶酪掉下来，直落进狐狸张开的嘴里。
“谢谢，”狐狸先生一边走开，一边甜言蜜语地说，“你的嗓子虽有些破，好歹也算有嗓子。不过，你的脑筋呢？”
爱拍马屁的人，正靠那些肯听他奉承的人过活。

source_paragraphs: A Traveler had hired an Ass to carry him to a distant part of the country. The owner of the Ass went with the Traveler, walking beside him to drive the Ass and point out the way.

The road led across a treeless plain where the Sun beat down fiercely. So intense did the heat become, that the Traveler at last decided to stop for a rest, and as there was no other shade to be found, the Traveler sat down in the shadow of the Ass.

Now the heat had affected the Driver as much as it had the Traveler, and even more, for he had been walking. Wishing also to rest in the shade cast by the Ass, he began to quarrel with the Traveler, saying he had hired the Ass and not the shadow it cast.
The two soon came to blows, and while they were fighting, the Ass took to its heels.
_In quarreling about the shadow we often lose the substance._
translated_paragraphs: 一位旅人雇了头驴，要它载自己到国内远处去。驴的主人也跟旅人同行，走在身旁，一路赶驴指路。
道路横穿一片一棵树也不生的平原，太阳毒辣地照下来。热得实在受不了，旅人终于决定停下来休息。旁边找不到别的阴凉，他就坐进驴身投下的影子里。
热气同样折磨着赶驴人，况且他一路步行，比旅人还难熬。他也想坐在驴影底下歇息，便和旅人争论起来，说雇出去的是驴，没有连驴投下的影子也租出去。
两人很快拳脚相向。而在他们扭打的时候，驴却撒腿跑了。
为了影子争执不下，常常连那投下影子的实物也要失去。

sections.title_en: THE MILLER, HIS SON, AND THE ASS
source_paragraphs: One day, a long time ago, an old Miller and his Son were on their way to market with an Ass which they hoped to sell. They drove him very slowly, for they thought they would have a better chance to sell him if they kept him in good condition. As they walked along the highway some travelers laughed loudly at them.
"What foolishness," cried one, "to walk when they might as well ride. The most stupid of the three is not the one you would expect it to be."
The Miller did not like to be laughed at, so he told his son to climb up and ride.
They had gone a little farther along the road, when three merchants passed by.
"Oho, what have we here?" they cried. "Respect old age, young man! Get down, and let the old man ride."
Though the Miller was not tired, he made the boy get down and climbed up himself to ride, just to please the Merchants.
At the next turnstile they overtook some women carrying market baskets loaded with vegetables and other things to sell.
"Look at the old fool," exclaimed one of them. "Perched on the Ass, while that poor boy has to walk."
The Miller felt a bit vexed, but to be agreeable he told the Boy to climb up behind him.
They had no sooner started out again than a loud shout went up from another company of people on the road.
"What a crime," cried one, "to load up a poor dumb beast like that! They look more able to carry the poor creature, than he to carry them."
"They must be on their way to sell the poor thing's hide," said another.

The Miller and his Son quickly scrambled down, and a short time later, the market place was thrown into an uproar as the two came along carrying the Donkey slung from a pole. A great crowd of people ran out to get a closer look at the strange sight.

The Ass did not dislike being carried, but so many people came up to point at him and laugh and shout, that he began to kick and bray, and then, just as they were crossing a bridge, the ropes that held him gave way, and down he tumbled into the river.
The poor Miller now set out sadly for home. By trying to please everybody, he had pleased nobody, and lost his Ass besides.
_If you try to please all, you please none._
translated_paragraphs: 很久以前的一天，老磨坊主和儿子赶着一头驴到集市上去，希望把它卖掉。他们走得很慢，心想得让驴保持精神健壮，才更容易卖个好价钱。正沿大路走着，有几位旅行的人大声嘲笑他们。
“多傻，”一个人喊道，“明明可以骑着，偏要自己走。三个里面最蠢的，可还不一定是你本来以为的那个。”
磨坊主不喜欢被人嘲笑，便吩咐儿子爬上去骑。
又沿路走了一小段，迎面经过三位商人。
“哎呀，瞧我们看见什么了！”他们喊道，“年轻人，要敬重长者！下来，让老先生骑。”
磨坊主尽管不累，为了让商人们满意，还是叫男孩下来，自己跨上去骑。
在下一道转门前，他们赶上几个女人。妇人们提着去赶集的篮子，装满蔬菜和各样待卖的东西。
“看看那个老糊涂，”其中一人说，“自己高高坐在驴上，那可怜的孩子却要步行。”
磨坊主心里有点恼火，可为了顺别人的心意，还是叫男孩爬上驴背，坐到身后。
他们刚重新上路，路上另一帮人又高声喊起来。
“太造孽啦，”一个人喊，“让可怜的牲口驮这么重，它又不会开口诉苦！看上去倒是他们更有力气扛那可怜的家伙，不是它有力气扛他们。”
“依我看，他们准是打算去卖这可怜家伙的皮。”另一个人说。
磨坊主和儿子赶快爬下驴背。过不了多久，集市上闹翻了天，原来这两个人用一根长杆抬着吊起来的驴出现了。一大群人奔出来，想凑近看看这稀奇的景象。
驴本来不讨厌给人抬着。可这么多人走上前，指着它又笑又叫，它就开始乱踢乱叫。他们正过桥，吊着驴的绳子突然断了，驴扑通掉进河里。
可怜的磨坊主悲伤地动身回家了。他一心要叫人人满意，末了一个也没讨好，连驴也丢了。
想讨好所有的人，结果谁也讨好不了。

source_paragraphs: A Dove saw an Ant fall into a brook. The Ant struggled in vain to reach the bank, and in pity, the Dove dropped a blade of straw close beside it. Clinging to the straw like a shipwrecked sailor to a broken spar, the Ant floated safely to shore.

Soon after, the Ant saw a man getting ready to kill the Dove with a stone. But just as he cast the stone, the Ant stung him in the heel, so that the pain made him miss his aim, and the startled Dove flew to safety in a distant wood.
_A kindness is never wasted._
translated_paragraphs: 一只鸽子看见一只蚂蚁掉进了小溪。蚂蚁拼命挣扎，还是够不着岸。鸽子可怜它，丢下一根稻草，正落在蚂蚁身边。蚂蚁紧紧抱住它，好比遇到海难的水手抱住一截断木，安然漂到了岸边。
不久，蚂蚁看见一个人拿着石头，正要打死鸽子。就在石头出手的时候，蚂蚁在他脚后跟上狠狠一蜇。那人一疼，石头打偏了。鸽子受了惊，一直飞进远处的树林，安全了。
你给出去的一点善意，总有它的用处。

source_paragraphs: A long time ago a Man met a Satyr in the forest and succeeded in making friends with him. The two soon became the best of comrades, living together in the Man's hut. But one cold winter evening, as they were walking homeward, the Satyr saw the Man blow on his fingers.
"Why do you do that?" asked the Satyr.
"To warm my hands," the Man replied.

When they reached home the Man prepared two bowls of porridge. These he placed steaming hot on the table, and the comrades sat down very cheerfully to enjoy the meal. But much to the Satyr's surprise, the Man began to blow into his bowl of porridge.
"Why do you do that?" he asked.
"To cool my porridge," replied the Man.
The Satyr sprang hurriedly to his feet and made for the door.
"Goodby," he said, "I've seen enough. A fellow that blows hot and cold in the same breath cannot be friends with me!"
_The man who talks for both sides is not to be trusted by either._
translated_paragraphs: 很久以前，有个人在森林中遇到一位半人半羊的林神萨堤尔，设法和他交上了朋友。不久，两位成了最亲密的伙伴，一起住在那人的小屋里。一个寒冬的傍晚，他们结伴回家时，萨堤尔看见那人正往自己的手指上呵气。
“你这么做是为什么？”萨堤尔问。
“让手暖和些。”那人回答。
到家后，那人备了两碗粥，热气腾腾地端上桌子。两个伙伴高高兴兴坐下来，准备享用这一餐。可叫萨堤尔十分惊讶的是，那人对着自己碗里的粥吹起气来。
“你这么做是为什么？”他问。
“让粥凉一凉。”那人回答。
萨堤尔匆匆跳起身，朝门口走去。
“再见，”他说，“我已经看得够多了。同样一口气，又能吹热，又能吹冷，这样的家伙可做不了我的朋友！”
今天替这一边说话，明天又替另一边说话，结果哪边都不该信他。

sections.title_en: THE WOLF, THE KID, AND THE GOAT
source_paragraphs: Mother Goat was going to market one morning to get provisions for her household, which consisted of but one little Kid and herself.
"Take good care of the house, my son," she said to the Kid, as she carefully latched the door. "Do not let anyone in, unless he gives you this password: 'Down with the Wolf and all his race!'"
Strangely enough, a Wolf was lurking near and heard what the Goat had said. So, as soon as Mother Goat was out of sight, up he trotted to the door and knocked.
"Down with the Wolf and all his race," said the Wolf softly.
It was the right password, but when the Kid peeped through a crack in the door and saw the shadowy figure outside, he did not feel at all easy.
"Show me a white paw," he said, "or I won't let you in."
A white paw, of course, is a feature few Wolves can show, and so Master Wolf had to go away as hungry as he had come.
"You can never be too sure," said the Kid, when he saw the Wolf making off to the woods.
_Two sureties are better than one._
translated_paragraphs: 一天早上，山羊妈妈要上集市给全家购置食物。她的家里只有一只小山羊和她自己。
“儿子，看好家门，”她一边小心扣好门闩，一边嘱咐小山羊，“谁来也别放进来，除非说出这个暗号，‘打倒狼和它的整个家族！’”
怪就怪在，近旁偏有一只狼潜伏着，把山羊妈妈说的话听得一清二楚。等她走得看不见了，狼便一路小跑来到门前，敲了敲门。
“打倒狼和它的整个家族。”狼轻声说。
暗号倒是没错，可小山羊从门缝里往外瞧，瞅着外面那个黑黢黢的身影，心里一点儿也不踏实。
“给我看一只白爪儿，”他说，“否则我不放你进来。”
白色的爪子，恐怕没几头狼亮得出来。狼先生只好饿着肚皮走了，跟来的时候一样饿。
“多问一声，总没坏处。”小山羊望着狼往树林里去，说道。
两重保证，总胜过一重。

source_paragraphs: The Swallow and the Crow had an argument one day about their plumage.
Said the Swallow: "Just look at my bright and downy feathers. Your black stiff quills are not worth having. Why don't you dress better? Show a little pride!"
"Your feathers may do very well in spring," replied the Crow, "but--I don't remember ever having seen you around in winter, and that's when I enjoy myself most."
_Friends in fine weather only, are not worth much._
translated_paragraphs: 一天，燕子和乌鸦为了身上的羽毛争论起来。
燕子说：“瞧瞧我这身鲜亮、柔软的羽毛。你那些又黑又硬的翎毛，有什么可要的？怎么不穿好一些？你也该有一点儿自尊心呀！”
“你那身羽毛春天穿穿也许很好，”乌鸦回答，“只是——我可不记得在冬天见过你。偏偏我最快乐的时候，就是冬天。”
只有风和日丽时才来往的朋友，不大值得看重。

source_paragraphs: There was once a baby show among the Animals in the forest. Jupiter provided the prize. Of course all the proud mammas from far and near brought their babies. But none got there earlier than Mother Monkey. Proudly she presented her baby among the other contestants.
As you can imagine, there was quite a laugh when the Animals saw the ugly flat-nosed, hairless, pop-eyed little creature.
"Laugh if you will," said the Mother Monkey. "Though Jupiter may not give him the prize, I know that he is the prettiest, the sweetest, the dearest darling in the world."
_Mother love is blind._
translated_paragraphs: 森林里的动物们举办过一场宝宝评比大会，由朱庇特提供奖品。远近各处自豪的妈妈们，自然都带来了自己的宝宝。不过，谁也没比猴妈妈到得早。她得意地把孩子放到其他参赛宝宝中间。
你准能想象，动物们见到这个扁鼻子、没什么毛、眼睛又凸的小丑怪，笑声可不小。
“要笑你们就笑吧，”猴妈妈说，“即使朱庇特不把奖品颁给他，我也知道，他是全世界最漂亮、最甜美、最亲爱的心肝宝贝。”
母亲的爱，看不见自己孩子的丑处。

sections.title_en: THE LION, THE ASS, AND THE FOX
source_paragraphs: A Lion, an Ass, and a Fox were hunting in company, and caught a large quantity of game. The Ass was asked to divide the spoil. This he did very fairly, giving each an equal share.
The Fox was well satisfied, but the Lion flew into a great rage over it, and with one stroke of his huge paw, he added the Ass to the pile of slain.
Then he turned to the Fox.
"You divide it," he roared angrily.

The Fox wasted no time in talking. He quickly piled all the game into one great heap. From this he took a very small portion for himself, such undesirable bits as the horns and hoofs of a mountain goat, and the end of an ox tail.
The Lion now recovered his good humor entirely.
"Who taught you to divide so fairly?" he asked pleasantly.
"I learned a lesson from the Ass," replied the Fox, carefully edging away.
_Learn from the misfortunes of others._
translated_paragraphs: 狮子、驴和狐狸结伴打猎，收获颇丰。大家请驴来分配战利品。驴分得十分公平，给每位的分量都一样多。
狐狸很满意，狮子却大发雷霆。他抬起巨爪，只打了一下，驴也成了那堆死猎物中的一具。
接着，他转向狐狸。
“你来分！”他怒气冲冲地吼道。
狐狸没浪费工夫多说一个字。他很快把猎物拢成一大堆，只从里面给自己挑出极小的一份，尽是些没人想要的零碎，比如山羊的角和蹄子，还有一截牛尾巴尖儿。
狮子这才完全恢复了好脾气。
“谁教你分得这么公平的？”他和颜悦色地问。
“我从驴身上学会的。”狐狸一边回答，一边小心往远处挪。
要懂得从旁人的不幸中吸取教训。

source_paragraphs: A long time ago, the Lion, the Fox, the Jackal, and the Wolf agreed to go hunting together, sharing with each other whatever they found.
One day the Wolf ran down a Stag and immediately called his comrades to divide the spoil.
Without being asked, the Lion placed himself at the head of the feast to do the carving, and, with a great show of fairness, began to count the guests.
"One," he said, counting on his claws, "that is myself the Lion. Two, that's the Wolf, three, is the Jackal, and the Fox makes four."
He then very carefully divided the Stag into four equal parts.
"I am King Lion," he said, when he had finished, "so of course I get the first part. This next part falls to me because I am the strongest; and _this_ is mine because I am the bravest."
He now began to glare at the others very savagely. "If any of you have any claim to the part that is left," he growled, stretching his claws meaningly, "now is the time to speak up."
_Might makes right._
translated_paragraphs: 很久以前，狮子、狐狸、胡狼和狼约好一块儿去打猎，得到什么，大家就分什么。
一天，狼追到一头雄鹿，立刻招呼伙伴们前来分配猎物。
不等旁人邀请，狮子就自己站到席首，动手切分，很公正似的数起了宾客。
“一，”他掰着爪子数，“是我，狮子。二，是狼。三，是胡狼。加上狐狸，合共四位。”
然后他极为仔细地把雄鹿分了均等的四份。
“我是狮王，”切完了，他说，“头一份当然归我。这下一份也该归我，因为我力气最大。还有这一份是我的，因为我最勇敢。”
接着他恶狠狠地瞪视同伴们。“留下的这一份，你们谁要是觉得自己有权要，”他低声咆哮，意味深长地伸出利爪，“现在就可以开口。”
有强权在手，便能把自己的话硬说成公理。

source_paragraphs: A little Mole once said to his Mother:
"Why, Mother, you said I was blind! But I am sure I can see!"
Mother Mole saw she would have to get such conceit out of his head. So she put a bit of frankincense before him and asked him to tell what it was.
The little Mole peered at it.
"Why, that's a pebble!"
"Well, my son, that proves you've lost your sense of smell as well as being blind."
_Boast of one thing and you will be found lacking in that and a few other things as well._
translated_paragraphs: 有一次，小鼹鼠对妈妈说：
“咦，妈妈，你说我眼睛瞎！可我敢肯定，我看得见！”
鼹鼠妈妈觉得，得设法叫他改掉这种自负。她把一小块乳香放在他面前，请他说出是什么东西。
小鼹鼠眯着眼睛瞧了瞧。
“这还用说，是块小石子！”
“好吧，孩子，这说明你不光看不见，连嗅觉也弄丢了。”
夸口说自己样样本领里有一项了得，可能反而叫人看出，你不只少了这一项，还少了别的几项。

sections.title_en: THE NORTH WIND AND THE SUN
source_paragraphs: The North Wind and the Sun had a quarrel about which of them was the stronger. While they were disputing with much heat and bluster, a Traveler passed along the road wrapped in a cloak.
"Let us agree," said the Sun, "that he is the stronger who can strip that Traveler of his cloak."
"Very well," growled the North Wind, and at once sent a cold, howling blast against the Traveler.

With the first gust of wind the ends of the cloak whipped about the Traveler's body. But he immediately wrapped it closely around him, and the harder the Wind blew, the tighter he held it to him. The North Wind tore angrily at the cloak, but all his efforts were in vain.

Then the Sun began to shine. At first his beams were gentle, and in the pleasant warmth after the bitter cold of the North Wind, the Traveler unfastened his cloak and let it hang loosely from his shoulders. The Sun's rays grew warmer and warmer. The man took off his cap and mopped his brow. At last he became so heated that he pulled off his cloak, and, to escape the blazing sunshine, threw himself down in the welcome shade of a tree by the roadside.
_Gentleness and kind persuasion win where force and bluster fail._
translated_paragraphs: 北风和太阳吵起来了，它们都说自己力气大。正当它们吵得火热、谁也不服谁的时候，路上走过一个裹着斗篷的旅人。
“咱们说好了，”太阳说，“谁能让那人脱下斗篷，谁就更厉害。”
“好哇！”北风低吼一声，立刻裹着寒气，呼啸着迎面扑向旅人。
头一阵风刮来，斗篷的下摆甩了起来，拍打着旅人的身子。他立刻把斗篷裹紧。风刮得越狠，他就攥得越紧。北风气得直撕扯那件斗篷，白费了好大一场劲。
轮到太阳了。起初，阳光柔柔地照着。刚挨过刺骨的寒风，旅人觉得暖和极了，便解开扣子，让斗篷松松地垂在肩头。阳光越来越暖。旅人摘下帽子，擦了擦额头。到后来，他热得干脆脱下斗篷，往路边可爱的树荫里一躺，好避一避火辣辣的太阳。
一味逞强办不成的事，温和地劝一劝，倒可能办成。

source_paragraphs: The Lion had been badly hurt by the horns of a Goat, which he was eating. He was very angry to think that any animal that he chose for a meal, should be so brazen as to wear such dangerous things as horns to scratch him while he ate. So he commanded that all animals with horns should leave his domains within twenty-four hours.

The command struck terror among the beasts. All those who were so unfortunate as to have horns, began to pack up and move out. Even the Hare, who, as you know, has no horns and so had nothing to fear, passed a very restless night, dreaming awful dreams about the fearful Lion.
And when he came out of the warren in the early morning sunshine, and there saw the shadow cast by his long and pointed ears, a terrible fright seized him.
"Goodby, neighbor Cricket," he called. "I'm off. He will certainly make out that my ears are horns, no matter what I say."
_Do not give your enemies the slightest reason to attack your reputation._
_Your enemies will seize any excuse to attack you._
translated_paragraphs: 狮子在吃一只山羊时，被羊角弄伤了，而且伤得不轻。他气坏了，自己挑中做食物的动物，居然胆大包天，敢长着犄角这样危险的东西，在他进餐时划伤他。于是他下令，凡是头上有角的动物，一律在二十四小时内离开他的领地。
这道命令让百兽陷入恐慌。凡是不幸长角的，都开始收拾行李搬走。连野兔这样一只如你所知、压根儿不长角、照理什么也不必怕的动物，也整夜没睡踏实，尽做有关可怕狮子的噩梦。
清早，他从兔窝钻进阳光里，看见自己那对又长又尖的耳朵投下的影子，一股惊恐顿时攥住了他。
“再见啦，蟋蟀邻居，”他喊道，“我这就出走。不管我怎么说，他肯定会一口咬定，我这对耳朵就是角。”
别让敌人抓着哪怕一点儿攻击你名声的由头。
你的敌人会抓住所能找到的任何借口向你发难。

source_paragraphs: A pack of Wolves lurked near the Sheep pasture. But the Dogs kept them all at a respectful distance, and the Sheep grazed in perfect safety. But now the Wolves thought of a plan to trick the Sheep.

"Why is there always this hostility between us?" they said. "If it were not for those Dogs who are always stirring up trouble, I am sure we should get along beautifully. Send them away and you will see what good friends we shall become."
The Sheep were easily fooled. They persuaded the Dogs to go away, and that very evening the Wolves had the grandest feast of their lives.
_Do not give up friends for foes._
translated_paragraphs: 一群狼潜伏在绵羊的草场附近。牧羊犬把它们远远挡在外头，绵羊安安稳稳地吃草。可这时候，狼想出一条骗羊的计策。
“为什么咱们总得这么针锋相对？”它们说，“要不是那些狗成天惹是生非，我们一定能相处得很愉快。把他们打发走吧，瞧瞧咱们能成为多好的朋友。”
绵羊很容易就上了当。他们劝走了狗。就在那天晚上，狼群享用了一生中最丰盛的一顿大餐。
别为了仇敌，放弃朋友。

source_paragraphs: A Fox was caught in a trap one fine morning, because he had got too near the Farmer's hen house. No doubt he was hungry, but that was not an excuse for stealing. A Cock, rising early, discovered what had happened. He knew the Fox could not get at him, so he went a little closer to get a good look at his enemy.
The Fox saw a slender chance of escape.

"Dear friend," he said, "I was just on my way to visit a sick relative, when I stumbled into this string and got all tangled up. But please do not tell anybody about it. I dislike causing sorrow to anybody, and I am sure I can soon gnaw this string to pieces."
But the Cock was not to be so easily fooled. He soon roused the whole hen yard, and when the Farmer came running out, that was the end of Mr. Fox.
_The wicked deserve no aid._
translated_paragraphs: 一个晴朗的早晨，狐狸靠农夫的鸡舍太近，中了圈套。他肚子饿，这毫无疑问，但肚饿并不是偷东西的理由。一只早起的公鸡看见了这一幕。他知道狐狸够不到自己，于是稍稍走近一点，想好好瞧一瞧这个敌人。
狐狸瞥见了一丝逃命的机会。
“好朋友，”他说，“我刚才是想去探望生病的亲戚，没留神让这根绳子绊住，才缠成这样。不过，还请你别告诉任何人。我最不愿意招得别人忧心，这根绳子，我相信自己很快就可以咬断。”
可是这只公鸡没那么容易上当。他立刻把整个鸡院叫醒了。等农夫奔出来的时候，狐狸先生也就走到了末日。
作恶的人不配得到援手。

sections.title_en: THE ASS IN THE LION'S SKIN
source_paragraphs: An Ass found a Lion's skin left in the forest by a hunter. He dressed himself in it, and amused himself by hiding in a thicket and rushing out suddenly at the animals who passed that way. All took to their heels the moment they saw him.

The Ass was so pleased to see the animals running away from him, just as if he were King Lion himself, that he could not keep from expressing his delight by a loud, harsh bray. A Fox, who ran with the rest, stopped short as soon as he heard the voice. Approaching the Ass, he said with a laugh:
"If you had kept your mouth shut you might have frightened me, too. But you gave yourself away with that silly bray."
_A fool may deceive by his dress and appearance, but his words will soon show what he really is._
translated_paragraphs: 一头驴在森林里找到一张被猎人丢下的狮皮。他披着狮皮，躲在密丛里，等别的动物经过时突然冲出去吓唬人，拿这当消遣。动物们一见他，纷纷拔腿逃开。
他看着大伙儿从自己面前逃走，好像自己当真是位狮王，不禁心花怒放，再也忍不住了，张嘴发出一声又响又难听的驴叫。狐狸原先也在跟着大伙儿逃，一听见叫声，猛然刹住脚步。他走近驴，笑着说：
“你要是闭紧了嘴，说不定连我也能叫你吓到。可惜你一声傻叫，让自己露了馅。”
蠢人靠衣着模样也许能骗人一时，一开口，很快就会露出本来面目。

sections.title_en: THE FISHERMAN AND THE LITTLE FISH
source_paragraphs: A poor Fisherman, who lived on the fish he caught, had bad luck one day and caught nothing but a very small fry. The Fisherman was about to put it in his basket when the little Fish said:
"Please spare me, Mr. Fisherman! I am so small it is not worth while to carry me home. When I am bigger, I shall make you a much better meal."
But the Fisherman quickly put the fish into his basket.
"How foolish I should be," he said, "to throw you back. However small you may be, you are better than nothing at all."
_A small gain is worth more than a large promise._
translated_paragraphs: 有个贫穷的渔夫，靠自己捕来的鱼度日。一天他运气不好，什么大鱼也没捞着，只打到一条很小的鱼苗。渔夫正要把它放进鱼篓，小鱼开口了：
“请饶我一命，渔夫先生！我还那么小，不值得您带回家。等我长大了，让您吃上一餐，肯定比现在强得多。”
渔夫却很快把小鱼放进了篓子。
“要把你扔回水里，”他说，“那我也太傻了。你再小，也比一无所得强。”
已经到手的一点点收获，比天大的许诺更有价值。

sections.title_en: THE FIGHTING COCKS AND THE EAGLE
source_paragraphs: Once there were two Cocks living in the same farmyard who could not bear the sight of each other. At last one day they flew up to fight it out, beak and claw. They fought until one of them was beaten and crawled off to a corner to hide.

The Cock that had won the battle flew to the top of the hen-house, and, proudly flapping his wings, crowed with all his might to tell the world about his victory. But an Eagle, circling overhead, heard the boasting chanticleer and, swooping down, carried him off to his nest.
His rival saw the deed, and coming out of his corner, took his place as master of the farmyard.
_Pride goes before a fall._
translated_paragraphs: 从前有两只公鸡住在同一个农家院里，彼此见面就不顺眼。终于有一天，它们飞扑上去，要用喙和爪分个胜负。它们一直斗到其中一只彻底落败，爬进角落里躲藏起来。
赢的那只公鸡飞上鸡舍屋顶，得意地拍动翅膀，扯足嗓门打鸣，让全世界知道自己赢了。偏偏一只鹰在头顶盘旋，听见这位神气的报晓郎自我夸耀，俯冲下来，把它带回了鹰巢。
它的对手亲眼目睹了这一幕，便从角落里出来，接替它做了农家院的主人。
人一得意忘形，跟头也就不远了。
